會試錄序

嘉靖庚戌春二月，天下士會試于禮部者幾四千五百人。尚書臣階、侍郎臣崇慶以試事請，上命臣治、臣德爲考試官。其同考試，則侍講臣一鳳，修撰臣炌用、臣維楨、臣鳴雷、臣春芳，編修臣臺、臣煦、臣陛、臣情，檢討臣紹儒、臣起，都給事中臣學易，左給事中臣廷𫛛，右給事中臣光裕，郎中臣煥、臣夢陽，員外郎臣家相。其監試，則御史臣如桂、臣嶠，暨百執事咸……
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

In the second month of spring in the gengxu year of Jiajing [1550], nearly 4,500 scholars from throughout the realm assembled to take the examination at the Ministry of Rites. Minister Jie and Vice Minister Chongqing, servants of the throne, submitted a request concerning the examination. His Majesty appointed his servants Zhi and De as Examiners. The Associate Examiners were Expositor Yifeng; Senior Compilers Kaiyong [?], Weizhen, Minglei, and Chunfang; Junior Compilers Tai, Xu, Bi, and Qing; Examining Editors Shaoru and Qi; Chief Supervising Secretary Xueyi; Left Supervising Secretary Ting𫛛 [given name uncertain]; Right Supervising Secretary Guangyu; Bureau Directors Huan and Mengyang; and Vice Director Jiaxiang—all servants of the throne. title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
備既如例三試之乃窮日夜
之力慎校擇焉遵
宸斷取三百二十人爰錄其名氏
及文之可式者二十篇以
獻臣治謹序之曰夫錄所以錄
士也然錄與士恒相焉重焉
窮居布衣之士業鉛槧遊鄉
===
邑必更十餘歲而後得錄於
鄉之有司又必更十餘歲而
後得錄於禮部有終身不與
者焉故士得與是錄者有餘
榮矣是士以錄而重也士錄
矣其終身所建立果足以濟
天下澤生民流聲光無窮焉

translation_en:
…were all in place. After the candidates had undergone the customary three examination sessions, the examiners exerted themselves day and night, carefully evaluating and selecting their work. In accordance with the imperial decision, 320 men were selected. Their names, together with twenty compositions worthy of serving as models, were then compiled for presentation to the throne. Your servant Zhi respectfully provides this preface:
A record serves to record the selected scholars. Yet the record and the scholars continually confer distinction upon one another [?]. A scholar of commoner status, living in obscurity, devotes himself to writing and pursues his studies in his home district. More than ten years must pass before he gains selection by the responsible provincial authorities, and another ten or more before he gains selection by the Ministry of Rites. Some go their whole lives without being selected. Thus, for a scholar to be included in this record is an ample honor. This is how scholars gain distinction through the record. Once scholars have been recorded, if what they accomplish throughout their lives truly suffices to benefit all under Heaven, bestow blessings upon the people, and perpetuate their illustrious reputations without end, …

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
後之人將敬而指之曰是錄
所得士也則錄其有餘榮矣
是錄以士而重也故曰錄與
士恒相爲重也夫國之錄士
何爲也欲其爲世用也士學
古之學而求錄於上之人亦
欲以其學用於世也然道有
===
升降世有古今君子惟隨其
所值而致行之要以濟天下
澤生民爲務然後爲有用之
學學之而弗可用用之而弗
宜於時則亦何取於錄哉我
高皇帝有天下也即位之三年庚
戌始開科錄天下士一時翊

澤生民爲務然後爲有用之

高皇帝有天下也即位之三年庚

punctuated:
後之人將敬而指之曰：「是錄所得士也。」則錄其有餘榮矣，是錄以士而重也。故曰：「錄與士恒相爲重也。」夫國之錄士何爲也？欲其爲世用也。士學古之學而求錄於上之人，亦欲以其學用於世也。然道有升降，世有古今，君子惟隨其所值而致行之，要以濟天下、澤生民爲務，然後爲有用之學。學之而弗可用，用之而弗宜於時，則亦何取於錄哉？
我高皇帝有天下也，即位之三年庚戌，始開科錄天下士，一時翊
translation_en:
…later generations will point to them with respect and say, “These are the scholars selected in this record.” Then the record will possess abundant glory: this is how a record gains weight through its scholars. Thus it is said, “The record and its scholars continually lend weight to one another.” Why does the state select scholars? It wishes them to serve the world. Scholars who pursue the learning of antiquity and seek selection by those above them likewise wish to put their learning to use in the world. Yet the Way rises and declines, and times differ between antiquity and the present. The gentleman must put it into practice according to the circumstances he encounters, making it his essential task to bring aid to all under Heaven and blessings to the people. Only then is his learning useful. If what he studies cannot be put to use, or if its application does not suit the times, what value is there in being selected?
When our Emperor Gao came to rule all under Heaven, in the third year of his reign, the gengxu year [1370], he first instituted the examinations to select scholars from throughout the realm. At that time, those who assisted …

text:

大業以傳之萬世上下咸有
大烈也
聖聖相承益謹于取士之度今
聖天子纘承大緒廓道德之塗拓
仁義之統遠撫長駕所以勤
萬民而章

translation_en:
…the ministers who supported him united their resolve and joined their strength, together establishing the great enterprise to transmit it to countless generations. Sovereign and subjects alike accomplished great deeds.
As sage sovereign succeeded sage sovereign, they exercised ever greater care in the standards for selecting scholars. Now the sagely Son of Heaven has inherited the great imperial undertaking, widened the path of the Way and virtue, and extended the tradition of benevolence and righteousness. His soothing influence reaches far, and his rule extends afar. In caring diligently for the myriad people and bringing glory to the great enterprise, he makes securing the benevolent and worthy his sole concern. Such was the intent of Yao and Shun. In these twenty-nine years, scholars have been selected ten times. His abundant grace has been widely bestowed, growing ever deeper with time. His supreme virtue shines manifestly, surpassing that of former ages. Scholars from distant regions ten thousand li away advance shoulder to shoulder and heel to heel. All who possess even a modest measure of talent or skill are available for official service: these are the means of securing an age of great peace. Yet when a single minister fails in his duties, his achievements bring no benefit to the common people, and there is concern…

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
澤不流群生寡遂政之在天
下若風草有所積有所虛視
祖宗之舊或少異焉此豈法之不
足哉士不素厲而弊所由滋
也說古道者則泥而不達於
時喜更張者又以其私智闘
乎天下而擾之不復典常之
===
師則其漸而至於敝也亦宜
是故明主不恃其有久安長
治之法而常恃于有保邦制
治之臣士者不患其無可為
之時而常患其無明體適用
之學書曰學古入官議事以
制政乃不迷其爾典常作之

澤不流，群生寡遂，政之在天下若風草，有所積，有所虛，視祖宗之舊或少異焉。此豈法之不足哉？士不素厲，而弊所由滋也。說古道者則泥而不達於時，喜更張者又以其私智闘乎天下而擾之，不復典常之師，則其漸而至於敝也亦宜。
是故明主不恃其有久安長治之法，而常恃于有保邦制治之臣；士者不患其無可為之時，而常患其無明體適用之學。《書》曰：「學古入官，議事以制，政乃不迷。其爾典常作之
translation_en:
…beneficence does not spread, and few among the multitude find fulfillment. Government’s influence throughout the realm is like wind upon grass: in some places it accumulates, while in others it is lacking. Compared with the old ways of the imperial ancestors, there are perhaps some slight differences. Could this be because the laws are inadequate? Rather, scholars have not disciplined themselves beforehand, and abuses consequently multiply. Those who expound the ancient Way cling rigidly to it and fail to understand present circumstances; those who delight in change pit their private cleverness against the world and throw it into disorder. When established norms are no longer taken as a guide, gradual deterioration is only to be expected.
Thus an enlightened ruler relies not on possessing laws that ensure enduring peace and lasting order, but always on having ministers who can safeguard the state and establish good government. Scholars should worry not that they lack an occasion to act, but that they lack the learning that clarifies fundamental principles and applies them appropriately. translation_en: …as your guide; do not let glib speech bring disorder to your office.” This speaks of understanding fundamental principles and applying them appropriately. Nothing is more essential than this to preserving the realm and governing it well. At the examination in the dingwei year (1547), your servant was graciously entrusted by imperial command with the responsibility of examining scholars. I greatly feared that I could not adequately discharge that duty. Now that I have again come to this responsibility, my fear is all the greater. I intend to exert myself respectfully, without negligence, hoping to find scholars who understand fundamental principles and can apply them appropriately. At the sage Son of Heaven’s direction, they may be employed to preserve together the achievement of great peace and bring about lasting order and security without limit. title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
創之始人周歷於艱險志勤
慮審故才皆可用而求之也
易治平之世人襲於所見之
安誦古人之言而不明乎當
世之務守成要之迹而不審
於治亂之原故才用鮮效而
求之也難夫以日敝之法而
===
重之鮮效之才其何以與語
保邦制治之理哉此臣所爲
竊憂而懼滋甚也夫法不足
於治者才不備也才不足於
用者學不備也爾多士學古
之學以售諸用則既錄於上
之人矣其必舉所學而善用

保邦制治之理哉此臣所爲
竊憂而懼滋甚也夫法不足
於治者才不備也才不足於

punctuated:
創之始，人周歷於艱險，志勤慮審，故才皆可用，而求之也易。治平之世，人襲於所見之安，誦古人之言而不明乎當世之務，守成要之迹而不審於治亂之原，故才用鮮效，而求之也難。夫以日敝之法，而重之鮮效之才，其何以與語保邦制治之理哉？此臣所爲竊憂而懼滋甚也。
夫法不足於治者，才不備也；才不足於用者，學不備也。爾多士學古之學，以售諸用，則既錄於上之人矣。其必舉所學而善用
translation_en:
…at the beginning of a founding, people have experienced hardships and dangers on every side; their resolve is diligent and their deliberations careful. Thus their talents can all be put to use, and finding such men is easy. In an age of peace and good government, people grow accustomed to the security they see around them. They recite the words of the ancients without understanding the affairs of their own age, and follow the outward forms of the essentials of preserving established rule [?] without examining the sources of order and disorder. Thus their talents produce little practical effect, and finding suitable men is difficult. With institutions deteriorating daily, compounded by talents that accomplish little, how can one discuss with such men the principles of safeguarding the state and establishing good government? This is why your servant privately worries and grows ever more fearful.
When institutions are inadequate for governing, it is because talent is insufficient; when talent is inadequate for practical service, it is because learning is insufficient. You assembled scholars have pursued the learning of antiquity in order to put it to practical use, and have now been selected by those above you. Surely you must bring all that you have learned to bear and use it well…

是重爲錄羞也吁可畏哉爾
多士勉之
資善大夫禮部尚書兼文淵
閣大學士張治謹序
punctuated:
之，務以濟天下，澤生民，上贊聖天子太平之業，而流聲光無窮焉，則錄其不有餘榮哉？乃若逐逐然與時汨沒，無所裨於世用，徒以羨榮名於錄也，雖錄之，天下後世有弗錄者矣，是重爲錄羞也。吁，可畏哉！爾多士勉之。
資善大夫、禮部尚書兼文淵閣大學士張治謹序。
translation_en:
…it, striving thereby to aid all under Heaven, bestow benefits upon the people, and support the sagely Son of Heaven’s undertaking of Great Peace, so that your renown and glory may endure without end. Would this record not then possess abundant honor? But if you merely bustle about, submerged in the currents of the times, contributing nothing to practical affairs and coveting only the glorious name conferred by inclusion in this record, then, though it records you, people throughout the realm and in later ages may refuse you recognition. This would heap shame upon the record. Alas, how fearful! You assembled scholars, exert yourselves!
Preface respectfully composed by Zhang Zhi, Grand Master for Fostering Goodness, Minister of Rites and concurrently Grand Secretary of the Wenyuan Hall.

translation_en:
Metropolitan Examination of the Twenty-ninth Year of Jiajing (1550)

Examination Administrators

Xu Jie, Grand Master for Aiding Goodness, Minister of Rites and concurrently Academician of the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Zisheng; he was from Huating County, Zhili, and was a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) of the guiwei year.

Wang Chongqing, Grand Master for Excellent Counsel and Left Vice Minister of Rites. His courtesy name was Dezheng; he was from Kai Subprefecture, Zhili, and was a metropolitan graduate of the wuchen year.

Examiners

Zhang Zhi, Grand Master for Aiding Goodness, Minister of Rites and concurrently Grand Secretary of the Wenyuan Pavilion. His courtesy name was Wenbang; he was from Chaling Subprefecture, Huguang, and was a metropolitan graduate of the xinsi year.

Ouyang De, Grand Master for Excellent Counsel, in charge of the Household Administration of the Heir Apparent, Left Vice Minister of Personnel and concurrently Academician of the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Chongyi; he was from Taihe County, Jiangxi, and was a metropolitan graduate of the guiwei year.

Associate Examiners

Xing Yifeng, Hanlin Academy Expositor. His courtesy name was Boyu; he was registered in the Longjiang Left Guard in Nanjing, was a native of Xiangfu County, Henan, and was a metropolitan graduate of the xinchou year.

Huang Tingyong, Hanlin Academy Senior Compiler, with the prestige title Gentleman for Scholarly Excellence. His courtesy name was Ruxing; he was from Putian County, Fujian, and was a metropolitan graduate of the yiwei year.

Wang Weizhen, Hanlin Academy Senior Compiler. His courtesy name was Yunning; he was from Hua Subprefecture, Shaanxi, and was a metropolitan graduate of the yiwei year.

Qin Minglei, Hanlin Academy Senior Compiler, with the prestige title Gentleman for Undertakings. His courtesy name was Ziyu; he was from Linhai County, Zhejiang, and was a metropolitan graduate of the jiachen year.

Li Chunfang, Hanlin Academy Senior Compiler, with the prestige title Gentleman for Undertakings. His courtesy name was Zishi; he was from Xinghua County, Zhili, and was a metropolitan graduate of the dingwei year.

Yin Tai, Hanlin Academy Junior Compiler, with the prestige title Gentleman for Literary Excellence. His courtesy name was Chongji; he was from Yongxin County, Jiangxi, and was a metropolitan graduate of the yiwei year.

Min Xu, Hanlin Academy Junior Compiler, with the prestige title Gentleman for Literary Excellence. His courtesy name was Heqing; he was registered in Renqiu County, Zhili, was a native of Shanghai County, and was a metropolitan graduate of the yiwei year.

Chen Sheng, Hanlin Academy Junior Compiler, with the prestige title Gentleman for Literary Excellence. His courtesy name was Jinfu; he was from Yuyao County, Zhejiang, and was a metropolitan graduate of the xinchou year.

Wu Qing, Hanlin Academy Junior Compiler, with the prestige title Gentleman for Rendering Service. His courtesy name was Yizhong; he was from Wuxi County, Zhili, and was a metropolitan graduate of the jiachen year.

Liang Shaoru, Hanlin Academy Examining Editor, with the prestige title Gentleman for Meritorious Service. His courtesy name was Cunye; he was from Dongping Subprefecture, Shandong, and was a metropolitan graduate of the xinchou year.

translation_en:
Mao Qi, Examining Editor in the Hanlin Academy, had the courtesy name Qianbin and was from Jiajiang County, Sichuan. He became a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) in 1547.
Liu Xueyi, Chief Supervising Secretary of the Office of Scrutiny for Personnel, had the courtesy name Daofu and was from Shouguang County, Shandong. He became a metropolitan graduate in 1538.
Zheng Tinghu, Left Supervising Secretary of the Office of Scrutiny for Works, had the courtesy name Yuanshi. He was registered in Hai Guard [?], Guangdong, and was a native of Deqing County, Zhejiang. He became a metropolitan graduate in 1538.
He Guangyu, Gentleman for Rendering Service and Right Supervising Secretary of the Office of Scrutiny for Personnel, had the courtesy name Siwen and was from Zitong County, Sichuan. He became a metropolitan graduate in 1541.
Zhang Huan, Gentleman for Fostering Virtue and a Secretary acting as Director of the Bureau of Honors in the Ministry of Personnel, had the courtesy name Maoshi. He was registered in Changzhou County in the directly administered territory and was a native of Wu County. He became a metropolitan graduate in 1538.
Lu Mengyang, Grand Master for Consultative Advice and Director of the Shaanxi Bureau in the Ministry of Justice, had the courtesy name Shaoming and was from Nanhai County, Guangdong. He became a metropolitan graduate in 1538.
Zhu Jiaxiang, Grand Master for Rectitude and Vice Director of the Bureau of Imperial Transport in the Ministry of War, had the courtesy name Bolin. He was registered in Shangqiu County, Henan, and was a native of Taicang Subprefecture in the directly administered territory. He became a metropolitan graduate in 1538.

Examination Invigilators:
Huang Rugui, Gentleman of Scholarly Excellence and Investigating Censor for the Shandong Circuit, had the courtesy name Dexin and was from Luling County, Jiangxi. He became a metropolitan graduate in 1538.
Gu Jiao, Gentleman of Scholarly Excellence and Investigating Censor for the Shaanxi Circuit, had the courtesy name Weisheng. He was registered in Xingzhou Front Garrison Guard in the directly administered territory and was a native of Xi County, Henan. He became a metropolitan graduate in 1538.

Proctors:
You Ying, Gentleman for Rectitude and Secretary in the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites, had the courtesy name Rubai and was from Wuxi County in the directly administered territory. He became a metropolitan graduate in 1544.
Liu Sijie, Gentleman for Rectitude and Secretary in the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites, had the courtesy name Yuanjing and was from Yi Subprefecture in the directly administered territory. He became a metropolitan graduate in 1547.

Officials Responsible for Printing Examination Papers:
Zhang Zitao, Grand Master for Consultative Advice and Director of the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites, had the courtesy name Zhongyu and was from Yin County, Zhejiang. He became a metropolitan graduate in 1541.
Wang Weizhong, Gentleman for Fostering Virtue and a Secretary acting as Vice Director of the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites, had the courtesy name Daoyuan and was from Jinjiang County, Fujian. He became a metropolitan graduate in 1541.

Wang Shangzhou, Gentleman for Undertakings, performed the duties of a Central Secretariat Drafter and served as Right Assistant Judge of the Right Court in the Court of Judicial Review [the title repeats “Right Court” in the transcription; ?]. text:
第壹場
四書
子貢問君子子曰先行其言而後從之
洋洋乎發育萬物峻極于天
既竭心思焉繼之以不忍人之政而仁覆
天下矣
易
上九自天祐之吉无不利象曰大有上吉
自天祐也
===
聖人久於其道而天下化成
非天下之至精其孰能與於此
天地之道貞觀者也日月之道貞明者也
天下之動貞夫一者也

惟帝臣惟帝時舉敷納以言明庶以功
車服以庸誰敢不讓敢不敬應
惟說式克欽承旁招俊乂列于庶位

punctuated:
第壹場

四書

子貢問君子。子曰：「先行其言，而後從之。」

洋洋乎！發育萬物，峻極于天。

既竭心思焉，繼之以不忍人之政，而仁覆天下矣。

易

上九，自天祐之，吉，无不利。象曰：「大有上吉，自天祐也。」

聖人久於其道，而天下化成。

非天下之至精，其孰能與於此？

天地之道，貞觀者也；日月之道，貞明者也；天下之動，貞夫一者也。

書

帝光天之下，至于海隅蒼生。萬邦黎獻，共惟帝臣。惟帝時舉，敷納以言，明庶以功，車服以庸。誰敢不讓，敢不敬應？

惟說式克欽承，旁招俊乂，列于庶位。
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

Zigong asked about the gentleman. The Master said: “He first puts his words into practice, and only afterward lets his words follow.”

How vast and abundant! It brings forth and nurtures the myriad things, and its lofty height reaches Heaven.

Having fully exerted his heart and thought, he follows this with government that cannot bear to see others suffer, and his benevolence then extends over all under Heaven.

Book of Changes (Yijing)

Top Nine: Heaven itself grants him aid. Good fortune; nothing is unfavorable. The Image commentary says: “The good fortune at the top of Great Possession comes from Heaven itself granting aid.”

The sage endures in his Way, and all under Heaven are transformed and brought to fulfillment.

Were it not the most subtle thing under Heaven, what could participate in this?

The Way of Heaven and Earth is displayed through constancy; the Way of the sun and moon shines through constancy; the movements of all under Heaven are made constant through unity.

Book of Documents (Shujing)

The emperor shed his light upon all beneath Heaven, reaching the people even at the seacoasts. The many worthy men of the myriad states were all the emperor’s servants. The emperor promoted them, receiving men widely on the basis of their words, testing them all by their achievements, and bestowing carriages and robes according to their service. Who dared not yield to others, or dared not respond respectfully?

Yue was thus able reverently to carry out the charge, seeking talented and capable men far and wide and placing them in the various offices.

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
凡厥庶民極之敷言是訓是行以近天子
之光曰天子作民父母以為天下王
其克詰爾戎兵以陟禹之迹方行天下至
于海表罔有不服以覲文王之耿光以
揚武王之大烈
詩
君曰卜爾萬壽無疆
織文鳥章白旆央央元戎十乘以先啟行
戎車既安如輊如軒四牡既佶既佶且
===
閑薄伐獫狁至于大原
卬盛于豆于豆于登其香始升上帝居歆
載穫濟濟有實其積萬億及秭為酒為醴
烝畀祖妣以洽百禮有飶其香邦家之
光有椒其馨胡考之寧
春秋
秋七月齊人降鄣莊公三十年
春王正月公會齊侯宋公陳侯衛侯鄭伯
許男曹伯侵蔡蔡潰遂伐楚次于陘

punctuated:
凡厥庶民，極之敷言，是訓是行，以近天子之光。曰：「天子作民父母，以為天下王。」
其克詰爾戎兵，以陟禹之迹，方行天下，至于海表，罔有不服，以覲文王之耿光，以揚武王之大烈。
詩
君曰：「卜爾萬壽無疆。」
織文鳥章，白旆央央。元戎十乘，以先啟行。
戎車既安，如輊如軒。四牡既佶，既佶且閑。薄伐獫狁，至于大原。
卬盛于豆，于豆于登，其香始升，上帝居歆。
載穫濟濟，有實其積，萬億及秭。為酒為醴，烝畀祖妣，以洽百禮。有飶其香，邦家之光。有椒其馨，胡考之寧。
春秋
秋七月，齊人降鄣。莊公三十年。
春王正月，公會齊侯、宋公、陳侯、衛侯、鄭伯、許男、曹伯侵蔡，蔡潰。遂伐楚，次于陘。
translation_en:
All the common people should follow the instruction of the proclaimed words of the supreme standard and act upon them, thereby drawing near to the Son of Heaven’s radiance. They will say: “The Son of Heaven acts as father and mother to the people and thus becomes king of all under Heaven.”
You must put your troops and weapons in good order, advance over the lands traversed by Yu, and march throughout the realm, reaching beyond the seas, with none failing to submit, thereby displaying King Wen’s brilliant radiance and exalting King Wu’s great achievements.

Book of Odes
The lord says: “I grant you boundless longevity.”
Woven patterns and bird emblems adorn the banners; white streamers flutter grandly. Ten great war chariots lead the way, opening the road.
The war chariots are steady, whether dipping forward or rising up. The four stallions are sturdy, both sturdy and well trained. We attack the Xianyun, reaching as far as Taiyuan.
We fill the wooden offering dishes and the earthenware vessels. Their fragrance begins to rise, and the Lord on High rests there, enjoying the offerings.
They reap in great numbers; full indeed are their heaps of grain, reckoned in myriads, hundreds of millions, and trillions. They make wine and sweet liquor, presenting them to their ancestral fathers and mothers, completing all the rites. Rich is their fragrance, bringing glory to the state and ruling house. Pungent is their aroma, bringing the peace of a long life.

Spring and Autumn Annals
In autumn, in the seventh month, the men of Qi compelled Zhang to surrender. The thirtieth year of Duke Zhuang.
In spring, in the first month of the royal calendar, the duke met with the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Chen, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Zheng, the Baron of Xu, and the Earl of Cao to invade Cai. Cai collapsed. They then attacked Chu and encamped at Xing. …

translation_en:
…Qu Wan of Chu came to conclude a covenant at the army’s encampment. Fourth year of Duke Xi. The duke joined the Marquis of Jin, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Cao, Guang, heir apparent of Qi, the Viscount of Ju, the Viscount of Zhu, the Viscount of Teng, the Earl of Xue, the Earl of Qi, and the Viscount of Xiaozhu in attacking Zheng; they met at Xiaoyu. The men of Chu seized Liang Xiao, the envoy of Zheng. Eleventh year of Duke Xiang.
The Viscount of Chu and the Marquis of Cai encamped at Juehe. Tenth year of Duke Wen. In spring, the Viscount of Chu attacked Jun. Eleventh year of Duke Wen.
In spring, the duke went to Qi. The duke returned from Qi. Tenth year of Duke Xuan.
Book of Rites
The ruler’s chariot has a lambskin cover with tiger-skin edging. A grand master’s purification chariot has a deerskin cover with leopard-skin edging; his court chariot and a serviceman’s purification chariot likewise have deerskin covers with leopard-skin edging.
When a sage faces south to govern all under Heaven, he must begin with the way of human relations.
In antiquity, Heaven and Earth were in harmony and the four seasons duly ordered; the people possessed virtue, and the five grains flourished.
This is the vital energy of the abundant virtue of Heaven and Earth; this is the benevolent vital energy of Heaven and Earth.
Second Session
Discourse
The mind of the sage is inexhaustible.
Imperial edicts, proclamations, and memorials: one topic from 〔among〕 these categories.

text:

勳後乃因一二委信失稱慨然有感遂

===

之義有相發明否與諸士抱器業以求
施用其必熟於人臣事君之道矧誦繹

事得失推於理亂相成之效反覆究之

translation_en:
…Emperor Taizu Gao, when founding the dynasty, first employed outstanding men from every quarter to accomplish his great achievements. Later, because one or two men whom he had trusted failed to meet his expectations, he was deeply moved and commanded his Confucian officials to select accounts from the histories of the Han and subsequent dynasties and arrange them by category as the Biographies of Worthy and Treacherous Ministers (Xianjian zhuan), to provide clear instruction at court and throughout the realm. Emperor Xuanzong Zhang, reflecting anew on the principle that enlightened rulers and worthy ministers of antiquity admonished one another, compiled accounts of the good and evil deeds of ministers over the two thousand years from the Spring and Autumn period to the Yuan into the Mirror for Ministers (Chen jian), and bestowed it upon his officials. The essential purport of these two books is fully set out in their imperially composed prefaces. Can you explain their meaning in full? In discussing the different kinds of ministers, no one, ancient or modern, has surpassed the account given by Mencius. Yet later generations also developed accounts of “weighty ministers” and “power-wielding ministers.” Do their descriptions shed further light on the meaning of these two books? You candidates possess abilities and learning that you seek to put into service, and must surely be well versed in the way a minister should serve his ruler. Moreover, having long recited and pondered the imperial teachings, might you have distinctive insights into their deeper meaning? Please comprehensively enumerate the successes and failures of ministers’ service through the ages, extend your inquiry to the effects of the mutual interaction of rulers and ministers in producing order or disorder, and examine these matters thoroughly from every side. Those administering this examination indeed wish to see where your aspirations lie.
Question: Human nature is the foundation of virtuous conduct. Only after understanding human nature can one avoid error in learning, and only after understanding learning can one perfect one’s virtue. Thus the true character of human nature must indeed be clearly distinguished. Yet in the time of Confucius and before, discussions of human nature were very brief, while among the scholars there were many…

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
才賢民亦渾樸孟子而下言性善者寖
詳寖明盖皆左右孟氏之說昭然而行
之矣然人才民俗寖不逮古豈性說之
明固無損益於世道之隆污邪然則惡
在其能有功於聖門也其他紛紛駕說
者各有所見其用歸之從善背惡於民
行良非小補乃不得與孟子同功顧辭
而闢之無乃執其說之異而未既其用
之同邪諸子之學所習各異然摩頂放
===
踵以利天下者豈無見於性之善而能
然乎乃無救於其習之偏者何也夫言
必稽諸致用而後可以審其是實用不
究而槩之空言則雖性善之說折諸所
謂不論氣者得無有所未備而何以異
於紛紛者歟故願與諸士深究其實也
問周官司馬戎政所為重也丘甸制賦乘
馬所出長師牧正董其事四時必祭得
牧職者賜姓賜邑其重可知已漢初自

才賢，民亦渾樸。孟子而下，言性善者寖詳寖明，盖皆左右孟氏之說，昭然而行之矣。然人才民俗寖不逮古，豈性說之明固無損益於世道之隆污邪？然則惡在其能有功於聖門也？其他紛紛駕說者，各有所見，其用歸之從善背惡，於民行良非小補，乃不得與孟子同功，顧辭而闢之，無乃執其說之異而未既其用之同邪？諸子之學，所習各異，然摩頂放踵以利天下者，豈無見於性之善而能然乎？乃無救於其習之偏者，何也？夫言必稽諸致用，而後可以審其是。實用不究而槩之空言，則雖性善之說，折諸所謂不論氣者，得無有所未備，而何以異於紛紛者歟？故願與諸士深究其實也。
問：周官司馬，戎政所為重也。丘甸制賦，乘馬所出；長師牧正，董其事；四時必祭；得牧職者，賜姓賜邑。其重可知已。漢初自
translation_en:
…talented and worthy, and the common people, too, were simple and unaffected. From Mengzi onward, accounts of the goodness of human nature became increasingly detailed and clear. They all supported Mengzi’s teaching and openly put it into practice. Yet men of talent and popular customs fell increasingly short of antiquity. Could it be that clarity in the teaching about human nature has no effect upon the flourishing or decline of the moral order? If so, wherein lies its contribution to the tradition of the sages? The many others who propound doctrines each have their own insights. In practice, their teachings lead people to follow good and turn away from evil, making no small contribution to popular conduct. Yet they are denied the same credit as Mengzi; instead, their teachings are rejected and refuted. Is this not to insist upon differences in their doctrines without fully examining the similarities in their practical effects? The various masters differed in what they studied and practiced. Yet could those who would wear themselves away from crown to heel for the benefit of all under Heaven have done so without some insight into the goodness of human nature? Why, then, did this fail to remedy the partiality of their learning?
Doctrines must be tested against their practical application before their correctness can be judged. If actual practice is not examined, and judgment rests merely on empty words, then even the doctrine of the goodness of human nature, when adjudicated in terms of what is called ‘not discussing qi’ [?], may be incomplete. How, then, would it differ from those competing doctrines? I therefore wish to investigate its substance deeply with you gentlemen.

Chiefs, masters, overseers, and directors supervised these affairs [?]. Sacrifices were invariably offered in all four seasons, and those who secured the office of managing the herds were granted surnames and fiefs. The importance attached to this can thus be understood. At the beginning of the Han, from …

text:
天子不能具純駟至孝武富庶始修馬
復令貞觀至麟德長興距清泰馬數蕃
耗而國之殷替因之我
聖祖首命劉惟謙申明馬政嚴督所司有不如
令者罪之夫法久則弊弊而後通今馬
政之不修也久矣欲捄偏補弊使飼牧
蕃孳足以裕國備兵必有通變宜常根
極畫一之方願相與言之
問聖帝明王必登崇儒雋以恢弘化理其
===
來遠矣然三代以上有儒之實而未聞
有儒之名何邪至漢唐宋始別為傳述
有儒林傳儒學道學傳其所紀載可得聞其
詳歟果皆名實俱茂無愧於儒歟抑猶
有遺論歟漢書不列董仲舒唐之韓愈
宋之周程張朱皆不列於儒亦何見歟
一時諸儒亦未聞有救時之實用豈儒
者顧不適于用歟抑未得為真儒歟不
然何皆不能致其治于三代之隆也茲

然何皆不能致其治于三代之隆也茲
punctuated:
天子不能具純駟，至孝武富庶，始修馬復令。貞觀至麟德，長興距清泰，馬數蕃耗，而國之殷替因之。我聖祖首命劉惟謙申明馬政，嚴督所司，有不如令者罪之。夫法久則弊，弊而後通。今馬政之不修也久矣，欲捄偏補弊，使飼牧蕃孳足以裕國備兵，必有通變宜常、根極畫一之方，願相與言之。
問：聖帝明王必登崇儒雋，以恢弘化理，其來遠矣。然三代以上，有儒之實，而未聞有儒之名，何邪？至漢唐宋，始別為傳述，有《儒林傳》《儒學》《道學傳》，其所紀載，可得聞其詳歟？果皆名實俱茂，無愧於儒歟？抑猶有遺論歟？《漢書》不列董仲舒，唐之韓愈、宋之周程張朱皆不列於儒，亦何見歟？一時諸儒亦未聞有救時之實用，豈儒者顧不適于用歟？抑未得為真儒歟？不然，何皆不能致其治于三代之隆也？茲
translation_en:
…even the Son of Heaven could not assemble a team of four horses of matching color. Only when wealth and population flourished under Emperor Xiaowu were the ordinances granting exemptions for keeping horses reinstated. From the Zhenguan to the Linde era, and from the Changxing to the Qingtai era, horse numbers increased or dwindled, and the state's prosperity or decline followed accordingly. Our Sagely Founder first ordered Liu Weiqian to clarify and reaffirm horse administration and strictly supervise the responsible offices, punishing those who failed to comply with the ordinances. Now, when laws have long been in force, abuses arise; once abuses arise, adjustments must follow. Horse administration has long been neglected. If we wish to correct its imbalances and remedy its abuses, so that feeding, pasturing, and breeding horses suffice to enrich the state and prepare its forces, there must be a comprehensive and uniform method, grounded in fundamentals, that accommodates change while remaining appropriate for lasting use. I invite you to discuss it together.
Question: Sagely emperors and enlightened kings have always promoted and honored outstanding Confucian scholars to extend moral transformation and good government; this practice has a long history. Yet in the Three Dynasties and earlier, there was the substance of Confucian learning, while we hear nothing of the name. Why is this? Only under the Han, Tang, and Song were separate biographical accounts compiled, including Biographies of Confucian Scholars, Confucian Learning, and Learning of the Way. May we hear in detail what these accounts record? Did all those included truly excel in both reputation and substance, worthily bearing the name of Confucian scholar? Or are there still judgments left unexpressed? The History of the Han does not include Dong Zhongshu among the Confucian scholars; nor are Han Yu of the Tang or Zhou, Cheng, Zhang, and Zhu of the Song included among them. What view underlies these decisions? Nor have we heard that the Confucian scholars of their respective times achieved practical results in rescuing their age. Could Confucian scholars actually be unsuited to practical service? Or had they not attained the status of true Confucians? Otherwise, why were they all unable to bring the government of their times to the flourishing heights of the Three Dynasties? Now…

text:

必何修而後可爾諸子居則為儒生出
則為儒臣必有槩于中也其究言之毋
畧
問我
國家建都北平以宣大薊州為肩背以遼東
為左臂謂其外與虜接而內距

者可為訓乎花當之子寇馬蘭谷也射

問：我國家建都北平，以宣大薊州為肩背，以遼東為左臂，謂其外與虜接，而內距京師不遠也。故先朝謀臣於此數鎮恒注筭焉。正德中，北虜突入宣大，寇白羊，南逼居庸，近矣。已而見我軍三面至，虜輒遁去，卒無所得。于時兵何卒辦，將何卒良？至今人有傳其事者，可為訓乎？花當之子寇馬蘭谷也，射傷裨將，桀矣。本兵請使責問，求執其子償其罪，以明朝廷之威。自是朵顏諸部畏威奉貢，何謀以制之也？成化末，海西建州諸夷數犯遼東，守臣議主撫，本兵議主勦，卒用本兵
translation_en:
…If we wish men wearing scholars’ caps to be worthy of the name of true Confucians, and their conduct to contribute to good government, what must they cultivate before this can be achieved? You gentlemen are Confucian students in private life and Confucian ministers upon entering office. You must surely have considered these matters deeply. Discuss them thoroughly, omitting nothing.

Question: Our dynasty established its capital at Beiping, taking Xuanfu, Datong, and Jizhou as its shoulders and back, and Liaodong as its left arm, because these regions border the northern foes on the outside and are not far from the capital on the inside. Thus the strategists of former reigns constantly devoted their planning to these several garrisons. During the Zhengde reign, the northern foes suddenly penetrated Xuanfu and Datong, raided Baiyang, and pressed south toward Juyong: they were close indeed. Shortly afterward, seeing our troops approaching from three directions, they fled, ultimately gaining nothing. How were troops made ready so quickly at that time, and how were such capable commanders found so suddenly? People still recount these events today. Can they serve as a lesson?

When Huadang’s son raided Malan Valley, he wounded an assistant commander with an arrow—a brazen act indeed. The Minister of War requested that an envoy be sent to call him to account and demand that his son be seized to answer for his crime, thereby demonstrating the imperial court’s authority. Thereafter, the various Doyan tribes feared that authority and presented tribute. By what strategy were they brought under control?

At the end of the Chenghua reign, the various non-Chinese peoples of Haixi and Jianzhou repeatedly invaded Liaodong. The officials defending the region advocated pacification, while the Minister of War advocated punitive military action. In the end, the court adopted the Minister of War’s…

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
議興師伐之遼東以寧由是言之則主
撫者非矣乃復有言勦之非者何哉今
朶顏諸部海西諸夷往往竊發為二境
患北虜益驚悍莫禦故就爾諸士訊所
聞而知者以裨邊計苟有自獻而足效
者即不襲故計可也

患北虜益驁悍莫禦禦故就爾諸士訊所

者即不襲故計可也
punctuated: 議，興師伐之，遼東以寧。由是言之，則主撫者非矣，乃復有言勦之非者，何哉？今朶顏諸部、海西諸夷往往竊發，為二境患；北虜益驚悍莫禦。故就爾諸士訊所聞而知者，以裨邊計。苟有自獻而足效者，即不襲故計可也。
translation_en: …the proposal was adopted, troops were raised to attack them, and Liaodong was thereby pacified. Judging from this, those who advocated pacification were wrong. Yet there are also those who say that the punitive campaign was wrong. Why is this? Now the various Duoyan tribes and the various peoples of Haixi frequently launch raids, afflicting both frontier regions; the northern barbarians grow ever fiercer and cannot be held in check. We therefore ask you gentlemen about what you have heard and know, to aid planning for the frontiers. If you have proposals of your own to offer that could prove effective, they need not follow past plans.

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
第壹塲
四書
子貢問君子子曰先行其言而後從之
傅夏器
同考試官署郎中章批親切有味非徒言者
同考試官左給事中鄭批是實能力行者
同考試官檢討梁批得夫子告子貢意
同考試官編修尹批是知尚實者
考試官學士歐陽批親切可錄
===
考試官大學士張批詞有警省處
賢者問君子聖人教以成德之實焉盖德之所
成則力行以為實也先其行而後其言其斯為
君子之學乎子貢之意若曰學者所以學為君
子也然君子之道非可以易能而學者之功必
知所用カ而後可幾及也賜嘗有志於是而未
之逮焉夫子其何以教之乎聖人告之以謂德
之不成不可語君子之學而成德之要則在乎
言行之間盖天下之事不貴于言而貴于行故

賢者問君子，聖人教以成德之實焉。盖德之所成，則力行以為實也。先其行而後其言，其斯為君子之學乎？子貢之意若曰：「學者所以學為君子也。然君子之道，非可以易能，而學者之功，必知所用カ而後可幾及也。賜嘗有志於是，而未之逮焉。夫子其何以教之乎？」聖人告之，以謂德之不成，不可語君子之學，而成德之要，則在乎言行之間。盖天下之事，不貴于言而貴于行，故

First Session

Four Books

Zigong asked about the gentleman. The Master said: “First put into practice what you would say, and afterward let your words follow it.”

Fu Xiaqi

Associate Examiner Zheng, Left Supervising Secretary, comments: “Here is someone truly capable of putting principles into practice.”
Associate Examiner Liang, Examining Editor, comments: “He grasps the intent of the Master's instruction to Zigong.”
Associate Examiner Yin, Compiler, comments: “Here is someone who knows to prize substance.”
Examiner Ouyang, Academician, comments: “Direct and apt; worthy of inclusion.”
Examiner Zhang, Grand Secretary, comments: “Some passages offer a salutary warning.”

A worthy man asked about the gentleman, and the sage instructed him in the substantive practice through which virtue is perfected. For virtue is perfected by taking earnest practice as its substance. To put action first and words afterward—is this not the learning of the gentleman?

Zigong's meaning was as though he said: “The purpose of learning is to learn to become a gentleman. Yet the way of the gentleman cannot easily be mastered, and those who study must know where to exert their effort [?] before they can hope to approach it. I, Ci, have long aspired to this but have not attained it. How might you, Master, instruct me?”

The sage instructed him, explaining that unless virtue is perfected, one cannot speak of the learning of the gentleman; and the key to perfecting virtue lies in the relationship between words and actions. For in the affairs of the world, what is prized is action rather than words. Therefore …

text:
君子之學必先其行而後其言何則行於未言
者其行果言於既行者其言信故必反求諸身
凡事物當然之理為性分所固有者皆俛焉以
盡其力動之幾微而驗之身心莫非天理之實

punctuated: 君子之學，必先其行而後其言。何則？行於未言者，其行果；言於既行者，其言信。故必反求諸身，凡事物當然之理，為性分所固有者，皆俛焉以盡其力。動之幾微而驗之身心，莫非天理之實，初無徇乎為人之私焉。實體諸己，凡人倫日用之常，為職分所當為者，皆踐之以致其誠。見之事為而措之功業，本以心得之餘，不徒事乎言語之末焉。可言也而未之能行，不敢以言也，懼其言之有餘而貽不逮之耻矣；可言也而不可以行，不苟以言也，懼其言之非義而有尚口之窮矣。蹈之而為道也，得之而為德也，然後從而言之，則言為有物，辭氣之出，固其至德之符乎！居之而為仁也，由之而為義也，夫惟不言則已，而言皆無擇，修辭立誠，固其居業之地乎！夫行之於未言之先，則行顧言矣；言之於既行之後，則言顧行矣。此德之所由以成，而君子之道也。賜也，尚可以他求哉？抑子貢之學病於多言，夫子蓋屢致意焉。何述之疑，一言終身之問，先後
translation_en:
…the learning of the gentleman must place action first and words afterward. Why? When one acts before speaking, one’s actions are resolute; when one speaks after acting, one’s words are trustworthy. Thus one must seek within oneself. All the principles of what is right in affairs and things, inherently possessed in one’s nature, must be pursued diligently with all one’s strength. In the subtlest beginnings of activity, tested in body and mind, everything embodies the reality of Heaven’s principle; there is from the outset no yielding to the selfish desire to impress others. One must personally embody these principles, sincerely putting into practice all the constant duties of human relationships and daily life that fall within one’s responsibilities. Their manifestation in deeds and application in achievements spring from the abundance of what one has grasped in the heart; one does not merely attend to the superficial business of words.

If something can be spoken of but one has not yet been able to carry it out, one dares not speak of it, fearing that one’s words will exceed one’s deeds and bring the shame of falling short. If something can be spoken of but cannot properly be put into practice, one does not speak carelessly, fearing that one’s words will violate righteousness and bring the distress that comes from prizing mere talk. What one treads is the Way; what one obtains within oneself is virtue. Only afterward does one speak of it, and then one’s words have substance. Surely the words and tone that emerge are signs of one’s consummate virtue! To dwell in it is benevolence; to follow it is righteousness. One may remain silent, but whenever one speaks, nothing in one’s words needs to be rejected. Refining one’s words and establishing sincerity are surely the foundation upon which one sustains one’s work! Acting before speaking makes one’s actions heed one’s words; speaking after acting makes one’s words heed one’s actions. This is how virtue is perfected, and this is the Way of the gentleman. Ci, can you still seek it elsewhere?

Moreover, Zigong’s learning suffered from excessive speech, and the Master repeatedly addressed this concern. His perplexity about what he would transmit, and his question about a single saying to be practiced throughout life—earlier and later…

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
言天載之神道也者流動不滯無有也而無乎
不有充滿無間無在也而無乎不在何如其洋
洋乎盖盈天地者萬物也親上親下咸適其品
類之宜成始成終各得其性命之理不相假借
不相妨害而生生化化於無窮者皆此道之發
見也其出也道之通也其入也道之復也天下
無處而無物亦無物而非道形下者之流布固
形上者之散殊乎盖道隱於無體而物則昭於

===
物觀道道何所不有哉覆萬物者惟天也周遍
廣闊而於穆昭不已之命往来屈伸而真元運
不息之機日月之代明四時之錯行其闔闢變
化之莫測者皆此道之呈露也其高也道之運

一物之不體至神之流行其至誠之充塞乎盖
道妙於無迹而天則顯於有象天之不能外乎
道則道其峻極于天矣觀道於天道其何有極
哉夫道著於上下如此此道之所以為大而不

punctuated:
言天載之神。道也者，流動不滯，無有也而無乎不有，充滿無間，無在也而無乎不在，何如其洋洋乎！盖盈天地者萬物也，親上親下，咸適其品類之宜；成始成終，各得其性命之理。不相假借，不相妨害，而生生化化於無窮者，皆此道之發見也。其出也，道之通也；其入也，道之復也。天下無處而無物，亦無物而非道。形下者之流布，固形上者之散殊乎！盖道隱於無體，而物則昭於有形。物之不能外乎道，則道其發育于物矣。以物觀道，道何所不有哉！
覆萬物者惟天也，周遍廣闊，而於穆昭不已之命；往来屈伸，而真元運不息之機。日月之代明，四時之錯行，其闔闢變化之莫測者，皆此道之呈露也。其高也，道之運也；其明也，道之顯也。天無一物之不覆，而道無一物之不體。至神之流行，其至誠之充塞乎！盖道妙於無迹，而天則顯於有象。天之不能外乎道，則道其峻極于天矣。觀道於天，道其何有極哉！夫道著於上下如此，此道之所以為大而不
translation_en:
…speak of the wondrous working of Heaven. The Way flows without obstruction. It has no determinate existence, yet there is nowhere it does not exist; it fills all without a gap. It has no fixed location, yet there is nowhere it is not present. How vast and abundant it is! The myriad things fill Heaven and Earth: those drawn upward and those drawn downward all find what suits their respective kinds; from their beginnings to their completion, each realizes the principle of its nature and allotted endowment. They neither borrow from nor impede one another, but endlessly generate and transform. All this is the manifestation of this Way. Their emergence is the Way’s outward passage; their withdrawal is the Way’s return. Under Heaven there is no place without things, and no thing that is not the Way. Surely the diffusion of what lies below form is the differentiated manifestation of what lies above form! The Way is hidden, having no bodily form, while things are manifest in visible shapes. Since things cannot stand outside the Way, it is the Way that brings them forth and nourishes them. Viewing the Way through things, where could it fail to exist?
Heaven alone overspreads the myriad things. All-encompassing and vast, it possesses a mandate profound and luminous, never ceasing; in its coming and going, contraction and expansion, its primal generative power operates without rest. The sun and moon shine in succession, and the four seasons proceed in alternation. Their unfathomable closing and opening, changes and transformations, are all disclosures of this Way. Heaven’s height is the operation of the Way; its brightness is the manifestation of the Way. There is no thing that Heaven does not overspread, and no thing that the Way does not embody. Surely the flow of the supremely numinous is the all-pervading fullness of utmost sincerity! The Way works wondrously without leaving traces, while Heaven manifests itself in visible phenomena. Since Heaven cannot stand outside the Way, it is the Way that reaches Heaven’s utmost heights. Viewing the Way in Heaven, how could the Way have any limit? Thus is the Way manifest above and below. This is why this Way is great and cannot…

可離也。欲體道者，可不知所用カ哉？何則？道者，率性而已，其原出於天，而實備諸己也。性無不具，則道無不有；推之天地萬物，莫不皆然。故求道者，求之於性，則天地萬物皆舉之矣。顧欲索之性分之外，則其於道也，不亦遠哉？此子思所以作《中庸》也。

translation_en:
…cannot be departed from. Can those who wish to embody the Way fail to know where to apply their effort [?]? Why is this so? The Way is simply following one's nature. Its source lies in Heaven, yet it is fully present within oneself. Since nothing is absent from human nature, nothing is absent from the Way. Extend this to Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things, and the same holds for all. Thus, those who seek the Way in their nature encompass Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things together. But if they seek it outside their inherent nature, are they not far removed from the Way? This is why Zisi wrote the Doctrine of the Mean.
“Having fully exerted their minds, they followed this with government that could not bear to see others suffer, and their benevolence sheltered all under Heaven.”
He Kuan

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
考試官大學士張批有關雎麟趾之意
大賢原仁心所由達以見仁政所當法也盖政
行而後心有所繼聖人所以達其仁於天下者
也為治者舎此將奚法哉孟子之意若曰人君
之為天下貴於有不忍之心尤貴於遵先王之
法夫法惡可以巳也昔者聖人仁以存心慮周
於物以四海皆天民而匹夫或未獲也寵綏堯
相之責心不容以自暇以五典本天敘而百姓
或未親也逸居無教之憂志豈得而少寧恫瘝
===
在身矣非法不能以徒遂乃推其意而創為之
法以極其裁成輔相之宜圖回於中矣而事不
可以無從乃舉斯心而措之於政以盡其勞來
匡直之方田里樹畜所以開衣食之道而經營
以厚民生者制度品節為甚詳焉學校禮義所
以啓會歸之路而鼓舞以正民德者綱紀文章
為甚備焉盖不忍民之凍餒而不能人人養之
也故道之以政庶上有揆下有守各率吾之養
人者以自養不忍民之昏瞀而不能人人啓之

大賢原仁心所由達，以見仁政所當法也。盖政行而後心有所繼，聖人所以達其仁於天下者也。為治者舎此，將奚法哉？孟子之意若曰：人君之為天下，貴於有不忍之心，尤貴於遵先王之法。夫法惡可以巳也？昔者聖人仁以存心，慮周於物。以四海皆天民，而匹夫或未獲也，寵綏堯相之責，心不容以自暇；以五典本天敘，而百姓或未親也，逸居無教之憂，志豈得而少寧？恫瘝在身矣，非法不能以徒遂，乃推其意而創為之法，以極其裁成輔相之宜；圖回於中矣，而事不可以無從，乃舉斯心而措之於政，以盡其勞來匡直之方。田里樹畜，所以開衣食之道，而經營以厚民生者，制度品節為甚詳焉；學校禮義，所以啓會歸之路，而鼓舞以正民德者，綱紀文章為甚備焉。盖不忍民之凍餒，而不能人人養之也，故道之以政，庶上有揆，下有守，各率吾之養人者以自養；不忍民之昏瞀，而不能人人啓之
translation_en:
Examiner Grand Secretary Zhang comments: “This conveys the spirit of ‘The Ospreys’ (Guan ju) and ‘The Qilin’s Hooves’ (Lin zhi).”

The great worthy traces how a benevolent heart finds full expression, thereby showing what should be emulated in benevolent government. For only when government is put into practice does the heart have something through which its intentions can be carried forward: this is how the sages extended their benevolence throughout the world. If those who govern abandon this, what will they take as their model? Mencius’s meaning is as if he said: When a ruler governs the world, it is precious to possess a heart that cannot bear others’ suffering; still more precious is adherence to the institutions of the former kings. How, then, can these institutions be dispensed with?

In antiquity, the sages preserved benevolence in their hearts, and their concern encompassed all beings. They regarded everyone within the four seas as Heaven’s people; if even one ordinary man had not received his due, they took upon themselves the responsibility of Yao’s minister to cherish and bring peace to the people, and their hearts allowed them no leisure. They regarded the five human relationships as grounded in Heaven’s ordering; if the people had not yet become attached to one another, their concern that people might live comfortably without instruction scarcely allowed their minds any peace. They felt the people’s suffering as though it were in their own bodies. Without institutions, their intentions could not be fulfilled unaided; thus they extended those intentions and created institutions, fully realizing the proper means of shaping and assisting the people’s lives. They pondered plans within their hearts, but affairs could not proceed without something to follow; thus they brought this heart to bear upon government, fully employing the means of encouraging, attracting, correcting, and setting people upright.

Fields and homesteads, planting and animal husbandry opened the way to clothing and food. In planning to enrich the people’s livelihood, their institutions and graded regulations were exceedingly detailed. Schools, ritual, and righteousness opened the path toward a shared moral end. In inspiring the people to rectify their virtue, their guiding principles and cultural forms were exceedingly complete. They could not bear to see the people cold and hungry, yet could not nourish each person individually. Therefore they guided them through government, hoping that those above would have standards and those below would have duties to uphold, and that all would follow the means by which the ruler nourished people in order to nourish themselves. They could not bear the people’s ignorance and confusion, yet could not enlighten each person individually …

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
也故一之以法庶上有教下有學各率吾之成
人者以自成由是政行於當時也稟其式而承
焉功之所加者廣大而無外矣法垂於後世也
師其意而修焉澤之所被者悠久而無疆矣故
聖人仁心所至不疾而速仁聞所動無遠弗届
皆其制法之善載而行之者也使不善其政則
仁隱於中無所藉以及乎人恩遏於近何所因
以達於遠雖有其心亦徒焉耳法之不可以已
也如是夫是則先王之政所以繼仁心於不匱
===
後王能法其政以有為焉天下之治也何有雖
然聖人之道亦竭其心思而政自不容已矣政
之不繼蓋心不能竭而或梏之亡耳然孟子猶
以為有其心者就其未梏未亡者牖之使自喜
其可進而不沮於難兹其為善成人之美與何
戰國之君知其非難而猶怠於自成往往自梏
而莫之竭也
易
聖人久於其道而天下化成

punctuated:
也，故一之以法，庶上有教，下有學，各率吾之成人者以自成。由是政行於當時也，稟其式而承焉，功之所加者廣大而無外矣；法垂於後世也，師其意而修焉，澤之所被者悠久而無疆矣。故聖人仁心所至，不疾而速；仁聞所動，無遠弗届，皆其制法之善載而行之者也。使不善其政，則仁隱於中，無所藉以及乎人；恩遏於近，何所因以達於遠？雖有其心，亦徒焉耳。法之不可以已也如是夫！是則先王之政所以繼仁心於不匱，後王能法其政以有為焉，天下之治也何有？雖然，聖人之道亦竭其心思，而政自不容已矣。政之不繼，蓋心不能竭，而或梏之亡耳。然孟子猶以為有其心者，就其未梏未亡者牖之，使自喜其可進而不沮於難，兹其為善成人之美與！何戰國之君知其非難而猶怠於自成，往往自梏而莫之竭也？

《易》
聖人久於其道而天下化成。
translation_en:
… Thus he brings them into unity through laws, so that those above teach and those below learn, each following the means by which he brings people to fulfillment in order to fulfill themselves. When his governance operates in his own time, people receive its patterns and carry them forward, and its achievements extend broadly, leaving nothing outside their reach. When his laws are handed down to later generations, people take his intentions as their guide and cultivate them, and his beneficence endures without limit. Thus, wherever the sage’s benevolent heart reaches, it advances swiftly without haste; wherever his reputation for benevolence moves people, no place is too distant to be reached. All this is because the laws he establishes effectively bear that benevolence and put it into practice. If he did not make his governance good, benevolence would remain hidden within, with no means of reaching others; kindness would be confined to those nearby—by what means could it reach those far away? Though he possessed such a heart, it would be of no avail. Such is the indispensability of laws! It is therefore the governance of the former kings that perpetuates their benevolent hearts without exhaustion. If later kings can model themselves on that governance and act upon it, what difficulty would there be in bringing order to all under Heaven?

Nevertheless, the sage’s Way also consists in fully exerting his heart and thought, so that governance follows of necessity. When governance fails to continue, it is because the heart has not been fully exerted, but has perhaps been fettered and lost. Yet Mencius still regarded such rulers as possessing that heart. Through what remained unfettered and unlost, he opened their understanding, enabling them to rejoice in their capacity to advance rather than be discouraged by difficulty. How skillfully he brought the good in others to fulfillment! Why did the rulers of the Warring States, knowing that this was not difficult, nevertheless remain remiss in fulfilling themselves, repeatedly fettering themselves instead of fully exerting their hearts?

Book of Changes
“When the sage perseveres in his Way, all under Heaven is transformed and brought to fulfillment.”

Associate Examiner Zhang, Acting Director, comments: “His exposition of the enduring character of the kingly Way is distinctive.”

Utmost sincerity never ceases, and thereby the achievements of government are brought to completion: this is the sage's constancy. In government, constancy is prized; only utmost sincerity is unceasing. The accomplishment of good government naturally includes results that come about without being deliberately sought. Is this not why the sage's Way constitutes the greatness of constancy? Such is the expansion of the meaning of Constancy in the Commentary on the Judgments of the Book of Changes.

Now, obtaining their place in Heaven and thus shining enduringly, changing and transforming and thus enduringly bringing things to completion—these are the constancy of the sun and moon and of the four seasons. The sage's Way accords with the sun and moon and the four seasons; his constancy can therefore be understood. Possessing the virtue of a sage, he occupies the position of the Son of Heaven. As Yao assisted the Lord on High, so his means of revering Heaven's Way and establishing an undertaking without limit is to continue in luminous virtue without cease, allowing no interruption for even a single breath. With the heart of a true king, he carries out the government of a true king, governing the people entrusted to him. 對時育物有篤實感發之意運之一心足以保
四海而無外也惟時惟幾安厥止而已矣正位
凝命有常永貞固之體行之一時足以垂永世
而成裕也吾見積之者久則推之者遠大順洋
溢帝德有廣運之神東漸西被四達而不悖也
感之者久則入之者深大化浸洽民心有從欲
之治淪膚浹髓萬世其永賴也無偏無黨遵王
之道也不識不知順帝之則也道德一而風俗
===

樂無聲而天下和也神祇格而鳥獸馴誕敷文
德之化矣是何也久則天天則神天下囿於聖
人之道而天下不知也聖人與天下相忘於道
而聖人不自知也是之謂至誠無息而功化之
極也恒之時不其大哉抑咸恒所以首經者也
咸言速恒言久何也盖速虛者也見聖人之神
焉久實者也見聖人之化焉要之一理而已雖
然唐虞之盛也而儆戒無虞周道之永也而詠

translation_en: …with not a single thought of slackening. It is simply a matter of being discerning and single-minded, holding fast to the mean. Responding to the seasons and nurturing all things, he possesses a sincere and substantial intent that moves and inspires others. Exercised through his own heart, it suffices to safeguard all within the four seas, leaving nothing outside its embrace. It is simply a matter of attending to the proper time and the first stirrings of change, resting securely where he ought to abide. Taking his rightful position and making Heaven’s mandate firm, he possesses an enduring, steadfast foundation. Put into practice in his own age, it suffices to bequeath abundance to all ages to come. I see that, when this accumulation continues long, its influence extends far. Great harmony overflows, and imperial virtue displays the wondrous power of its far-reaching operation: reaching eastward and spreading westward, it penetrates all four quarters without discord. When its moving influence continues long, it enters deeply. Great transformation thoroughly permeates the people, bringing about an order that accords with their hearts’ desires. It sinks through their skin and penetrates their marrow; ten thousand generations will rely upon it forever. Without partiality or faction, they follow the king’s Way; without conscious knowledge or awareness, they accord with the sovereign’s pattern. Moral principles become one and customs become uniform, forever securing the livelihood of the multitude. Perfect ritual requires no yielding, yet all under Heaven is ordered; perfect music has no sound, yet all under Heaven is harmonious. The spirits of Heaven and Earth arrive, and birds and beasts become tame: the transforming influence of cultured virtue spreads far and wide. Why is this? Endurance makes one like Heaven; being like Heaven makes one numinous. All under Heaven lives within the sage’s Way without knowing it. The sage and all under Heaven forget one another in the Way, and the sage himself is unaware of it. This is what is meant by utmost sincerity without cessation, the pinnacle of achievement and transformation. Is not the significance of the time of Constancy (Heng) great indeed? Moreover, Influence (Xian) and Constancy are placed at the beginning of the classic. Why does Influence speak of swiftness, and Constancy of duration? Swiftness pertains to receptive emptiness: therein we see the sage’s numinous efficacy. Duration pertains to substance: therein we see the sage’s transforming influence. In essence, they are but one principle. 陳則常示而不隱四時行焉百物生焉其教顯
於上下之察者亘古今無少改也日月之升降
其運無端也然懸象之著則常明而不息日之
照焉月之臨焉其明生於往来之推者窮天地

Yet the patterns and images they display are constantly revealed, never hidden. The four seasons proceed, and the myriad things are born. Their teaching, manifest in what is evident above and below, has not changed in the slightest throughout antiquity and the present. The sun and moon rise and descend, their revolutions without end. Yet the celestial images they display shine constantly, without cease. The sun illuminates; the moon looks down. Their light, arising through the successive movement of coming and going, is never exhausted for as long as Heaven and Earth endure. Viewed in this way, it becomes clear how the movements of all under Heaven are represented in the Changes.

Beneficial in use, in going forth and coming in, it contains the incipient basis for transforming and fitting things to circumstances. Although genuine and false conduct lead to different outcomes, the constant norms of canonical rites operate wherever affairs and things converge and interconnect; there is naturally something here that cannot be transgressed. Contraction and expansion stimulate each other, and from this emerges the basis for carrying things forward. The actual conditions of the myriad things are exceedingly intricate and cannot be fixed; yet although things have no fixed form, principle is fixed. The ordering of the myriad affairs is exceedingly changeable and cannot remain constant; yet although affairs are inconstant, principle is constant. Hence, if one accords with this principle, what brings good fortune will arrive; if one opposes it, what brings misfortune will arrive. text:
此言
大臣自任事君以人之責其所感者深矣夫以
人事君大臣之職業也說之所以欽承於商宗
者孰大於是且說之意謂夫上下志同莫不欲
得賢而用之然賢不易致恒視君之成德耳吾
王典學之功既深造于罔覺法祖攸行復永底
于無愆則德一而樂於取善心純而急於用賢
說於是弗克承之是不敢巳今也幸大君之有
作而祇若之不遑念盛時之可為而薦賢以圖
===
治以天之生俊乂也所以異乎人者也禮之不
優鮮有至矣俊乂之生也非止於一方也求之
不廣鮮不遺矣必篤同升之義舉所知以及所
不知庸詎知善之在於人乎大翕受之公惟其
人而不惟其類庸詎知人之賢於我乎上而為
德下而為民所與共天位者集衆思以廣忠益
而大小各稱其職焉入使治之出使長之所與
代天工者具衆美以分猷念而中外皆得其人
焉由是百官承式而君臨之有輔同心匡辟真

punctuated:
此言。
大臣自任事君以人之責，其所感者深矣。夫以人事君，大臣之職業也。說之所以欽承於商宗者，孰大於是？且說之意謂：夫上下志同，莫不欲得賢而用之，然賢不易致，恒視君之成德耳。吾王典學之功，既深造于罔覺；法祖攸行，復永底于無愆。則德一而樂於取善，心純而急於用賢。說於是弗克承之，是不敢巳。今也幸大君之有作，而祇若之不遑；念盛時之可為，而薦賢以圖治。以天之生俊乂也，所以異乎人者也，禮之不優，鮮有至矣。俊乂之生也，非止於一方也，求之不廣，鮮不遺矣。必篤同升之義，舉所知以及所不知，庸詎知善之在於人乎？大翕受之公，惟其人而不惟其類，庸詎知人之賢於我乎？上而為德，下而為民，所與共天位者，集衆思以廣忠益，而大小各稱其職焉。入使治之，出使長之，所與代天工者，具衆美以分猷念，而中外皆得其人焉。由是百官承式，而君臨之有輔；同心匡辟，真
translation_en:
…these words.

When a great minister takes upon himself the responsibility of serving his ruler by providing worthy men, profoundly does this move him. Serving the ruler by providing worthy men is the proper duty of a great minister. What could be more important than this in Yue’s reverent service to the Shang sovereign? Yue’s meaning was this: when those above and below share the same purpose, all wish to obtain worthy men and employ them. Yet worthy men are not easily attracted; this always depends upon the ruler’s perfected virtue. My king’s efforts in constant study have already brought him to profound attainment without conscious awareness; by following the deeds of his ancestors, he has also attained lasting freedom from error. His virtue is therefore undivided, and he delights in accepting what is good; his mind is pure, and he is eager to employ the worthy. Yue would not dare fail to respond to this. Now, fortunate to witness the great ruler’s vigorous undertaking, he hastens to comply reverently. Mindful of what can be accomplished in this flourishing age, he recommends worthy men to achieve good government.

Heaven endows outstanding men with qualities that distinguish them from others. Unless they are treated with exceptional courtesy, few will come. Nor are outstanding men born in only one region. Unless the search is broad, some will almost certainly be overlooked. One must firmly uphold the obligation to advance together with others, recommending those one knows and extending the search to those one does not know—for how can one know where goodness resides among men? One must enlarge the impartial spirit of embracing all, considering the individual rather than merely his kind—for how can one know who is worthier than oneself? Above, this serves the ruler’s virtue; below, it serves the people. Those with whom one shares Heaven’s offices pool their thinking to broaden their loyal contributions, so that each, whether in a great or a minor office, fulfills his duties fittingly. Those appointed at court are made to govern; those sent out are made to lead. Those with whom one carries out Heaven’s work bring together their various excellences and share the work of planning and deliberation, so that suitable men fill posts both at court and outside it. Thus the hundred officials follow the prescribed standards, and the ruler has assistance in governing them. United in purpose, they uphold and correct their sovereign, truly …

…there would indeed be a means of extending this to your colleagues. The ministers would reverently comply, taking as their model the assistance rendered to Heaven. Mutually correcting one another and guiding the ruler’s intentions would not have to depend entirely upon Fu Yue. Thus, the way in which he sought to render service lay precisely in the demanding expectations he earnestly set before the ruler. Was this not a very great expression of reverence? Moreover, to labor in seeking talent and enjoy ease in employing the worthy—this was invariably how the sage kings of antiquity advanced the Way and achieved good government. Thus, only after reverent, silent reflection came the dream in which the Supreme Lord bestowed a worthy assistant; only after the search for someone matching the likeness came the summoning of outstanding men. By obtaining a worthy man to assist him, the king brought about the flourishing of Yin’s royal Way. Since Tang and Yi Yin, such a partnership had been seen only this once. Had Gaozong not reflected upon how difficult it was to encounter such a man, how could he have understood the purport of Yue’s offering admonition and assisting his virtue?

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
宛然在目
考試官學士歐陽批得守成之要可録
考試官大學士張批周公保治之意可想
見也録之
周臣勉君飭武以懷遠所以繼前王之德業也
盖文武之盛德大業而善繼之者在我後人也
周公詰兵之訓夫豈徒哉今夫刑以齊天下兵
以威天下勿誤庶獄王固知刑之當慎而不知
兵之不可以已也是必當熙洽之世而亟為先
===
事之防嚴武備之修而豫為不虞之戒由是王
靈丕振聲教訖於四方使禹服弼成之舊自此
其允升焉聖武布昭德威廣於天下雖海隅蒼
生之地亦罔不率俾焉疆宇闢而尺地莫非其
有式廓以增矣人心服而一民莫非其臣亂畧
以遏矣兹固守成之道而前王德業不因之有
賴乎惟我文王聖德緝煕著而為四方之光西
土之顯者煥乎日月之照臨矣覲之者文孫責
也今則武衛張而文命益敷有以宣重輝於奕

…is vividly before our eyes.

Examiner Zhang, Grand Secretary, comments: “The Duke of Zhou’s intention to preserve good government can be discerned here. Include it.”
A minister of Zhou urged his ruler to put military affairs in order so as to win over distant peoples: this was the means of carrying forward the virtue and achievements of the former kings. For the abundant virtue and great achievements of Kings Wen and Wu depend upon us, their descendants, to carry them forward well. Could the Duke of Zhou’s injunction to put the armed forces in order have been without purpose? Punishments bring order to all under Heaven; armed forces inspire awe throughout it. ‘Do not err in the many judicial cases’: the king certainly understood that punishments must be applied cautiously, but did not understand that military preparedness could not be discontinued. Precisely in an age of flourishing harmony, therefore, he must urgently take precautions before trouble arises, rigorously attend to military preparations, and guard beforehand against the unforeseen. Thus the king’s majesty would be greatly strengthened, and his renown and transforming instruction would reach the four quarters, ensuring that the inherited achievement of securing Yu’s domains would henceforth truly advance. His sagely martial power would be manifest everywhere, and the awe inspired by his virtue would spread throughout the realm. Even among the common people in the farthest coastal regions, none would fail to follow and obey. His territory would expand, with not a foot of land outside his possession: thus would his domain be enlarged and augmented. The people’s hearts would submit, with not a single person outside his subjecthood: thus would disorder and aggression be checked. This is indeed the way to preserve an established achievement. Would not the virtue and achievements of the former kings thereby find their support?
Our King Wen’s sagely virtue shone continually, manifesting itself as a light to the four quarters. Its radiance in the western lands was as brilliant as the illumination of sun and moon. To make it manifest [?] is the responsibility of his cultured grandson. title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
世丕顯之謨天下之所快覩者也孰得而遏之
哉惟我武王天休震動奮而為燮伐之功永清
之治者翕然天人之順應矣揚之者文子責也
今則武功振而王基益固有以延景命於萬年
丕承之烈天下所望而震焉者也孰得而禦之
哉是則一戎兵之詰而係於守成者如此知恤
之君其可忽乎抑文武無二道用之惟其時而
已武成戢兵示天下弗服武之時周公相之也
傳至成王天下不復知有兵故周公詰兵之戒
===

非聖人得已惟其時可矣

本旨
punctuated:
世。丕顯之謨，天下之所快覩者也，孰得而遏之哉？惟我武王，天休震動，奮而為燮伐之功；永清之治者，翕然天人之順應矣。揚之者，文子責也。今則武功振而王基益固，有以延景命於萬年。丕承之烈，天下所望而震焉者也，孰得而禦之哉？是則一戎兵之詰，而係於守成者如此，知恤之君，其可忽乎？抑文武無二道，用之惟其時而已。《武成》戢兵，示天下弗服，武之時，周公相之也。傳至成王，天下不復知有兵，故周公詰兵之戒，深致意焉。時之所在，雖聖人不能違也。故兵者，非聖人得已，惟其時可矣。
詩
君曰：「卜爾萬壽無疆。」
陳斗南

同考試官郎中盧批：「修辭微婉，太得詩人本旨。」
translation_en:
…for successive generations. This splendidly illustrious design is what all under Heaven delight to behold: who could obstruct it? Our King Wu, receiving Heaven’s favor, stirred mightily and accomplished the work of chastisement through arms. His rule, bringing lasting peace, met with the united and willing response of Heaven and humankind. To exalt it was the responsibility of his cultivated son. Now military achievements flourish and the royal foundation grows firmer, thereby extending Heaven’s great mandate for ten thousand years. This splendid achievement of carrying on the inheritance is what all under Heaven look upon with awe: who could resist it? Thus, even this single matter of putting arms in readiness bears so closely upon preserving an established realm. Could a ruler mindful of his responsibilities neglect it? Yet civil and military governance are not two different Ways; their use depends only upon the times. In “The Completion of the War” (Wucheng), arms were laid away to show all under Heaven that they would no longer be used. This was in King Wu’s time, when the Duke of Zhou assisted him. By the time the throne passed to King Cheng, all under Heaven had ceased even to be aware of arms. Thus the Duke of Zhou gave profound attention to his admonition to maintain military readiness. Even a sage cannot act against what the times require. Hence the employment of arms is something even a sage cannot always avoid; it is enough that it accord with the times.

Book of Odes
“The lord says: ‘I foretell for you ten thousand years of life without limit.’”
Chen Dounan

君之詞
考試官大學士張批臣子愛君之情藹然可掬
托神嘏而期以永年周臣祝君之意也盖人君
===
之壽至于萬年者可謂永矣周臣托之神嘏以
期其君焉忠愛之情何至哉其意若曰吾君奉
神靈之統而作之君也其福之獲豈惟天保之
而已哉嘗於神保而有徵矣盖吾君之奉祀也
盡志盡物既孚於禴祠之餘而神明之来格也
是饗是宜自昭於陟降之頃先公先王雖曰遠
矣然一誠之所感召而神則無弗惠焉来宗来
止致嘉告矣盖一氣之所流通而惠則無弗福
焉其必將曰仁者壽之基也今爾之孝享既我

To invoke the spirits’ blessings and thereby hope for enduring years: this is the intention with which the ministers of Zhou wished their ruler well. A ruler whose life reaches ten thousand years may indeed be called long-lived. The ministers of Zhou invoked the spirits’ blessings in expressing this hope for their ruler. How profound [?] was their loyal affection! Their meaning was as though they said: Our ruler upholds the succession handed down by the divine spirits and acts as sovereign. In obtaining blessings, does he merely enjoy Heaven’s protection? There has already been confirmation through the impersonator of the spirits. For when our ruler performs sacrifices, he devotes his whole purpose and provides every offering; his sincerity has already won trust through the seasonal sacrifices. And when the spirits arrive, they accept and approve the offerings, making this manifest as they ascend and descend. Though the former lords and former kings may be said to be distant, wherever wholehearted sincerity moves and summons them, none of the spirits fails to bestow favor. They come to the ancestral temple, they arrive, and deliver an auspicious message. For wherever the single vital force circulates, their favor invariably brings blessings. They will surely say: Benevolence is the foundation of longevity. Now your filial offerings have already, to me …

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
將矣則永錫爾類而篤之以壽考之祜者其寧
有窮哉壽者福之先也今爾之昭明既有融矣
則保佑爾命而引之以綿長之慶者其何有極
哉長守其富也長守其貴也合天下之渙而萃
之所以紹耿光而揚休烈者自今伊始殆萬斯
年而無替乎宗廟享之也子孫保之也承前人
之緒而繹之所以守宗祧而為祭主者過此以
往殆萬斯年而無疆乎夫明之於幽其理同也
孝享之禮既至則其感通之者必速祖之於孫
===
其氣同也詒燕之謀未已則其願望之者必深
即其所卜而吾君之萬壽也信乎有徵矣抑周
之臣子頌禱其君而必本之天與祖何也文王
之詩曰命之不易言天心之難諶也又曰無念
爾祖言祖德之不可忘也周之盛王既有以得
乎天而又有以得乎祖君人之道於是盡矣古
人之善頌禱如此夫
載穫濟濟有實其積萬億及秭為酒為醴
烝畀祖妣以洽百禮有飶其香邦家之光

則保佑爾命而引之以綿長之慶者其何有極
哉長守其富也長守其貴也合天下之歡而萃
之所以紹耿光而揚休烈者自今伊始殆萬斯
年而無替乎宗廟享之也子孫保之也承前人
之緒而繹之所以守宗祧而爲祭主者過此以
往殆萬斯年而無疆乎夫明之於幽其理同也
孝享之禮既至則其感通之者必速祖之於孫
===
其氣同也詒燕之謀未已則其顧望之者必深
即其所卜而吾君之萬壽也信乎有徵矣抑周
之臣子頌禱其君而必本之天與祖何也文王
之詩曰命之不易言天心之難諶也又曰無念
爾祖言祖德之不可忘也周之盛王既有以得
乎天而又有以得乎祖君人之道於是盡矣古
人之善頌禱如此夫
載穫濟濟有實其積萬億及秭爲酒爲醴
烝畀祖妣以洽百禮有飶其香邦家之光
punctuated:
將矣，則永錫爾類，而篤之以壽考之祜者，其寧有窮哉？壽者，福之先也。今爾之昭明既有融矣，則保佑爾命，而引之以綿長之慶者，其何有極哉？長守其富也，長守其貴也，合天下之渙而萃之，所以紹耿光而揚休烈者，自今伊始，殆萬斯年而無替乎？宗廟享之也，子孫保之也，承前人之緒而繹之，所以守宗祧而為祭主者，過此以往，殆萬斯年而無疆乎？夫明之於幽，其理同也。孝享之禮既至，則其感通之者必速。祖之於孫，其氣同也。詒燕之謀未已，則其願望之者必深。即其所卜，而吾君之萬壽也，信乎有徵矣。抑周之臣子頌禱其君，而必本之天與祖，何也？《文王》之詩曰：「命之不易。」言天心之難諶也。又曰：「無念爾祖。」言祖德之不可忘也。周之盛王既有以得乎天，而又有以得乎祖，君人之道於是盡矣。古人之善頌禱如此夫！

載穫濟濟，有實其積，萬億及秭。為酒為醴，烝畀祖妣，以洽百禮。有飶其香，邦家之光。
translation_en:
…have been presented, then can there ever be an end to granting blessings forever to you and your kind, and enriching you with the blessing of long life? Longevity comes first among blessings. Now that your radiant virtue shines forth, how could there be any limit to protecting your allotted life and prolonging it with enduring blessings? Long may you retain your wealth; long may you retain your noble station. Gathering together all that is scattered under Heaven, you continue the glorious light and proclaim the splendid achievements of your forebears. Beginning now, shall this not endure for ten thousand years without decline? The ancestral temples shall receive offerings, and your descendants shall preserve this inheritance. Taking up and carrying forward the legacy of your predecessors, you maintain the ancestral shrines and preside over their sacrifices. From this time onward, shall this not continue for ten thousand years without end?

The visible and invisible realms share the same principle. Once the rites of filial offering are performed to perfection, the response and communion they elicit must be swift. Ancestors and descendants share the same vital essence. Since the ancestors’ designs to bequeath peace to their descendants never cease, their hopes for them must be profound. Judging by what these foretell, there is indeed evidence that our ruler will enjoy myriad years of life. Yet why did the ministers and subjects of Zhou, in praising their ruler and praying for him, invariably ground their words in Heaven and the ancestors? The ode “King Wen” says, “The Mandate is not easy to retain,” expressing how difficult it is to rely upon Heaven’s favor. It also says, “Will you not keep your ancestor in mind?” expressing that ancestral virtue must never be forgotten. The illustrious kings of Zhou secured the favor of Heaven and also that of their ancestors. In this they fulfilled the Way of ruling others. Such was the skill of the ancients in offering praise and prayer!

Then they reap in great throngs;
Full indeed are their heaps of grain,
In myriads, hundreds of millions, and trillions.
They make wine and sweet liquor,
Presenting them to their ancestral fathers and mothers,
To fulfill the hundred rites.
Fragrant is their aroma,
The glory of the state and royal house…

周人叙豐年之入，而國之大典舉焉。夫事神禮人，國之所重也，而備舉之，則豐年之利大矣。其可忘所自哉？此周人修報所以歸德於神也。其意曰：國用之盈縮，視年穀之豐歉。然服勤之勞者，固農之力，而有收之利者，實神之錫焉。今也
translation_en:
…Its fragrance is that of pepper; there is peace in ripe old age.

Wan Yulong

Associate Examiner Zhu, Vice Director, comments: “The exposition is rigorously ordered, and the phrasing vigorous and forceful. The writer must be deeply versed in classical learning.”

Associate Examiner Lu, Director, comments: “The Zhou people's concern for agriculture and their observance of rites of thanksgiving emerge beyond the words themselves.”

Associate Examiner Wu, Compiler, comments: “The language and ideas are concise and disciplined, capturing the form of the hymn.”

Associate Examiner Li, Senior Compiler, comments: “Through the abundant harvest, the essay evokes the scene of supreme harmony under the fully established Zhou dynasty, profoundly capturing the form of the hymn.”

Associate Examiner Wang, Senior Compiler, comments: “It takes as its theme that the abundance or scarcity of resources for state expenditure depends upon whether the year's harvest is plentiful or poor. Its overall bearing is distinctive.”

Examiner Ouyang, Academician, comments: “It reveals the Zhou people's conviction that sowing and reaping alone are treasures. It merits inclusion.”

Examiner Zhang, Grand Secretary, comments: “It brings out the Zhou dynasty's concern for agriculture. It merits acceptance.”

The Zhou people recount the produce of a plentiful year, through which the great ceremonies of the state are performed. Serving the spirits and treating people with ritual propriety are matters of great importance to the state. If all these observances can be performed in full, then great indeed are the benefits of a plentiful year. Could their source be forgotten? This is why the Zhou people, in performing rites of thanksgiving, attributed their blessings to the spirits. The meaning is this: the abundance or scarcity of resources for state expenditure depends upon whether the year's grain harvest is plentiful or poor. Yet although the toil of diligent labor certainly comes from the farmers' exertions, the benefit of obtaining a harvest is truly a gift from the spirits. Now…

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
農事方畢稼穡既成矣穫之也時而趨事之人
濟濟其衆焉蓋地有餘利故人無遺力矣納之
也同而露積之實萬億及秭焉蓋生之者衆而
入之者多矣夫如是則凡所以洽神人和上下
而為國之彛典寧有墜而不舉者哉于焉為之
酒也有思柔之美矣為之醴也皆維醹之嘉矣
由是幽之以事神也烝畀祖妣則享祀妥侑足
以綏孝子之心而無違於禮焉獻酬交酢足以
盡威儀之時而不愆於度焉報本追遠之誠胥
===
此乎達矣然所以致此者豐年之慶有以成之
也否則三酒五齊無所於備其何以將誠信而
交神明哉祀事不其缺乎由是明之以禮人也
則有飶其香足以成上下之交而錫邦家之光
焉有椒其馨足以將引翼之敬而貽胡考之寧
焉養賢及民之政胥此焉舉矣然所以致此者
豐年之慶有以成之也否則尊酒簋貳無所用
享其何以尚有德而尊高年哉典禮其不廢乎
此皆昭受田祖先農之賜有國者所深願而不

此皆昭受田祖先農之賜有國者所深頼而不
punctuated: 農事方畢，稼穡既成矣。穫之也時，而趨事之人濟濟其衆焉，蓋地有餘利，故人無遺力矣。納之也同，而露積之實萬億及秭焉，蓋生之者衆，而入之者多矣。夫如是，則凡所以洽神人、和上下而為國之彛典，寧有墜而不舉者哉？于焉為之酒也，有思柔之美矣；為之醴也，皆維醹之嘉矣。由是幽之以事神也，烝畀祖妣，則享祀妥侑，足以綏孝子之心而無違於禮焉；獻酬交酢，足以盡威儀之時而不愆於度焉。報本追遠之誠，胥此乎達矣。然所以致此者，豐年之慶有以成之也。否則三酒五齊無所於備，其何以將誠信而交神明哉？祀事不其缺乎？由是明之以禮人也，則有飶其香，足以成上下之交而錫邦家之光焉；有椒其馨，足以將引翼之敬而貽胡考之寧焉。養賢及民之政，胥此焉舉矣。然所以致此者，豐年之慶有以成之也。否則尊酒簋貳無所用享，其何以尚有德而尊高年哉？典禮其不廢乎？此皆昭受田祖先農之賜，有國者所深願而不
translation_en:
…the farm work has just ended, and the growing of grain is complete. The harvest is gathered at the proper time, and great numbers of people hasten to the work. Since the land yields abundant benefits, no one spares any effort. The grain is brought in together, and the heaps piled in the open number in the countless millions. Since those producing it are numerous, what they bring in is plentiful. Under such circumstances, could any of the state's established rites, which bring spirits and people into accord and harmonize those above and below, fall into neglect and remain unperformed? From this grain they make wine, admirable for its mellowness; they make sweet liquor, excellent for its richness.

Thus, in the unseen realm, they serve the spirits, presenting offerings to their ancestral fathers and mothers. The offerings and sacrifices, the settling of the ancestral impersonators in their places and the urging of them to partake, suffice to comfort the hearts of filial descendants without departing from ritual propriety. The presentation, return, and exchange of wine cups suffice to fulfill the timely requirements of dignified bearing without transgressing the prescribed measure. Through these rites, their sincerity in repaying their origins and remembering their distant ancestors finds full expression. Yet what enables all this is the blessing of a plentiful year. Otherwise, there would be no means to prepare the three kinds of wine and the five grades of sacrificial liquor. How, then, could they convey their sincerity and good faith and commune with the spirits? Would not the sacrifices be deficient?

Thus, in the visible realm, they treat people with ritual propriety. The rich fragrance of the offerings suffices to bring those above and below into fellowship and bestow glory upon the state; their peppery aroma suffices to convey the respect shown in guiding and assisting the aged and to confer the peace of a long life. Through these rites, the policies of nourishing the worthy and extending benefits to the people are all put into practice. Yet what enables all this is the blessing of a plentiful year. Otherwise, there would be no means to offer even a vessel of wine and two baskets of grain. How, then, could they honor the virtuous and revere the aged? Would not the established rites fall into disuse? All this plainly shows their receipt of blessings from the Ancestor of the Fields and the First Husbandman—blessings that those who possess a state deeply desire but cannot…

開國是故上之人所以勞民而勸功下之人所

translation_en:
…could be certain of obtaining. How, then, could the rites of thanksgiving and repayment to the gods be discontinued? Zhou founded its state upon agriculture. Thus, the efforts of those above to reward the people’s toil and encourage their work, and the practices and songs of those below, concerned nothing beyond this. How great is the importance of agriculture! In the poem “The Seventh Month” and the admonitions of “Against Idleness,” the Duke of Zhou earnestly instructed King Cheng on this very matter. This shows that ruler and ministers, high and low alike, were anxious and diligent, watchful and resolute, putting the hardships of sowing and harvesting first, and only afterward sharing together in the flourishing of great peace. Was this not the foundation of their eight hundred years of enduring rule in accordance with the Way?
Spring and Autumn Annals
“In spring, in the first month of the royal calendar, the duke joined the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Chen, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Zheng, the Baron of Xu, and the Earl of Cao in invading Cai. Cai’s forces collapsed. They then attacked Chu and encamped at Xing. Qu Wan of Chu came to conclude a covenant at the army’s camp.” Fourth year of Duke Xi.
“The duke joined the Marquis of Jin, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Cao, Guang, heir apparent of Qi, the Viscount of Ju, the Viscount of Zhu, the Viscount of Teng, the Earl of Xue, the Earl of Qi, and the Viscount of Little Zhu in attacking Zheng. They met at Xiaoyu. The men of Chu seized Liang Xiao, the diplomatic envoy of Zheng.” Eleventh year of Duke Xiang.
Wang Yingshi
Associate Examiner Liu, Chief Supervising Secretary, comments: “Powerful and ample; worthy of selection.”
Associate Examiner Qin, Senior Compiler, comments: “Such was the sage’s intent in approving Duke Huan of Qi and Duke Dao of Jin.”

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
考試官學士歐陽批聖人善不戰屈人此作
能發之
考試官大學士張批此聖人予善之恕子能
言之可録
春秋兩紀霸主駕外服內也皆予其不戰焉盖
不戰屈人王者之事也桓悼之於楚鄭其庶幾
哉昔大道隱而舞干因壘之風不繼見於天下
矣何幸桓悼之進於此邪方桓之伐楚也兵連
八國潰首蔡師力已强矣孰不曰可翦此後食
===
也桓則不然謂威天下有道而兵革不以為利
矧楚可義折者何忍勦民為哉於是干戈載戢
爰修文告之詞同好是徵用張柔服之道陘亭
次而桓之駕楚以不戰矣果而軍門納款屈完
惠來遂帖服於齊焉噫漢水方城楚非易勝者
也自桓折以義故險無所用之否則背城借一
俘馘所不免矣桓其善駕楚哉若悼之討鄭也
抗楚三駕觀兵東門鋒云銳矣孰不曰可脅之
使從也悼則不然謂懷天下有德而强大難於
