Examiner Ouyang, Academician, comments: “The Sage commends subduing others without fighting. This composition brings out that meaning.”
Examiner Zhang, Grand Secretary, comments: “Such is the Sage’s generosity in giving credit for good deeds. You have expressed it well; this merits selection.”
The Spring and Autumn Annals twice records hegemonic lords bringing outer states under control and securing the submission of inner states, in both cases approving their success without battle. For subduing others without fighting is the work of a true king. Did not Duke Huan and Duke Dao come close to this in their dealings with Chu and Zheng? Long ago, when the Great Way became obscured, the practice of dancing with shields and ‘relying on ramparts’ [?] ceased to appear in the world. How fortunate that Huan and Dao advanced so far toward this ideal!
When Huan attacked Chu, he joined the forces of eight states and first routed the army of Cai; his strength was already formidable. Who would not have said, “We can destroy this enemy before taking our meal”? But Huan thought otherwise. He held that there was a proper way to inspire awe throughout the realm, and that weapons and armor were not to be treated as a means of advantage. Moreover, since Chu could be brought to yield through righteousness, how could he bear to slaughter its people? Thus he put away his weapons and composed a formal proclamation. Invoking their shared amity, he advanced the way of winning submission through gentleness. He halted at Xingting, and thus brought Chu under control without fighting. Sure enough, an offer of submission was presented at his army’s gates: Qu Wan graciously came, and Chu thereupon submitted to Qi.
Ah! With the Han River and Fangcheng as its defenses, Chu was no easy state to defeat. Because Huan brought it to yield through righteousness, its natural defenses served no purpose. Otherwise, it would have made a last stand beneath its city walls, and the taking of captives and severed ears would have been unavoidable. How skillfully Huan brought Chu under control!
As for Dao’s punitive expedition against Zheng, he opposed Chu with three campaigns and displayed his troops at the eastern gate; his forces were indeed formidable. Who would not have said, “We can threaten Zheng into obedience”? But Dao thought otherwise. He held that virtue was the means to win the allegiance of all under Heaven, while sheer strength and power could hardly …

圖成，知鄭可誠感者，何假窮兵為哉？於是納堠禁侵，推心以置其腹；禮囚遣告，虛懷以俟其歸。蕭魚會，而悼之服鄭以不戰矣。果而如楚咎絕，良霄被執，遂堅事夫晋焉。噫！尋盟尋叛，鄭非可信者也。自悼感以誠，故詐無所用之；否則玉帛待强，兵爭無寧日矣。悼其善服鄭哉！是則楚强也，而屈於義；鄭叛也，而服於誠。彼善戰者，實不容於聖人之世，而欒武子之師不遷戮，所以見予於《春秋》也。雖然，桓之兵善矣，使楚之奉使無人焉，則境外之君命，誰其裁之？悼之兵善矣，使鄭之謀國無人焉，則二三之國是，誰其定之？至如管仲內政之作、魏絳息民之謀，又二霸之烈所由成也。賢者之有益於人國如此夫！

…to bring the undertaking to completion. Knowing that Zheng could be moved by sincerity, why resort to exhausting military force? He therefore withdrew the scouts [?] and prohibited incursions, opening his heart and placing it, as it were, within theirs. He treated the prisoners courteously and sent them back with a message, awaiting Zheng’s allegiance with an open mind. At the meeting at Xiaoyu, Duke Dao thus brought Zheng into submission without fighting. Indeed, communications with Chu were severed [?], and Liang Xiao was detained; Zheng thereafter served Jin steadfastly. Ah! Repeatedly renewing alliances and then betraying them, Zheng could hardly be trusted. But once Duke Dao moved it through sincerity, its deceit had no further use. Otherwise, its offerings of jade and silk would have gone to whichever power was stronger, and armed conflict would never have ceased. How skillfully Duke Dao brought Zheng into submission! Thus Chu, though powerful, yielded to righteousness; Zheng, though rebellious, submitted to sincerity. Those who excel merely at warfare truly have no place in the age of a sage. This is why Luan Wuzi’s army, which did not extend its slaughter to others [?], received approval in the Spring and Autumn Annals.
Nevertheless, skillful as Duke Huan’s military conduct was, had Chu lacked a capable envoy, who could have exercised discretion over his ruler’s commands beyond the borders? Skillful as Duke Dao’s military conduct was, had Zheng lacked capable statesmen, who could have settled its wavering national policy? Moreover, Guan Zhong’s establishment of domestic administration and Wei Jiang’s plans to give the people respite were also what enabled these two hegemons to achieve their great deeds. Such is the benefit that worthy men bring to a state!
“The Viscount of Chu and the Marquis of Cai encamped at Juehe”—the tenth year of Duke Wen. “In spring, the Viscount of Chu attacked Jun”—the eleventh year of Duke Wen.

Examiner Ouyang, Academician, comments: Careful and rigorous.
Examiner Zhang, Grand Secretary, comments: The wording is rigorous and orderly. Include it.
The Spring and Autumn Annals records military affairs, and those who oppress the Xia states or attach themselves to the Yi barbarians alike receive censure. This shows how scrupulously the Sage guarded the boundary between Yi and Xia. Ever since Langyuan, Chu had not passed a day without contemplating designs upon the north. Now it joined four states in encamping at Juehe, while its ruler personally led an attack upon Mi. Yet Duke Huan of Qi also encamped when conducting campaigns. Why, then, is Chu alone censured?
The gentleman says: That the Yi should not throw the Hua states into disorder is an enduring principle of Heaven and Earth; moreover, Song descended from a former royal dynasty. What standing had Chu that it dared capitalize on the fear inspired by its destruction of small states, flaunt its achievements in pacification, and encamp at Juehe? It stationed its army and plotted, watching for an opening before acting. Had Song not held the hunt at Mengzhu, the campaign at Xixue [?] would have been directed against Song rather than Mi. In compiling the Classic, the Sage regarded Duke Huan of Qi’s encampment as undertaken to frame diplomatic declarations that would intimidate the enemy. Chu, however, harbored unruly ambitions to encroach upon the Xia states. How could the two be spoken of in the same breath? Thus the attack on Mi is recorded after the encampment at Juehe. This is what constitutes the censure.
As for joining Chu, Chen, Zheng, and Song did so too. Why, then, is Cai alone censured? The gentleman says: To transform the Yi through Xia civilization is a principle valid throughout antiquity and the present, whereas Chu was indeed a barbarian state that usurped royal prerogatives. What was Cai doing, abandoning the honorable standing of the Ji-lineage states, willingly accepting the company of an alien people, and following Chu to Juehe? Humiliating itself and lowering its aspirations, descending from lofty trees into a dark valley, in the end…

…in the end, when Jin convened the covenant at Xincheng, Cai alone did not participate: here is clear evidence of its determination to abandon righteousness. In compiling the Classic, the Sage regarded the three states’ following Chu as a means of alleviating danger and securing their own safety. Cai, however, persisted without cause. How could they all be judged alike? Thus he placed the Marquis of Cai below the Viscount of Chu: this, too, is what is meant by censuring him. When this principle prevails, the central states remain the central states, and the Yi and Di remain the Yi and Di; the central states do not stray beyond their bounds, and the Yi and Di do not enter. Thus the great boundary safeguarding all under Heaven is established. How true the saying that none but a sage could have compiled the Spring and Autumn Annals!
Yet the greatest good fortune of the central states lies in having capable men. At that time, Chu oppressed the Xia states—but who opened the way for it? Cai sided with Chu—but who permitted it? Jin presided over the covenants of the Xia states, but authority did not rest with the feudal lords. Zhao Dun and the other ministers cannot evade their responsibility. At this, the gentleman cannot but look back longingly upon Duke Huan’s earlier age and lament that Duke Dao came so late.

text:
立舉而措之天下無難矣聖人為治而始諸此
有以哉且夫篤近者舉遠之機守約者施博之
道審所尚而治體可識矣是故聖人繼離明以
普照而答陽宣化君臨乎萬邦秉乾剛以獨斷
而正位凝命宰制乎羣動撫世酬物以容保天
下也將以溥樂利之休奠麗陳教以敷錫斯民
也欲以臻熈皥之治此豈無所始哉亦曰人道
而已矣盖人道惟在於洽親化理莫先於惇族
聖人不徧物而治也道隆於天合彝倫攸敘以
===
端萬化之基情篤於所親人紀肇修以立庶政
之極于其本之一而恩孚焉達統同之和而仁
民愛物胥此推之矣于其分之殊而理秩焉廣
辨異之宜而家邦四海舉此加之矣斯則盡倫
敦化以涵時出之源施為緩急自裕推行之利
其曰報功舉賢使能存愛雖均為治道所先而
要之必自人道始是故聖人南面而立而天下
大治也不然求治雖切而本之則無近者未洽
而化難遠被其何以治天下乎古稱盛治者惟

translation_en:
…once the root is established, there is no difficulty in extending it to all under Heaven. There is good reason for the sage to begin his government here! Deepening devotion to those close at hand is the key to reaching those far away; holding to what is essential is the way to extend one's influence broadly. By examining what is given precedence, one can understand the essential character of government. Thus the sage perpetuates the brightness of Li, the trigram of fire, to illuminate all, responding to the yang force and spreading transforming influence as he rules the myriad states. He upholds the firmness of Qian, the trigram of Heaven, to decide with sole authority, rectifying his position and securing the Mandate as he governs all activity. In tending the age and responding to affairs so as to embrace and protect all under Heaven, he intends to spread the blessings of happiness and prosperity. In establishing settled attachments [?] and promulgating instruction so as to bestow benefits upon the people, he seeks to attain an enlightened and harmonious order. Could this have no starting point? That starting point is simply the Way of human relationships.

For the Way of human relationships lies in harmony among kin, and nothing takes precedence over strengthening familial bonds in transforming and ordering the people. The sage achieves order without attending individually to every being. The Way flourishes within the bonds formed by Heaven, and the constant human relationships are duly ordered, thereby setting right the foundation of all transformation. Affection is deepened toward one's kin, and the principles of human relationships are first cultivated, thereby establishing the standard for every affair of government. Through the unity of their common root, his kindness inspires trust: he extends the harmony that unites them, and from this proceeds benevolence toward the people and love for all creatures. Through the distinctions between their respective positions, principle establishes due order: he broadens the proper recognition of differences, applying this throughout the family, the state, and all within the Four Seas.

Thus, by fulfilling human relationships and deepening transforming influence, he nurtures the source from which timely action flows. Whether his measures are gradual or urgent, he naturally has ample means to carry them into effect. What are called rewarding merit, elevating the worthy, employing the capable, and preserving loving care are all priorities in the way of government; yet, in essentials, one must begin with the Way of human relationships. Thus the sage stands facing south, and all under Heaven is brought into great order. Otherwise, however earnestly one seeks good government, it has no foundation. If harmony has not been achieved among those nearby, transforming influence can hardly reach far away: how could one govern all under Heaven? Among those of antiquity celebrated for flourishing government, only…

translation_en:
…Yao and Shun. Their fostering of kinship and ordering of the splendid institutions were founded upon illustrious virtue and successive brilliance. Thus one’s own person is also the root of affection for one’s kin, and the source from which moral transformation spreads. To judge the governance of the realm, look to the household; to judge the governance of the household, look to the person. How true this is!

“Now, in antiquity, Heaven and Earth were harmonious and the four seasons properly ordered; the people possessed virtue and the five grains flourished.”

Li Zuan

Associate Examiner Chen, a Hanlin Compiler, comments: “The subtlety of their mutual dependence is something others have not brought out. He must have penetrated deeply into its mysteries.”

Associate Examiner Min, a Hanlin Compiler, comments: “The composition is dignified and its language richly elegant.”

Examiner Ouyang, a Hanlin Academician, comments: “Clear and fluent.”

Examiner Zhang, a Grand Secretary, comments: “The atmosphere of a flourishing age appears vividly before us.”

The worthy speaks of the harmonious response of the Three Powers in a flourishing age, revealing how music arises. How abundant was the transforming vital energy of high antiquity! When the Three Powers respond in harmony, surely music can be made! When Zixia answered Marquis Wen, did he not say: “Heaven has its place above, Earth its place below, and the people dwell between them: this is the Way of the Three Powers”? Without observing the abundance of resonance and response in antiquity, how could one understand the origins of music?

The four seasons depend on Heaven and Earth for their transformations. If Heaven and Earth are not harmonious, the workings of vital energy cease, and it is difficult to expect the seasons to proceed in their alternating courses. In antiquity, however, the primal unity was blended into a whole, and the clarity of Heaven and tranquillity of Earth established the enduring order displayed before us; the Supreme Ultimate brought all together, and ease and simplicity manifested…

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
無私之教天地順矣吾知主宰以職則流行不
愆其序奠位以正則代謝各適其常陰陽相感
而化生焉寒暑相推而歲成焉天地官而四時
因之以不忒也使非世道之隆天地且不順况
四時乎五穀以養民民之不德則咎徵感而欲
其蕃廡難矣惟夫古者純朴天固而大道以為
公沕穆風行而敦厚以成俗民有德矣將見協
氣嘉生栽培以茂其化太和瑞應美利以溥其
施豐穰而百室盈焉順成而八蜡通焉民平康
===
===
而五穀因之以用成也使非世道之盛民且不
德况五穀乎夫造化之和既妙無聲之體民德
所召又涵聲氣之元此樂作於大定而平心宣
化豈溺音所得同哉抑論萬古此天地萬古此
民人則應感之盛何獨於古為然惟天子建中
和之極則與天地四時合德合序成民以阜物
而天人之和應矣是故天人者作樂之原君身
者參贊之本

所召又涵聲氣之元此樂作於大定而平心宣

而天人之和應矣是故天人者作樂之原君身
者參贊之本
第貳場
punctuated:
無私之教。天地順矣，吾知主宰以職，則流行不愆其序；奠位以正，則代謝各適其常。陰陽相感而化生焉，寒暑相推而歲成焉。天地官，而四時因之以不忒也。使非世道之隆，天地且不順，况四時乎？五穀以養民，民之不德，則咎徵感，而欲其蕃廡難矣。惟夫古者純朴天固，而大道以為公；沕穆風行，而敦厚以成俗。民有德矣，將見協氣嘉生，栽培以茂其化；太和瑞應，美利以溥其施。豐穰而百室盈焉，順成而八蜡通焉。民平康，而五穀因之以用成也。使非世道之盛，民且不德，况五穀乎？夫造化之和，既妙無聲之體；民德所召，又涵聲氣之元。此樂作於大定，而平心宣化，豈溺音所得同哉？抑論萬古此天地，萬古此民人，則應感之盛，何獨於古為然？惟天子建中和之極，則與天地四時合德合序，成民以阜物，而天人之和應矣。是故天人者，作樂之原；君身者，參贊之本。

第貳場
translation_en:
…the teaching of impartiality. Heaven and Earth are in accord. I know that when the governing power fulfills its office, their operations do not depart from their proper sequence; when their positions are rightly established, their successive changes each follow their constant course. Yin and yang act upon one another, bringing things into being through transformation; cold and heat succeed one another, completing the year. Heaven and Earth discharge their offices, and consequently the four seasons do not err. Were the order of the age not flourishing, even Heaven and Earth would lack accord—how much more so the four seasons?

The five grains nourish the people. If the people lack virtue, signs of calamity arise in response, and it is difficult to expect the grains to flourish abundantly. In antiquity, however, simplicity was firmly rooted in people's Heaven-given nature, and the Great Way served the common good; a profound harmony spread like the wind, and sincerity and generosity formed the customs. The people possessed virtue. Thus one would see harmonious vital forces bringing forth fine growth, nurturing it so that its transformations flourished; auspicious responses to supreme harmony spreading benefits abundantly. Harvests were plentiful, and every household's stores were full; crops ripened in due season, and the year-end sacrifices to the eight agricultural spirits were all performed. The people enjoyed peace and well-being, and consequently the five grains came to maturity. Were the order of the age not flourishing, even the people would lack virtue—how much more could one expect the five grains to thrive?

The harmony of creation already embodies the subtle workings of a soundless substance; what the people's virtue calls forth also contains the wellspring of sound and vital force. This music arises amid great stability, bringing hearts into balance and spreading moral transformation. How could corrupting music compare with it? Yet throughout the ages Heaven and Earth remain the same, and throughout the ages the people remain the same: why, then, should such flourishing mutual responsiveness belong to antiquity alone? Only let the Son of Heaven establish the supreme standard of equilibrium and harmony: he will then accord in virtue with Heaven and Earth and in sequence with the four seasons, perfecting the people and making all things abundant, so that Heaven and humanity respond to one another in harmony. Thus Heaven and humanity are the source of the making of music, while the ruler's own person is the foundation for participating in and assisting the transforming work of Heaven and Earth.

translation_en:
Discourse

“The Sage’s Mind Is Inexhaustible”

You Lie

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhang, Acting Director: “The sage’s inexhaustible mind can be apprehended inwardly, but is difficult to exhaust in words. This composition describes it with subtlety and care; its language is refined and its meaning fully realized. Reading it leaves a lingering savor. It merits inclusion.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Zheng, Left Supervising Secretary: “The sage fully realizes benevolence, and thus his mind is naturally inexhaustible; fundamentally, no forced effort is involved. Through the principle of resting at ease in benevolence without departing from it, this composition elucidates the sage’s mind almost completely. Its author must have cultivated a profound inner understanding.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Liang, Examining Editor: “The sage’s mind, benevolent toward all under Heaven, cannot bear to yield to circumstances that prevent its fullest realization; hence it is inexhaustible. This composition fully brings this out and also comprehensively presents the meaning of the mutual admonition through which the rulers and ministers of Tang and Yu helped one another achieve perfection. Reading it inspires awe and admiration.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Yin, Compiler: “Benevolence is the human mind. The sage’s mind is pure in its benevolence; thus benevolence is inexhaustible, and his mind is likewise inexhaustible. This composition elucidates the matter so thoroughly that almost no hidden meaning remains. One can tell that its author has long devoted effort to this.”

Comment by Examiner Ouyang, Academician: “To say that the sage’s mind is pure in its benevolence and therefore inexhaustible shows a sound understanding of the sage.”

text:
無窮之心玩之有餘味矣可錄以式
聖人仁覆天下而未甞□乎其已能故自視常
未盡自視未盡斯其為盡仁者乎夫仁天地之
大德而性於人人所以體萬物而為天地之心

…the sage’s inexhaustible heart. Pondering it leaves a lingering savor. It may be selected as a model.

The sage’s benevolence embraces all under Heaven, yet he has never [?] what he has already been able to accomplish; thus he always regards himself as having fallen short. Is it not precisely this sense of falling short that makes him one who fully realizes benevolence? Benevolence is the great virtue of Heaven and Earth, endowed in human beings as their nature. Through it, human beings embody the myriad things and serve as the heart of Heaven and Earth. As a Way, it is supremely great yet supremely close at hand, supremely subtle yet supremely numinous. Embracing all and benefiting all, it extends throughout the world without any discoverable limit; vast and deep as a wellspring, it issues from the human heart without any discernible boundary. Thus, benefiting things may count as benevolence, but if even one thing remains unbenefited, one cannot yet speak of completeness. A single impartial and all-embracing thought may embody benevolence, but if even one thought interrupts it, one cannot yet speak of purity. The sage rests naturally in benevolence and never departs from it. Yet the world is so vast that he may not be able to benefit everyone without exception. He therefore always regards whatever his beneficence has not reached as a failure of completeness, and never regards his own undeviating benevolence as purity already attained. This is why Yao and Shun, whose influence flowed together with Heaven above and Earth below, still found it difficult to cultivate themselves so as to bring peace to the common people. Hence the saying: “The sage’s heart is inexhaustible.” Who but one of the utmost benevolence under Heaven could attain this?

Some say: “Whenever people exhaust their strength and dare not stop carelessly, it is because the undertaking is possible, yet they themselves have not mastered it; although they have not mastered it, they must do so. title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
盡舉而安之勢有所必不能豈聖人顧汲汲焉
必能之也噫聖人之於百姓豈敢曰勢不能盡
安遂委之於不必能邪人以天地萬物為體其
安百姓盖安其四體也委四體於不必盡安惟
不仁其身者能之仁者之心固宜有汲汲不懈
者矣則夫修之已者亦豈敢曰吾已盡已能而
不復有所進邪夫人以修已為易能易盡也盖
以身為已而未嘗於其感應者觀之也今夫視
聽言動之用喜怒好惡之情凡接物而應焉者
===
已也而莫非物也微物則惡所視聽而好惡喜
怒之哉親疎遠邇智愚貴賤與夫貧窮煢獨凡
對已而感焉者物也而莫非已也微已則惡覩
其為親疎與煢獨者哉故聖人之於天下視惟
明聽惟聰而休戚誠偽之隱靡所不周言忠信
行篤敬而順逆睽合之志靡所不通喜怒不遷
好惡無作而愛憎取舍之情靡所不同兹其修
之已也皆加乎民而安之者也其於百姓惇親
及疎篤近舉遠皆在所懷而各得其敘貴貴下

… to bring peace to every one of them: circumstances must place some things beyond one’s power. Would even a sage nevertheless strive anxiously to accomplish them? Ah! In dealing with the common people, how could a sage dare say that circumstances prevent him from bringing peace to all, and therefore abandon the task as something he need not accomplish? A person takes Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things as his own body. Bringing peace to the common people is thus bringing peace to his own four limbs. Only someone without benevolence toward his own person could abandon his limbs as things that need not all be brought to ease. The benevolent heart must indeed strive urgently and without rest. In cultivating himself, then, how could he dare say, “I have already done everything and accomplished all I can,” and cease making further progress?

People consider self-cultivation easy to accomplish and easy to complete because they identify the self with the individual body and have never examined it through its interactions and responses. Consider the operations of seeing, hearing, speaking, and acting, and the feelings of joy, anger, liking, and dislike. Whatever encounters things and responds to them is the self; yet none of it is apart from things. Without things, what would there be to see or hear, to like or dislike, or to feel joy or anger about? Those bound to us closely or loosely, those near or far, the wise and foolish, the eminent and humble, together with the impoverished and solitary—all that confronts the self and moves it belongs to the realm of things; yet none of it is apart from the self. Without the self, how could their being close or distant, or solitary, be perceived?

Thus, in his dealings with the world, the sage sees clearly and hears keenly, comprehending every hidden aspect of well-being and distress, sincerity and deceit. His words are loyal and trustworthy, his conduct earnest and reverent, and he understands every intention, whether compliant or contrary, estranged or harmonious. His joy and anger do not shift onto other objects, and his likes and dislikes do not arise arbitrarily; his feelings of love and aversion, acceptance and rejection, are shared with all. His cultivation of himself thus extends in every respect to the people and brings them peace. In dealing with the common people, he is generous toward his kin and extends his care to those less closely connected; he is devoted to those nearby and reaches out to those far away. text:
賤尊賢容衆皆在所愛而各得其辨老老幼幼
恤不辜矜無告皆在所慈而各得其所茲其安
之也皆出乎身而修焉者也故修己者修安民
之道於己百姓安而後己之分盡自修之事畢
矣聖人有見於感應之一也以為己之分無時
而可盡自修之事無時而可畢何也百姓之衆
惡能盡舉而全安之也夫天地之大也而萬物
有未生未育人不能無憾於天地聖人之大也
而百姓有未安人不能無望於聖人而聖人豈
===
能自安於其心哉昔者堯舜大聖人也其明德
以親民者盖至於萬邦協和而四方風動矣然
其訓迪庶官勸之勿壞與其所以慎修思永者
孳孳爾也盖舜之稱堯也謂舍己稽衆不虐無
告不廢困窮惟帝能之則知人安民之道矣而
禹又以為知人則哲安民則惠雖帝亦難能焉
豈非道未易盡而堯之所能者堯亦有難焉者
哉則舜之所以孳孳如堯又可知也矣故當時
之戒羣臣也曰弼違曰無面從曰汝為汝翼汝

…the lowly, honoring the worthy and embracing the multitude: all fall within his love, and each receives the distinctions appropriate to them. Treating the aged as elders and the young as children, caring for the innocent and pitying those with no one to appeal to: all fall within his compassion, and each finds a proper place. Thus, his bringing peace to them proceeds entirely from the cultivation of his own person. Accordingly, to cultivate oneself is to cultivate within oneself the Way of bringing peace to the people. Only when the common people are at peace is one’s own duty fulfilled and the work of self-cultivation complete. The sage perceives the unity of stimulus and response and holds that there is never a time when his duty can be exhausted, nor a time when the work of self-cultivation can be completed. Why? With so many common people, how could he encompass them all and bring complete peace to every one of them? Great as Heaven and Earth are, among the myriad things there are some not yet brought into being or nurtured; people cannot be without regret concerning Heaven and Earth. Great as the sage is, among the common people there are some not yet at peace; people cannot cease to have expectations of the sage. How, then, could the sage himself rest content in his heart?
In antiquity, Yao and Shun were great sages. Through illuminating their virtue and drawing the people close, they indeed attained harmony among the myriad states, and their influence stirred the four quarters like the wind. Yet they remained diligent in instructing and guiding the various officials, urging them not to let their work fall into ruin, and in carefully cultivating themselves with enduring consequences in mind. In praising Yao, Shun said that he set aside his own views and consulted the multitude, did not oppress those with no one to appeal to, and did not cast aside those in hardship and poverty: only the emperor could accomplish this. This was the Way of knowing people and bringing peace to the people. Yet Yu further held that knowing people required discernment and bringing peace to the people required beneficence, and that even the emperor found these difficult to accomplish. Was this not because the Way was not easily fulfilled in its entirety, and because even Yao found difficulty in what he was capable of accomplishing? We can therefore also understand why Shun was as diligent as Yao. 明汝聽羣臣之進戒也亦曰怠曰傲曰違道干
譽咈人從已喜起交修時幾交勅昌言交拜惴
惴焉若勉修其德而未能若經綸屯否而未底
其績者此豈不見天下理亂之形而故以為未
理不見已心危微之幾而故以為未盡哉心同
天運無有止足其視天下之大也阻飢之民豈
盡康食五品豈盡遜五刑豈盡措典禮豈盡叙
神人豈盡和蠻夷之猾夏者豈盡率服鳥獸草
木上下之物豈盡樂生則吾之所以明峻德於
===
天下者猶有未至而豈能泰然忘戒也夫堯舜
聖神與天合德其必不至如禹益諸臣所戒也
夫人知之矣然未能泰然忘戒也則惟諸臣知
之諸臣之克艱與君同心其不以無虞而忘自
儆也堯舜信之矣因而致儆其君之所或未儆
也亦惟堯舜能行之推堯舜之心即庶績盡凝
萬物咸若矣然所以制未亂之治者猶未可以
已也況天下之大有必不能盡慊其志者邪推
諸臣之心非不知帝德廣運萬邦作乂矣然所

夫堯舜聖神，與天合德，其必不至如禹益諸臣所戒也，夫人知之矣。然未能泰然忘戒也，則惟諸臣知之。諸臣之克艱，與君同心，其不以無虞而忘自儆也，堯舜信之矣。因而致儆其君之所或未儆也，亦惟堯舜能行之。
推堯舜之心，即庶績盡凝、萬物咸若矣，然所以制未亂之治者，猶未可以已也，況天下之大，有必不能盡慊其志者邪？推諸臣之心，非不知帝德廣運、萬邦作乂矣，然所
translation_en:
…your sight and your hearing.” When the assembled ministers offered admonitions, they likewise spoke of indolence, arrogance, departing from the Way to seek acclaim, and opposing others to follow one’s own inclinations. In mutual joy and encouragement to action, ruler and ministers cultivated one another; they admonished one another concerning every occasion and incipient development, and bowed to one another upon hearing excellent counsel. They remained apprehensive, as though striving to cultivate their virtue but still falling short, as though bringing order amid difficulty and stagnation but not yet accomplishing their work. Could this have been because they failed to perceive whether the realm was orderly or disordered, and therefore deliberately regarded it as not yet ordered, or failed to perceive the subtle stirrings of peril and refinement within their own hearts, and therefore deliberately regarded their efforts as incomplete? Their hearts moved with Heaven, never stopping or becoming satisfied. Looking upon the vast realm, they asked: Have all those afflicted by hunger obtained secure sustenance? Are the five human relationships all harmonious? Have the five punishments all been set aside? Are the established rites all properly ordered? Are spirits and human beings all in harmony? Have all the Man and Yi peoples who disturb the Chinese lands submitted? Do birds, beasts, plants, trees, and all beings above and below delight in life? If not, then my work of making lofty virtue manifest throughout the realm still falls short. How could I rest at ease and forget vigilance?
Yao and Shun were sagely and divine, their virtue united with Heaven’s. Everyone knew that they would surely never fall into the faults against which Yu, Yi, and the other ministers warned them. Yet only those ministers understood that they still could not rest at ease and forget vigilance. Yao and Shun trusted that their ministers could undertake difficult duties with hearts united with their ruler’s, and would not forget to caution themselves merely because no danger threatened. Accordingly, to give effect to warnings concerning matters about which their ruler might not yet be vigilant—this, too, only Yao and Shun could do.
If we consider the hearts of Yao and Shun, even supposing that every undertaking had been fully accomplished and all things were in accord, the means of securing order before disorder arose still could not be abandoned. How much more so in so vast a realm, where there would inevitably be matters that could not fully satisfy their aspirations! If we consider the hearts of the ministers, it was not that they failed to recognize that the sovereign’s virtue extended broadly and that the myriad states had become well governed. Yet that by which…

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
以致無斁之保者猶未可以已也况人心靡常
有未能必其無動於罔念者邪故唐虞之德光
被上下真如天地之化雖未能無一物之未生
未育然不害其為無不生育而其屈伸往來闔
闢變化則未嘗因物而有所加損蓋穆然常運
而不已也是聖人之心也聖人豈有特異于人
者哉亦曰純乎仁而已仁者心之德也人心虛
靈天地合德其真誠惻怛明昭不昧一夫不獲
惕焉恫瘝於厥躬而一念必謹戰戰焉若氷淵
===
之臨是心體本然聖人無以異乎衆人者也衆
人之異於聖人則自雜之也是故物我相形私
利相奪忿疾暴慢猜疑刻忌紛然交作故不自
見其過而常自覺其所能則其於人也寖見其
可惡而不盡見其可愛見我之愛人者無不至
而人之不蒙吾愛者為自絕而不知愛人之心
久矣其窮也矣然其始蓋亦善端之動而過焉
者意有所向忽而未察其究也浸淫固滯日入
於頗側而罔覺爾聖人純乎仁而不蔽於我者

利相奪忿疾慢猜疑刻忌紛然交作故不自
見其過而常自覺其所能則其於人也寖見其
可惡而不盡見其可愛見我之愛人者無不至
而人之不蒙吾愛者為自絶而不知愛人之心

於頗僻而罔覺爾聖人純乎仁而不敝於我者
punctuated:
以致無斁之保者，猶未可以已也。况人心靡常，有未能必其無動於罔念者邪？故唐虞之德，光被上下，真如天地之化，雖未能無一物之未生未育，然不害其為無不生育；而其屈伸往來、闔闢變化，則未嘗因物而有所加損，蓋穆然常運而不已也。是聖人之心也。聖人豈有特異于人者哉？亦曰純乎仁而已。仁者，心之德也。人心虛靈，天地合德，其真誠惻怛，明昭不昧，一夫不獲，惕焉恫瘝於厥躬；而一念必謹，戰戰焉若氷淵之臨。是心體本然，聖人無以異乎衆人者也。

衆人之異於聖人，則自雜之也。是故物我相形，私利相奪，忿疾暴慢、猜疑刻忌，紛然交作。故不自見其過，而常自覺其所能，則其於人也，寖見其可惡，而不盡見其可愛；見我之愛人者無不至，而人之不蒙吾愛者為自絕，而不知愛人之心，久矣其窮也矣。然其始，蓋亦善端之動而過焉者，意有所向，忽而未察；其究也，浸淫固滯，日入於頗側而罔覺爾。聖人純乎仁而不蔽於我者
translation_en:
…the means of securing unwearied protection must still not be abandoned. How much more so when the human heart is inconstant, and one cannot be certain that it will never be stirred into action in a lapse of mindfulness! Thus the virtue of Tang and Yu shone upon all above and below, truly resembling the transforming work of Heaven and Earth. Though there might still be some creature not yet brought forth or nurtured, this did not detract from their giving life and nurture to all. Their contraction and expansion, coming and going, closing and opening, and transformation were never increased or diminished on account of particular things. Rather, they moved constantly in silent harmony, without ceasing. Such is the heart of the sage. Does the sage possess anything uniquely different from other people? It is simply purity in benevolence. Benevolence is the virtue of the heart. The human heart is empty and numinous, its virtue consonant with Heaven and Earth. Its sincerity and compassion shine clearly, unobscured. If even one person fails to find his proper place, it takes alarm and feels his suffering as its own; it guards every thought, trembling as though treading on ice or standing above an abyss. This is the original condition of the heart’s essential substance, in which sages do not differ from ordinary people.

Ordinary people differ from sages because they themselves introduce impurities into it. Thus external things and the self are set against one another, private interests contend, and anger, resentment, violence, arrogance, suspicion, harshness, and jealousy arise together in confusion. Consequently, people fail to see their own faults, while remaining constantly aware of their abilities. In their dealings with others, they increasingly see what is hateful in them, without fully seeing what is lovable. They consider their own love for others complete in every respect, and regard those who do not receive it as having cut themselves off. They do not realize that their heart’s capacity to love others has long since been exhausted. Yet at the beginning, this too was probably an impulse arising from the sprouts of goodness that went too far: their intention turned in a particular direction, and through carelessness they failed to examine it. In the end, this gradually permeated them and became entrenched; day by day they slipped into partiality and deviation without realizing it. The sage is pure in benevolence and unobscured by the self…

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
也無蔽故常覺無我故常愛故不待熾然之過
而能密察其意向之萌兢兢業業日乾夕惕若
有迫乎其中以追及乎其前雖欲已之而不得
者盖不徒以己之未易盡百姓之不能盡安而
始汲汲若是也其常覺而常愛者無待於外也
故聖人之心非警之使無窮仁本無窮也修己
以敬之極也仁道不明外安民以修己者是內
非外而不知萬物之備於我外敬以安民者徇
外遺內而不知強恕之本諸心是皆未得夫精
===
一不二之道縱使作之不怠然有所舉者必有
所廢有所作者必未能恒而無輟即斃而後已
猶未足以語聖人無窮之心夫仁故也孔子曰
仁者人也親親為大故思修身不可以不事親
思事親不可以不知人事親者安民之始知人
者知仁者也雖然仁亦惡可易言者何也仁者
性之生理非有聲臭方體可求而執之者也無
體故無盡無可執故無為而成人之道也實天
之命也詩有之維天之命於穆不已盖曰天之

translation_en:
… Being unobscured, the sage is always aware; being without self, he always loves. Thus he does not wait for a fault to become glaring before closely examining the first stirrings of his intentions. Cautious and earnest, diligent by day and watchful at night, he seems impelled from within to catch up with what lies ahead; even if he wished to stop, he could not. It is surely not merely because self-cultivation is difficult to complete, or because the common people cannot all be brought to peace, that he begins to exert himself so urgently. His constant awareness and constant love depend on nothing external. Thus the sage’s heart is not made inexhaustible by keeping it on the alert: benevolence itself is inexhaustible. This is the culmination of cultivating oneself through reverence.

When the Way of benevolence is not understood, those who cultivate themselves while treating bringing peace to the people as something external affirm the inward and reject the outward, failing to understand that the myriad things are fully present within themselves. Those who seek to bring peace to the people while treating reverence as something external pursue the outward and neglect the inward, failing to understand that striving to treat others as oneself is rooted in the heart. Neither has grasped the Way of refinement and singleness, without division. Even if they act tirelessly, whenever they take up one thing they must abandon another; whatever they undertake, they cannot sustain it constantly without interruption. Even if they stop only at death, this is still insufficient to speak of the sage’s inexhaustible heart, for its inexhaustibility comes from benevolence.

Confucius said: “Benevolence is what makes us human; loving one’s kin is its greatest expression.” Thus, wishing to cultivate oneself, one cannot fail to serve one’s parents; wishing to serve one’s parents, one cannot fail to understand people. Serving one’s parents is the beginning of bringing peace to the people; understanding people is understanding benevolence. Yet how could benevolence be spoken of lightly? Why is this? Benevolence is the life-generating principle of human nature. It has no sound or smell, shape or substance that one could seek out and grasp. Having no bodily form, it has no limit; having nothing that can be grasped, it accomplishes things without deliberate action. It is the Way of humanity, and truly the mandate of Heaven. The Book of Odes says: “Heaven’s mandate—ah, how profound and unceasing!” This speaks of Heaven’s…

…that by which Heaven is Heaven. “Ah, how illustrious was the purity of King Wen’s virtue!” This speaks of that by which King Wen continued to illuminate his virtue and abode in reverence. Thus, knowing Heaven, one knows human nature; knowing human nature, one knows benevolence; knowing benevolence, one knows the Way, and thereby knows how to cultivate oneself. Therefore one is vigilant and cautious where nothing is seen, as though always seeing something; one is apprehensive where nothing is heard, yet never has any particular object of fear. This is the profound meaning of earnest reverence, the essential principle of cultivating oneself to bring peace to the people, and the reason the sage’s heart is pure in benevolence and inexhaustible.

漢承富挑師每歲殫勤於塞外晉遺戎乎
失徙隋耗國乎窮征雪恥除凶靡奇莫用
申和結好恥屈何功是以明君不黷武以
殘民夫惟上聖善修文而附衆苟非威德
之並茂庸覩柔化之克從自石晉棄燕雲
十六州之民俾屬犬羊之籍迄

考試官大學士張批：以典則之詞，寓經世之畧，真天下之俊才乎！錄之。

…in all their particulars, extending to more than a thousand words without repetition or confusion, as though the man himself were speaking. This could not have been achieved without familiarity with the affairs of that time. These are all your strategies for defending against the Rong [?].
Examiner and Grand Secretary Zhang comments: “In language worthy of a model, this conveys strategies for ordering the world. Truly an outstanding talent of the realm! Include it in the record.”
Your servant Song Qi, holding the designated office, respectfully submits the Discourse on Defending against the Rong that he has composed.
I humbly consider that, when the sage rules over the Chinese lands, he assuredly cultivates virtue, giving priority to plans for ordering his own realm. Since the Son of Heaven’s defenses lie among the barbarians of the four quarters, he must attend to military affairs as a strategy for suppressing disorder. Because fixed methods cannot readily be applied to controlling them, negligence and indolence must be guarded against in times of peace. Consider these Hu of the remote deserts: they have never been reached by our civilizing teachings. To govern them by not governing them, a flourishing dynasty employs only loose control; to impose upon them what ought not to be imposed, earlier ages accordingly demonstrated limited punitive warfare [?].
Qin relied upon its strength to extend its territory, and a commoner first raised rebellion east of the mountains. Han inherited wealth and provoked military conflict, exhausting its efforts beyond the frontier year after year. Jin left the Rong as a source of trouble through its failure to relocate them [?]; Sui depleted the state through unrestrained campaigning. Washing away humiliation and eliminating the wicked—these were empty boasts without practical effect. Renewing peace and forming friendly ties—what achievement was there in shameful submission? Thus an enlightened ruler does not indulge in warfare and thereby ruin his people. Only the highest sage excels in cultivating civil virtue and winning the allegiance of the multitude. title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
國家空滄兾數百里之地鞠為萑葦之墟旃
裘併混於中華冠帶孰分於左衽惟
藝祖始平天下急思恢復之圖暨
太宗再克河東深注安攘之畫雖中令之深謀
有監顧北陲之勝畧已隳百年見子河之
功可稱
雄斷萬里傳白池之捷獨擅
丕猷尋當景德之興乃有澶淵之役三驅縱寇
金繒反入於穹廬
===
六御要盟烽燧曾閒於斥堠蠢爾鴟張之既久
居然狡黠之益猖豕突誰攖操虚強以撼
中國狼求弗饜侈雄大而詫北荒頃緣羌
難之弗戡寝啓戎心之橫肆軍書互擾諸
州禍慘於枕骸誓約公渝二虜勢成於掎
角國步因之多故民財已竭征輸矧井陘
密邇乎敵防而河朔實當乎劇鎮增城列
戍山川之險隘雖包守塞防邊士馬之精
強竟秏苟不借籌於先畫何由税駕於後

punctuated: 國家空滄兾數百里之地，鞠為萑葦之墟。旃裘併混於中華，冠帶孰分於左衽？惟藝祖始平天下，急思恢復之圖；暨太宗再克河東，深注安攘之畫。雖中令之深謀有監，顧北陲之勝畧已隳。百年見子河之功，可稱雄斷；萬里傳白池之捷，獨擅丕猷。尋當景德之興，乃有澶淵之役。三驅縱寇，金繒反入於穹廬；六御要盟，烽燧曾閒於斥堠。蠢爾鴟張之既久，居然狡黠之益猖。豕突誰攖，操虚強以撼中國；狼求弗饜，侈雄大而詫北荒。頃緣羌難之弗戡，寝啓戎心之橫肆。軍書互擾諸州，禍慘於枕骸；誓約公渝，二虜勢成於掎角。國步因之多故，民財已竭征輸。矧井陘密邇乎敵防，而河朔實當乎劇鎮。增城列戍，山川之險隘雖包；守塞防邊，士馬之精強竟秏。苟不借籌於先畫，何由税駕於後
translation_en:
…under our dynasty, several hundred li of land around Cang and Ji lay empty, reduced entirely to a wilderness of reeds. Wearers of felt and fur mingled within the Central Lands: who could distinguish those wearing caps and sashes from those whose robes fastened on the left? When the founding ancestor first pacified All under Heaven, he urgently considered plans to recover the lost territory. When Taizong subsequently conquered Hedong, he devoted close attention to plans for securing the realm and repelling outsiders. Although the profound counsel of the Director of the Secretariat offered a warning [?], the strategy for victory on the northern frontier had already come to ruin. A hundred years later, the achievement at Zihe displayed heroic resolve; news of the victory at Baichi traveled ten thousand li, manifesting an unrivaled grand design. Then, with the opening of the Jingde era, came the campaign at Chanyuan. As in a hunt that drives game from only three sides, the enemy was allowed to escape, and gold and silk instead flowed into their domed tents. The imperial carriage was constrained to a sworn agreement, and for a time the beacon fires at the frontier watchposts fell idle.

Those benighted foes had long spread their wings like owls, and their cunning grew ever more rampant. Who could withstand their boar-like charges? With a hollow show of strength they shook the Central Kingdom. Insatiable in their wolf-like demands, they vaunted their might and boasted throughout the northern wastes. Recently, because the Qiang troubles remained unsuppressed, the enemy’s ambitions gradually became unrestrained. Military dispatches threw the various prefectures into turmoil; the calamity was so grievous that the dead lay pillowed upon one another’s bones. Sworn agreements were openly violated, and the two enemy peoples established positions from which to attack us on two sides. The fortunes of the state consequently suffered many troubles, while the people’s wealth was already exhausted by levies and deliveries of supplies. Moreover, Jingxing lies very close to the enemy’s defenses, and Heshuo is indeed a crucial military command. Though enlarged walls and deployed garrisons encompass the mountain and river passes, guarding the fortresses and defending the frontier have ultimately depleted the strength of our picked troops and horses. Unless we devise plans beforehand, how can we bring our journey to rest amid the subsequent…

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
艱伏念臣章句菲材詩書素業昔秉筆以
承
制既慙奉職之弗堪茲分符以課功庸免曠官
之益甚馳驅一路恐無裨補於秋毫出入
三年敢愛糜捐於暮齒昔賈誼憤匈奴苦
漢遂陳三表五餌之謀洎晁錯患謫戍危
秦因列四里十連之制雖陋如班固詆之
為疎而明若孝文用之即效爰取歲時之
更歷兼裒日夜之講求耳目得諸見聞既
臚陳而可指首尾識其情狀豈詮述之無
稽是因括論以成篇欲使循文而責實託
更端於客難反覆以昭利害之原借形喻
於物情校量而得短長之數言無文而可
采計施今而易行
廟議弘深豈可令
國威之不振忠思廣集將無惜虜勢之莫支
茲蓋伏遇

艱。伏念臣章句菲材，詩書素業。昔秉筆以承制，既慙奉職之弗堪；茲分符以課功，庸免曠官之益甚？馳驅一路，恐無裨補於秋毫；出入三年，敢愛糜捐於暮齒？昔賈誼憤匈奴苦漢，遂陳三表五餌之謀；洎晁錯患謫戍危秦，因列四里十連之制。雖陋如班固，詆之為疎，而明若孝文，用之即效。爰取歲時之更歷，兼裒日夜之講求。耳目得諸見聞，既臚陳而可指；首尾識其情狀，豈詮述之無稽？是因括論以成篇，欲使循文而責實。託更端於客難，反覆以昭利害之原；借形喻於物情，校量而得短長之數。言無文而可采，計施今而易行。廟議弘深，豈可令國威之不振？忠思廣集，將無惜虜勢之莫支？

translation_en:
…difficulties. I humbly reflect that your servant possesses scant talent for textual learning, with the Odes and Documents as my customary occupation. Formerly, when I wielded the brush in obedience to imperial commands, I already felt ashamed of my inability to discharge my duties. Now, entrusted with a tally of office and charged with achieving results, how can I avoid still graver neglect of my post? As I travel throughout this circuit, I fear that I contribute not the slightest benefit; after three years of service, how could I begrudge sacrificing myself in my declining years?
Formerly, Jia Yi, indignant that the Xiongnu were afflicting the Han, presented his plan of the “three demonstrations and five baits.” Later, Chao Cuo, concerned that banishment to frontier garrison service had imperiled the Qin, set out his system of four neighborhood units and ten associated groups. Although someone as limited in understanding as Ban Gu disparaged these proposals as impractical, a ruler as enlightened as Emperor Xiaowen put them into practice with immediate results.
Accordingly, I have drawn upon the experience accumulated over the years and gathered together what I have investigated day and night. What my eyes and ears have apprehended can be set forth in detail and specifically identified; since I understand the circumstances from beginning to end, how could my exposition lack a foundation? Thus I have assembled my arguments into an essay, wishing its words to provide a basis for demanding practical results. Through objections voiced by an imagined guest, I introduce new topics, examining them repeatedly to illuminate the sources of benefit and harm. Drawing illustrative analogies from the circumstances of things, I weigh and compare them to determine their relative strengths and weaknesses. My words lack ornament but deserve consideration; my plans can readily be put into practice today. With court deliberations so comprehensive and profound, how could the empire’s prestige be allowed to remain unasserted? With loyal counsel gathered so widely, surely there need be no regret that the enemy’s power cannot hold out [?].
Now, indeed, I humbly have the good fortune to serve under 〇〇〇〇…

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
恭儉宜民
寬和得衆駿業承
祖宗之盛式康庶政之惟熙
鴻仁協上下之休允底烝民於有乂納諫并
容乎訐直信賢不惑以讒邪三事無偏將
相得承於獨任四方有敗
聰明毎徹於先知顧
黼扆宵旰之紆思在椎結叛回之阻化邕渠
昨殄南徼幸平夏孽今遺西陲豈靖乃耶
===
律一姓起沙漠幾二百年即靺鞨諸酋入
服屬已數十國自濫
中朝之幣予益空大内之帑藏虎北諸防既
失險以成虜據關南十縣復齎償而饋寇
資索求快遂於探囊搖脅動輕於振槁念
諸臣左計已持倒柄之泰阿迹此虜驕心
方掠縱置之脫兎毀要言於宿好甘仇寇
之偽臣羌狄何親必中畔而復其隙舅甥
相絆聊暫連以飽所私况狠弟貪惏之方

punctuated: 恭儉宜民，寬和得衆，駿業承祖宗之盛，式康庶政之惟熙。鴻仁協上下之休，允底烝民於有乂。納諫并容乎訐直，信賢不惑以讒邪。三事無偏，將相得承於獨任；四方有敗，聰明毎徹於先知。顧黼扆宵旰之紆思，在椎結叛回之阻化。邕渠昨殄，南徼幸平；夏孽今遺，西陲豈靖？乃耶律一姓起沙漠，幾二百年；即靺鞨諸酋入服屬，已數十國。自濫中朝之幣予，益空大内之帑藏。虎北諸防既失險以成虜據，關南十縣復齎償而饋寇資。索求快遂於探囊，搖脅動輕於振槁。念諸臣左計，已持倒柄之泰阿；迹此虜驕心，方掠縱置之脫兎。毀要言於宿好，甘仇寇之偽臣。羌狄何親？必中畔而復其隙。舅甥相絆，聊暫連以飽所私。况狠弟貪惏之方
translation_en:
…Reverent and frugal, you benefit the people; generous and harmonious, you win the multitude. Your great undertaking continues the flourishing achievements of your ancestors, bringing settled order to the many affairs of government. Your vast benevolence unites the blessings enjoyed by high and low, truly bringing all the people under orderly rule. In accepting remonstrance, you tolerate even blunt accusations; in trusting the worthy, you remain undeceived by malicious slander. The Three Dukes show no partiality, and generals and chief ministers receive your undivided trust. When failures occur anywhere in the realm, your perceptive intelligence invariably apprehends them in advance. Yet what occupies your thoughts behind the imperial screen, from before dawn until late at night, is the resistance to civilizing influence of those rebellious people with mallet-shaped topknots. The rebel chief of Yong was recently destroyed, and the southern frontier is fortunately pacified; but remnants of Xia survive today—how can the western frontier be at peace?

Now the Yelü clan arose in the desert nearly two hundred years ago. Even among the chiefs of the Mohe, several dozen states have already submitted to its authority. Since excessive gifts of silk began to be granted by the central court, the treasury within the palace has been increasingly depleted. The defenses north of Hu [?] have already lost their strategic advantages and become enemy strongholds; the ten counties south of the passes have, moreover, supplied compensation [?], furnishing resources to the enemy. Their demands are satisfied as readily as reaching into a purse; they resort to threats and intimidation as easily as shaking dry stalks. Consider the mistaken calculations of our ministers: they already hold the sword Tai’a with its hilt turned toward the enemy. Judging by these enemies’ arrogant intentions, they are now plundering like a hare released to run free [?]. They break solemn pledges made in longstanding friendship and willingly become sham vassals of our foes [?]. What affection binds the Qiang and Di? They will surely betray one another midway and renew their breach. Bound together as maternal uncle and nephew, they merely maintain a temporary alliance to satisfy their private desires. Moreover, the ruthless younger brother’s greed is just now…

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
恣而大臣屏輔之未周鼠首以觀豈無中
說尉陀之輩蝟毛而奮何止新羅靺鞨之
人觀其中外之相猜加以華番之交亂兵
有五間操施必
仁聖而後能國無兩強爭裂豈懦庸之可制事
不圖於先試功何冀其有成欲振武以示
威在養馬練兵之弗怠思設竒而取勝惟
環車擾騎之兼長要之因外服以輯內寧
豈得惜一勞而忘永佚三空早實先占廐
===
廩之充盈五蠧速除盍究公私之匱乏由
因循之弊積故怯弱之患滋任一則權不
分莫若廢監軍而專任將威伸則和可守
大宜省歲幣而益治兵將求我志之克揚
必謹敵来之有備擁堅却銳立畫守於春
徂夏入之交批亢擣虛奮麾征於我出彼
歸之會離二虜之援於始合作三軍之氣
於方衰不畏彼侵患所以来其侵毋幸敵
亂恃已之不可亂安危在計豈容勦襲於

歸之會離二虜之援於始合作三軍之氣
於方衰不畏彼侵患所以來其侵毋幸敵
亂恃已之不可亂安危在計豈容勦襲於
punctuated: 恣，而大臣屏輔之未周，鼠首以觀，豈無中說、尉陀之輩？蝟毛而奮，何止新羅、靺鞨之人？觀其中外之相猜，加以華番之交亂，兵有五間，操施必仁聖而後能；國無兩強，爭裂豈懦庸之可制？事不圖於先，試功何冀其有成？欲振武以示威，在養馬練兵之弗怠；思設竒而取勝，惟環車擾騎之兼長。要之，因外服以輯內寧，豈得惜一勞而忘永佚？三空早實，先占廐廩之充盈；五蠧速除，盍究公私之匱乏？由因循之弊積，故怯弱之患滋。任一則權不分，莫若廢監軍而專任將；威伸則和可守，大宜省歲幣而益治兵。將求我志之克揚，必謹敵来之有備。擁堅却銳，立畫守於春徂夏入之交；批亢擣虛，奮麾征於我出彼歸之會。離二虜之援於始合，作三軍之氣於方衰。不畏彼侵，患所以来其侵；毋幸敵亂，恃已之不可亂。安危在計，豈容勦襲於

Among those who watch hesitantly like a mouse peering out, could there be none like Zhong Yue [?] or Commandant Tuo? Those who rise like a hedgehog’s bristling spines would hardly be limited to the people of Xinluo and Mohe. Consider the mutual suspicion between those within and those outside, compounded by turmoil involving Chinese and foreign peoples alike. Warfare employs five kinds of spies, but only a humane and sagely ruler can put them to use. A state cannot accommodate two powerful rivals: how could the timid and mediocre control their struggle and division? Unless affairs are planned beforehand, how can one hope to succeed when putting one’s abilities to the test? To display military might and inspire awe requires unremitting attention to raising horses and training troops. To devise unexpected tactics and secure victory requires proficiency both in encircling with chariots and in harassing with cavalry [?]. In essence, external submission should secure internal peace. How could one begrudge a single exertion and forget lasting ease? Remedy the three depletions early, first ensuring that stables and granaries are full; eliminate the five vermin promptly—should we not investigate the shortages in public and private resources? Accumulated abuses born of habitual neglect have allowed timidity and weakness to spread. When responsibility is unified, authority is not divided: nothing would be better than abolishing army supervisors and entrusting command exclusively to generals. When our might is asserted, peace can be maintained: we should certainly reduce the annual tribute payments and devote greater effort to preparing our forces. To ensure that our purposes prevail, we must take care to be ready for the enemy’s arrival. Hold firm defenses and repel their sharp assault, promptly planning defensive measures [?] at the transition from departing spring to approaching summer. Strike at vital points and attack undefended places, vigorously directing campaigns when our advance coincides with their withdrawal. Sever the mutual support of the two enemy peoples just as they begin to unite; rouse the spirit of our armies just as it begins to flag. Do not fear their invasion; be concerned about what invites it. Do not count on disorder among the enemy; rely on our own immunity to disorder. 故談。勝敗無常，可以監觀於往事。臣才不稱位，力靡逮心。久悉咨詢，方畧足陳於指掌；叨承任使，艱憂何止於恫身？恐逡巡指畫之莫施，即緩急韜籌之焉濟？兵難遥度，時違則變，不可預期；事貴權宜，勢易則謀，何所卒用？仰効芻蕘千慮之得，冀抒葵藿一念之忠。伏惟采之廷猷，酌以聖算。九重决勝，録書生樽俎之長；千里折衝，舒將士鼓鼙之氣。舉事必推乎天道，考功罔奪於人時。兵出萬全，必致两階之舞羽；治熈一統，允歌四海之建櫜。臣無任瞻天仰聖、激切屏營之至，謹以《禦戎論》七篇隨表上進以聞。

第叁塲
策五道
translation_en:
… stale arguments. Victory and defeat are inconstant; past events offer lessons for scrutiny. Your servant’s talents do not match his office, and his strength falls short of his intentions. Long familiar with consultations, I can set forth strategies as plainly as if pointing to my palm. Yet, unworthily entrusted with service, how could my anxieties over these difficulties be confined to concern for myself? I fear that hesitation will prevent my plans from being put into effect; in an emergency, what help could my military schemes then provide? Warfare is difficult to assess from afar: when circumstances depart from expectations, changes cannot be foreseen. Affairs require expedient judgment: when the situation changes, what use will a plan ultimately have? I humbly offer the one sound thought among a thousand reflections of a woodcutter or grass-gatherer, hoping to express the single-minded loyalty of the mallow that turns toward the sun.

I humbly beg Your Majesty to incorporate this into the court’s deliberations and weigh it with your sagely calculations. Determining victory from within the imperial palace, recognize a scholar’s ability to prevail at the ceremonial banquet table; repelling the enemy a thousand li away, give scope to the martial spirit of officers and soldiers stirred by their drums. In undertaking affairs, always follow the Way of Heaven; in assessing accomplishments, do not disregard the opportunities afforded by human affairs. Dispatching troops with complete assurance of success will surely bring about the dance with feathered plumes between the two stairways—a peaceful submission. With flourishing government and unified rule, all within the Four Seas may truly sing of weapons returned to their cases [?]. Your servant, looking up to Heaven and reverently toward Your Sageliness, cannot contain his intense emotion and trembling apprehension. I respectfully submit herewith, accompanying this memorial, the seven essays of Discourses on Resisting the Rong (Yu Rong Lun), for Your Majesty’s hearing.

Third Session
Five Policy Questions

First Policy Question
Fu Xiaqi

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhang, Acting Bureau Director: These two books are works that our imperial ancestors prepared for those who serve as subjects throughout all generations. You have drawn out their meaning and expounded it from various angles; your loyalty and sincerity overflow beyond your words. Could this be because you have taken the sagely instructions to heart and gained insight from them?

Comment by Associate Examiner Zheng, Left Supervising Secretary: Nowhere is the meaning of a subject’s service to his ruler more fully set forth than in these two books. You have answered point by point, omitting nothing, and elucidated our imperial ancestors’ authoritative teachings and admonitions as clearly as if pointing to something in your palm. In depth and breadth of understanding and in extensive learning and ability, none could surpass you.

Comment by Associate Examiner Liang, Examining Editor: The way of the minister, past and present, is recorded in these two books. Through them our imperial ancestors bequeathed instruction to all officials and established a standard for all generations. You have expounded their teachings without omission, speaking earnestly of the loyalty with which a subject serves his ruler. Are you not one who has been steeped in the sagely transforming influence and reflects on how to repay it? A worthy scholar! A worthy scholar!

Comment by Associate Examiner Yin, Compiler: Our imperial ancestors compiled these two books to bequeath models and warnings to subjects for all generations. You have deeply explored their purport and meaning and set them forth in detail; moreover, your words reveal an ardent loyalty that you wish to put into practice. Judging from your aspirations, what you establish and exemplify in the future will surely exert a stirring influence upon your age.

Comment by Examiner Ouyang, Academician: The essential purport of the two books is fully recorded …

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
御製二序中為教至明切矣策問正欲諸士子知自辨自鑒得
事君之道因子之言以占其志殆誦繹
聖訓而有槩於中者乎
考試官大學士張批賢姦傳與臣鑒二書我
祖宗所以教天下人臣事君之義至詳切也子能敷繹其說而援證
有據其亦知為臣之道者他日立朝必有可觀矣
得士若此良以自慶
人君以人立政莫先擇臣之術人臣以身
任事莫急徇君之義術不先於擇臣是以
===
失委政之明義不急於徇君是以忘致身
之忠夫惟明君辨邪正於幾微以施擇臣
之術故能有所察於下而臣得自效天下
之政可立矣賢臣推得失於事理以致徇
君之義故能有所信於上而君莫之疑天
下之事可任矣此我
太祖高皇帝賢姦傳之纂
宣宗章皇帝臣鑒之錄雖專以訓臣義亦兼以
明君術也臣嘗仰讀

punctuated:
御製二序中，為教至明切矣。策問正欲諸士子知自辨、自鑒，得事君之道。因子之言以占其志，殆誦繹聖訓而有槩於中者乎？
考試官大學士張批：《賢姦傳》與《臣鑒》二書，我祖宗所以教天下人臣事君之義，至詳切也。子能敷繹其說，而援證有據，其亦知為臣之道者。他日立朝，必有可觀矣。得士若此，良以自慶。
人君以人立政，莫先擇臣之術；人臣以身任事，莫急徇君之義。術不先於擇臣，是以失委政之明；義不急於徇君，是以忘致身之忠。夫惟明君辨邪正於幾微，以施擇臣之術，故能有所察於下，而臣得自效，天下之政可立矣。賢臣推得失於事理，以致徇君之義，故能有所信於上，而君莫之疑，天下之事可任矣。此我太祖高皇帝《賢姦傳》之纂、宣宗章皇帝《臣鑒》之錄，雖專以訓臣義，亦兼以明君術也。臣嘗仰讀
translation_en:
…in the two imperially composed prefaces, whose instruction is exceptionally clear and pointed. The policy question expressly seeks to make the candidates understand how to distinguish right from wrong for themselves and examine themselves, thereby grasping the way to serve their sovereign. Judging your aspirations from your words, have you not recited and pondered the imperial teachings and been deeply moved within?
Examiner Zhang, Grand Secretary, comments: The two books, Biographies of the Worthy and the Treacherous (Xianjian zhuan) and Mirror for Ministers (Chen jian), are the means by which our imperial ancestors taught ministers throughout the realm their duty in serving their sovereign. Their instruction is exceptionally detailed and pointed. You can expound their teachings and support your citations with sound evidence; you too understand the way of being a minister. When you take your place at court in the future, you will surely have noteworthy achievements. To obtain a scholar such as you is truly cause for congratulating ourselves.
A ruler establishes government through the people he employs: nothing takes precedence over the art of selecting ministers. A minister undertakes affairs through his own person: no duty is more urgent than devotion to his sovereign. If the ruler’s art does not give priority to selecting ministers, he loses discernment in entrusting government to others; if the minister’s duty does not give urgency to devotion to his sovereign, he forgets the loyalty that requires him to dedicate himself fully. Only an enlightened ruler distinguishes the wicked from the upright in the subtlest signs and thereby exercises the art of selecting ministers. Thus he can discern the qualities of those below him, and his ministers can demonstrate their abilities; government throughout the realm can then be established. A worthy minister examines what is gained and lost in light of the principles governing affairs, thereby fulfilling his duty of devotion to his sovereign. Thus he can win the trust of his superior, and the ruler has no doubts about him; the affairs of the realm can then be undertaken. This is why our Emperor Taizu Gao’s compilation of Biographies of the Worthy and the Treacherous and Emperor Xuanzong Zhang’s compilation of Mirror for Ministers, though devoted specifically to teaching the duties of ministers, also elucidate the arts of rulership. Your servant has reverently read…

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
聖製諸序而竊敢繹其義知君臣之道必相待
而後成不可以獨競焉則二書其可為萬
世君臣之法詔矣請因執事之問究悉其
愚夫人君能以人立政不知擇臣之術不
可以言明人臣能以身任事不知徇君之
義不可以語忠是故古之明君之擇臣也
因能而授之官辨材而處之任夷能典禮
不咨以治樂契能敷教不勑以明刑開心
以受其道平志以入其謀懽然如父子之
===
相得而不可間翕然如身首之相應而無
所疆是以心志通孚之有素而意氣感合
之能常即有大姦慝動於其側則聞其聲
有以推其形觀其表有以識其裏蓋所以
用其明者審矣是故君子有所效以盡其
材小人有所懼而不得為姦愚所謂辨邪
正於幾微以施擇臣之術者此也是君之
所當察也古之人臣奮勞而不知有身竭
忠而不知有家父殛而當罪不敢以親懟

===
所疆是以心志通乎之有素而意氣感合
之能常即有大姦慝動於其側則聞其聲
有以推其形觀其表有以識其裏蓋所以
用其明者審矣是故君子有所效以盡其
材小人有所懼而不得爲姦愚所謂辨邪
正於幾微以施擇臣之術者此也是君之
所當察也古之人臣奮勞而不知有身竭
忠而不知有家父殛而當罪不敢以親懟
punctuated:
聖製諸序，而竊敢繹其義，知君臣之道必相待而後成，不可以獨競焉。則二書其可為萬世君臣之法詔矣。請因執事之問，究悉其愚。
夫人君能以人立政，不知擇臣之術，不可以言明；人臣能以身任事，不知徇君之義，不可以語忠。是故古之明君之擇臣也，因能而授之官，辨材而處之任。夷能典禮，不咨以治樂；契能敷教，不勑以明刑。開心以受其道，平志以入其謀，懽然如父子之相得而不可間，翕然如身首之相應而無所疆。是以心志通孚之有素，而意氣感合之能常。即有大姦慝動於其側，則聞其聲有以推其形，觀其表有以識其裏，蓋所以用其明者審矣。是故君子有所效以盡其材，小人有所懼而不得為姦。愚所謂辨邪正於幾微以施擇臣之術者，此也。是君之所當察也。
古之人臣，奮勞而不知有身，竭忠而不知有家。父殛而當罪，不敢以親懟
translation_en:
…the imperially composed prefaces, and I have humbly ventured to unfold their meaning. I understand that the way of ruler and minister can be fulfilled only through their mutual dependence; neither can accomplish it alone. These two books may thus serve as exemplary injunctions [?] for rulers and ministers for ten thousand generations. Allow me, in response to your question, to set forth my humble understanding in full.
A ruler may establish government through the men he employs, but unless he understands the art of selecting ministers, he cannot be called discerning. A minister may personally undertake affairs, but unless he understands the duty of serving his ruler with devotion, he cannot be called loyal. Thus, when discerning rulers of antiquity selected ministers, they conferred offices according to ability and assigned responsibilities after distinguishing their talents. Yi could oversee ritual, so they did not consult him about administering music; Xie could spread moral instruction, so they did not command him to make punishments clear. They opened their hearts to receive their ministers’ principles and quieted their own intentions to admit their counsel. Their joyful accord resembled that of father and son, admitting no estrangement; their harmony resembled the coordination of body and head, knowing no bounds. Consequently, mutual trust between their hearts and purposes was long established, and the sympathetic accord of their dispositions could endure. Even if a deeply treacherous person began to act at their side, they could infer his true character from hearing his words and recognize his inner nature by observing his outward appearance. Such was the care with which they exercised their discernment. Thus, gentlemen had opportunities to offer service and fully employ their talents, while petty men had cause for fear and could not practice treachery. This is what I humbly mean by distinguishing the wicked from the upright in the slightest signs, thereby exercising the art of selecting ministers. This is what a ruler ought to scrutinize.
Ministers of antiquity labored strenuously without a thought for themselves and exhausted their loyalty without a thought for their families. When a father was put to death and the punishment fitted his crime, they did not dare harbor resentment on account of kinship…

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
也讎舉而合公不敢以私嫉也分定而無
所陵志協而無所忌位以讓叙如五官相
使而不争業以和成如四時相宣而不悖
是以材智攄於殫究而職業成於儆恪即
有大變患臨於其前則可隕其身而不可
詘其節可奪其位而不可易其志盖所以
篤其忠者素矣是故投之以負扆六尺之
託而不危懾之以横分九死之禍而不畏
愚所謂推得失於事理以急殉君之義者
===
此也是臣之所當厲也夫君之於臣孰不
欲擇之顧擇之有術莫要於其始也其始
何也邪正之幾微是也不審於幾微則雖
有擇臣之明其邪正無由辨矣臣之於君
孰不思殉之顧殉之有義莫難於其終也
其終何也成敗之事理是也不觀於事理
則雖有殉君之忠其得失無由論矣孟子
曰有事君人者事是君則為容悅者也有
安社稷臣者以安社稷為悅者也後之言

曰有事君人者事是君則爲容悅者也有

punctuated:
也。讎舉而合公，不敢以私嫉也。分定而無所陵，志協而無所忌，位以讓叙，如五官相使而不争；業以和成，如四時相宣而不悖。是以材智攄於殫究，而職業成於儆恪。即有大變患臨於其前，則可隕其身而不可詘其節，可奪其位而不可易其志，盖所以篤其忠者素矣。是故投之以負扆六尺之託而不危，懾之以横分九死之禍而不畏。愚所謂推得失於事理，以急殉君之義者，此也。是臣之所當厲也。
夫君之於臣，孰不欲擇之？顧擇之有術，莫要於其始也。其始何也？邪正之幾微是也。不審於幾微，則雖有擇臣之明，其邪正無由辨矣。臣之於君，孰不思殉之？顧殉之有義，莫難於其終也。其終何也？成敗之事理是也。不觀於事理，則雖有殉君之忠，其得失無由論矣。孟子曰：「有事君人者，事是君則為容悅者也；有安社稷臣者，以安社稷為悅者也。」後之言
translation_en:
…. When an enemy is recommended for office in accordance with the public good, they dare not resent him out of private animosity. With their respective duties settled, they do not encroach upon one another; with their purposes aligned, they harbor no mutual suspicion. Their positions are ordered through deference, like the five offices serving one another without contention; their work is accomplished through harmony, like the four seasons furthering one another without conflict. Thus their talents and intelligence find full expression in exhaustive inquiry, and their official duties are accomplished through vigilance and respect. Even if great upheaval or calamity confronts them, their lives may be destroyed, but their integrity cannot be bent; their positions may be taken away, but their resolve cannot be altered. This is because their loyalty has long been firmly cultivated. Hence, when entrusted with a young sovereign who sits before the imperial screen, they do not imperil him; when threatened with violent dismemberment [?] and a hundred deaths, they feel no fear. This is what I mean by weighing right and wrong according to the principles underlying affairs, and giving priority to the duty of sacrificing oneself for one’s ruler. This is what ministers should strive to fulfill.
What ruler does not wish to choose his ministers carefully? Yet choosing them requires a method, and nothing matters more than the beginning. What is this beginning? The barely perceptible signs of wickedness and uprightness. Unless these subtle signs are scrutinized, even a ruler with the discernment to select ministers will have no means of distinguishing the wicked from the upright. What minister does not think of sacrificing himself for his ruler? Yet such sacrifice must accord with righteousness, and nothing is more difficult than carrying it through to the end. What is this end? The principles underlying success and failure in affairs. Unless these principles are examined, even a minister possessing the loyalty to sacrifice himself for his ruler will have no means of judging whether his conduct is right or wrong. Mencius said: “There are men who serve a ruler merely to ingratiate themselves with him and please him. There are ministers who secure the altars of soil and grain, and take pleasure in securing them.” Later commentators …

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
者乃曰天下有權臣有重臣二者其迹相
似而實不類夫權臣所為重臣之所深疾
重臣所取權臣之所不顧也故權臣天下
不可一日有而重臣天下不可一日無也
甚哉有味乎其言也由今觀之權臣内固
其君之心而外竊其威柄以予奪天下非
即孟子之所謂容悅事君者邪我
聖祖所傳之姦臣與臣鑒所載田蚡而下七十
有餘人者固皆其類也此惡可為戒者也
===
重臣内引其君於道而外謹其法制以齊
整百司非即孟子之所謂安社稷之臣者
邪我
聖祖所傳之賢臣與臣鑒所載子產而下二百
有餘人者固皆其類也此善可為法者也
以愚觀之歷代人臣賢姦之辨雖已大備
於二書然夷考
二聖序列之意所以示章癉於既往垂法戒於
方來盖其微哉不可以不詳也執事乃欲

不可一日有而重臣天下不可一日無也
甚哉有味乎其言也由今觀之權臣內固
其君之心而外竊其威柄以子奪天下非

有餘人者固皆其類也此惡可爲戒者也
===
重臣內引其君於道而外謹其法制以齊

邪我
聖祖所傳之賢臣與臣鑑所載子產而下二百
有餘人者固皆其類也此善可爲法者也
以愚觀之歷代人臣賢姦之辨雖已大備
於二書然夷考
二聖序列之意所以示章癉於既往垂法戒於
方來蓋其微哉不可以不詳也孰事乃欲
punctuated:
者乃曰：「天下有權臣，有重臣，二者其迹相似而實不類。夫權臣所為，重臣之所深疾；重臣所取，權臣之所不顧也。故權臣，天下不可一日有；而重臣，天下不可一日無也。」甚哉，有味乎其言也！由今觀之，權臣内固其君之心，而外竊其威柄以予奪天下，非即孟子之所謂容悅事君者邪？我聖祖所傳之姦臣，與《臣鑒》所載田蚡而下七十有餘人者，固皆其類也。此惡可為戒者也。

重臣内引其君於道，而外謹其法制以齊整百司，非即孟子之所謂安社稷之臣者邪？我聖祖所傳之賢臣，與《臣鑒》所載子產而下二百有餘人者，固皆其類也。此善可為法者也。

以愚觀之，歷代人臣賢姦之辨，雖已大備於二書，然夷考二聖序列之意，所以示章癉於既往，垂法戒於方來，盖其微哉！不可以不詳也。執事乃欲
translation_en:
…said: “There are ministers who usurp power, and there are ministers of weight. Their outward conduct may appear similar, but in substance they belong to different kinds. What usurping ministers do, ministers of weight deeply detest; what ministers of weight choose, usurping ministers disregard. Thus, the realm cannot tolerate usurping ministers for even a single day, yet cannot do without ministers of weight for even a single day.” How profound and full of meaning these words are! Viewed from the present, usurping ministers secure their hold upon their ruler’s heart within the court, while outside it they steal his authority to grant and withhold throughout the realm. Are these not precisely those whom Mengzi described as serving their ruler by accommodating and pleasing him? The treacherous ministers whose lives our Sagely Founder recounted, together with the more than seventy men beginning with Tian Fen recorded in the Mirror for Ministers (Chen jian), all belong to this category. These are examples of evil that can serve as warnings.

Ministers of weight guide their ruler toward the Way within the court, while outside it they uphold his laws and institutions with care, bringing order to all the offices. Are these not precisely those whom Mengzi described as ministers who secure the altars of soil and grain—that is, the state? The worthy ministers whose lives our Sagely Founder recounted, together with the more than two hundred men beginning with Zichan recorded in the Mirror for Ministers, all belong to this category. These are examples of goodness that can serve as models.

In my humble view, although the distinction between worthy and treacherous ministers through successive dynasties is already fully set out in these two books, a careful examination of the intentions expressed in the two sagely sovereigns’ prefaces reveals how subtle is their purpose: to make manifest praise and condemnation of the past, and to transmit models and warnings to the future! This must be examined in detail. You, sir, now wish to…

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
使承學反覆究之其敢黙焉已乎夫二書
所載賢與善者皆古重臣忠君之事也其
為道也有四以敬正事不敢冀君之知也
以道責難不敢阿君之好也內交可合曰
援黨以比周吾弗為之矣外譽可致曰違
道以要衆吾弗取之矣此四者重臣之所
執也然推其忠之所存要在殉君以行義
爾故我
聖祖於序賢臣稱其智哉忠於君而不變而臣
===
鑒序善可法者亦以為秉仁循義心天理
之公去之千載而有輝光矣則所謂天下
不可一日無重臣也非以其能益於國邪
所載姦與惡者皆古權臣蔽君之事也其
為道也亦有四壅主之聽將以得國之柄
也動衆之爭將以致已之威也引之以好
善之名而陰致其誣善之實欲君之善可
惑焉疆之以難從之事而因揣其易從之
志欲君之從可易焉此四者權臣之所託

之公去之千載而有輝光矣則所謂天下
不可一日無重臣也非以其能益於國耶
所載姦與惡者皆古權臣蔽君之事也其
為道也亦有四壅主之聽將以得國之柄
也動衆之爭將以致巳之威也引之以好
善之名而陰致其誣善之實欲君之善可
惑焉疆之以難從之事而因揣其易從之
志欲君之從可易焉此四者權臣之所託
punctuated:
使承學反覆究之，其敢黙焉已乎？夫二書所載賢與善者，皆古重臣忠君之事也。其為道也有四：以敬正事，不敢冀君之知也；以道責難，不敢阿君之好也；內交可合，曰：「援黨以比周，吾弗為之矣。」外譽可致，曰：「違道以要衆，吾弗取之矣。」此四者，重臣之所執也。然推其忠之所存，要在殉君以行義爾。故我聖祖於序賢臣，稱其智哉，忠於君而不變；而《臣鑒》序善可法者，亦以為秉仁循義，心天理之公，去之千載而有輝光矣。則所謂天下不可一日無重臣也，非以其能益於國邪？

所載姦與惡者，皆古權臣蔽君之事也。其為道也亦有四：壅主之聽，將以得國之柄也；動衆之爭，將以致已之威也；引之以好善之名，而陰致其誣善之實，欲君之善可惑焉；疆之以難從之事，而因揣其易從之志，欲君之從可易焉。此四者，權臣之所託
translation_en:
…have us students investigate these matters repeatedly; how could we dare remain silent and leave it at that? The worthy men and good deeds recorded in these two books are all instances of great ministers of antiquity serving their rulers loyally. Their way of proceeding had four aspects. They rectified affairs with reverence, without daring to hope for their ruler’s recognition. By the Way they demanded difficult achievements of him, without daring to flatter his preferences. When they could have forged connections within the court, they said: “I will not enlist a faction to engage in partisan collusion.” When they could have gained renown outside the court, they said: “I will not depart from the Way to court the multitude.” These four principles were what great ministers upheld. Yet, tracing the source of their loyalty, its essential purpose was to devote themselves to their ruler and put righteousness into practice. Thus, in his preface concerning worthy ministers, our sagely founder praised their wisdom [?] and their unchanging loyalty to their ruler. The preface to the Mirror for Ministers (Chen jian), discussing good deeds worthy of emulation, likewise held that they embraced benevolence, followed righteousness, and took the impartiality of Heaven’s principle to heart [?], so that even a thousand years later they retained their radiance. Hence the saying that the realm cannot go a single day without great ministers: is this not because they can benefit the state?

The treacherous men and evil deeds recorded there are all instances of power-wielding ministers of antiquity keeping their rulers in ignorance. Their way of proceeding likewise had four aspects. They blocked their sovereign’s access to information in order to gain control of the state. They stirred up contention among the multitude in order to establish their own authority. They drew the ruler in under the name of loving goodness, while secretly bringing about the actual slander of good men, seeking to make his love of goodness susceptible to deception. They pressed him with matters difficult to comply with, then used this to gauge his disposition to comply with easier ones, seeking to make his compliance easy to obtain [?]. These four practices were what power-wielding ministers relied upon…

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
也然推其欺之所著要在蔽君以行私爾
故我
聖祖於序姦臣指其恃要持權窺覘人主之意
臣鑒序惡可戒者亦斥其挾姦縱私傷仁
敗德百世聞其姓名猶起人忿憾不平之
氣矣則所謂天下不可一日有權臣也非
以其能害於政邪夫語其不可無也不能
預蓄之以有待知其不可有也不能决去
之而無疑斯則人主擇臣之失術往記所
===
以垂之論誡者也且夫不察其心而求其
迹則重臣之直行不顧孰與權臣之恭退
有禮也不觀其度而信其才則權臣之敏
給便事孰與重臣之質疆少文也慶賞爵
予君所以惠下重臣用之以張公朝權臣
亦用之以厚私門而有不知其竊者矣刑
罰誅奪君所以威衆重臣取之以行公法
權臣亦取之以快私志而有不知其假者
矣故處有重臣之朝者君子赴義小人畏

punctuated:
也。然推其欺之所著，要在蔽君以行私爾。故我聖祖於序姦臣，指其恃要持權、窺覘人主之意；《臣鑒》序惡可戒者，亦斥其挾姦縱私、傷仁敗德，百世聞其姓名，猶起人忿憾不平之氣矣。則所謂天下不可一日有權臣也，非以其能害於政邪？夫語其不可無也，不能預蓄之以有待；知其不可有也，不能决去之而無疑：斯則人主擇臣之失術，往記所以垂之論誡者也。
且夫不察其心而求其迹，則重臣之直行不顧，孰與權臣之恭退有禮也？不觀其度而信其才，則權臣之敏給便事，孰與重臣之質疆少文也？慶賞爵予，君所以惠下，重臣用之以張公朝，權臣亦用之以厚私門，而有不知其竊者矣。刑罰誅奪，君所以威衆，重臣取之以行公法，權臣亦取之以快私志，而有不知其假者矣。故處有重臣之朝者，君子赴義，小人畏
translation_en:
…Yet if we trace the manifestations of their deceit, its essence lies simply in keeping the ruler in ignorance so as to pursue private interests. Thus, when our Sagely Founder wrote about treacherous ministers, he pointed out how they relied on powerful positions, wielded authority, and probed the sovereign’s intentions. The Mirror for Ministers (Chen jian), in recounting evils that should serve as warnings, likewise condemned their harboring treachery, indulging selfish interests, injuring benevolence, and corrupting virtue. Even after a hundred generations, hearing their names still stirs indignation and resentment at injustice. Thus, when it is said that the realm cannot tolerate power-usurping ministers for even a single day, is this not because they can harm its government? To say that weighty ministers are indispensable, yet fail to cultivate them in advance against future need; to know that power-usurping ministers must not be tolerated, yet fail to remove them decisively and without hesitation—these are failures in a ruler’s method of choosing ministers, against which earlier records have handed down judgments and admonitions.
Moreover, if one does not examine their hearts but looks only at their outward conduct, how can a weighty minister’s forthright actions, taken without regard for consequences, compare with a power-usurping minister’s respectful deference and observance of propriety? If one does not observe their moral bearing but trusts their talents, how does a power-usurping minister’s quick-witted facility in handling affairs compare with a weighty minister’s plain firmness and lack of polish? Rewards and grants of rank are the means by which the ruler bestows favors upon those below. Weighty ministers use them to strengthen the public authority of the court; power-usurping ministers also use them to enrich their own households, yet some rulers fail to recognize this appropriation. Punishments, executions, and deprivation of rank or property are the means by which the ruler holds the multitude in awe. Weighty ministers employ them to enforce public law; power-usurping ministers also employ them to gratify their private desires, yet some rulers fail to recognize this borrowing of their authority. Thus, in a court with weighty ministers, gentlemen hasten toward righteousness, and petty men fear…

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
法天下之政無一不出於公者國家所以
日興於治也處有權臣之朝者小人赴勢
君子畏禍天下之政無一不出於私者國
家所以日入於亂也是故人君綜攬萬幾

法，天下之政無一不出於公者，國家所以日興於治也。處有權臣之朝者，小人赴勢，君子畏禍，天下之政無一不出於私者，國家所以日入於亂也。是故人君綜攬萬幾，觀化原於物理之著，攝御群臣，辨人品於心術之微，察事之無形以推其形之所示，審幾之欲動以知其動之所由。夫然後天下之材可得而知，天下之情可得而校，而重與權之分、賢與姦之判，不待數計物索，已昭昭乎不可盖匿矣。
抑權臣之不可有，世皆知之，而重臣之不可無，非深明於治體者不足與識之也。盖天下有危疑不制之變，非重臣孰能定之？人君有沮易難持之計，非重臣孰能决之？故僕固之難，六師攻之不克，汾陽一出，卒著免胄之勳；光獻之疑，天下憂之莫解，稚圭數語，迄成撤簾之功。彼其德信感人之深，故意動而中外咸服；威望繫人之久，故語出而上下不疑。
translation_en:
…the law; every act of government under Heaven proceeds from public considerations. This is why the state advances daily toward good order. In a court with overmighty ministers, petty men flock to power and gentlemen fear disaster; every act of government under Heaven proceeds from private interests. This is why the state descends daily into disorder. Thus the ruler, comprehensively directing the myriad affairs of government, must discern the sources of transformation in the manifest patterns of things. In controlling his ministers, he must distinguish their character through the subtleties of their intentions. He must examine affairs before they take shape to infer what their eventual form will reveal, and scrutinize incipient developments on the verge of movement to understand what drives them. Only then can the talents of all under Heaven be known and their true circumstances assessed. The distinction between ministers of weight and overmighty ministers, and the division between the worthy and the wicked, will then be so clear that they cannot be concealed, without requiring exhaustive reckoning and investigation of each particular.
Everyone knows that overmighty ministers must not be allowed to exist. Yet only those who deeply understand the essentials of government can appreciate that ministers of weight are indispensable. When dangerous and uncertain upheavals arise under Heaven and cannot be controlled, who but a minister of weight can settle them? When the ruler has plans that are obstructed or unsettled and difficult to maintain, who but a minister of weight can bring them to a decision? Thus, during Pugu’s rebellion, the imperial armies attacked without success; but once the Prince of Fenyang appeared, he ultimately won distinction by removing his helmet. When uncertainty concerning Guangxian arose, all under Heaven worried, unable to resolve it; yet a few words from Zhigui eventually accomplished the withdrawal of the curtain of regency. Such ministers’ virtue and trustworthiness move people profoundly, so that when their intentions stir, those within the court and beyond it all submit. Their authority and prestige have long secured people’s allegiance, so that when they speak, neither high nor low harbors doubt…

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
以之靖亂則吳楚之難淮蔡之功不動聲
色而可定以之寄命則産禄之變思訓之
謀無煩指顧而能安後世惟不得重臣用
之故帷幄無參决之倚則弘石之姦得肆
莞樞乏耆舊之託則李鄭之難由作此禍
亂所為相尋於無窮也然所謂重臣者豈
可遽得於一旦哉非君任之素專則其體
無由而尊養之素篤則其節無由而完優
寵之素厚則其英毅果敢之氣幾何不至
===
遂撓屈也故體能使之尊明主之專任也
唐文皇之於房玄齡是已節能使之完明
主之篤養也宋太宗之於寇準是已氣能
使之不撓屈明主之素優予也漢文帝之
於申屠嘉是已故曰天下之政舉而修之
在臣天下之材作而成之在君此明主之
獨鑒不以語人者也
二聖纂録之深意得無有出於是乎書曰克綏
先王之禄永底烝民之生一德交修上下

二聖纂錄之深意得無有出於是乎書曰克綏
先王之祿永底烝民之生一德交儆上下
punctuated:
以之靖亂，則吳楚之難、淮蔡之功，不動聲色而可定；以之寄命，則産禄之變、思訓之謀，無煩指顧而能安。後世惟不得重臣用之，故帷幄無參决之倚，則弘石之姦得肆；莞樞乏耆舊之託，則李鄭之難由作。此禍亂所為相尋於無窮也。然所謂重臣者，豈可遽得於一旦哉？非君任之素專，則其體無由而尊；養之素篤，則其節無由而完；優寵之素厚，則其英毅果敢之氣，幾何不至遂撓屈也？故體能使之尊，明主之專任也，唐文皇之於房玄齡是已；節能使之完，明主之篤養也，宋太宗之於寇準是已；氣能使之不撓屈，明主之素優予也，漢文帝之於申屠嘉是已。故曰：天下之政，舉而修之在臣；天下之材，作而成之在君。此明主之獨鑒，不以語人者也。
二聖纂録之深意，得無有出於是乎？《書》曰：「克綏先王之禄，永底烝民之生。」一德交修，上下
translation_en:
…By employing such ministers to quell disorder, crises like the rebellion of Wu and Chu and campaigns like those against Huai and Cai can be brought to a settled conclusion without any outward display of agitation. By entrusting them with the fate of the state, disturbances like that involving Lü Chan and Lü Lu, or the plot involving Sixun [?], can be pacified without so much as the trouble of giving directions. In later ages, rulers simply failed to obtain and employ weighty ministers. Thus, when they had no one to rely on for counsel and decisions within their inner councils, the villainy of Hong Gong and Shi Xian could run unchecked; when pivotal offices [?] lacked trusted elder statesmen, disasters like that involving Li and Zheng arose. This is why calamity and disorder followed one another without end.
Yet could such weighty ministers be obtained suddenly, in a single day? Unless the ruler has long entrusted them with undivided confidence, their standing has no means of becoming exalted; unless he has long nurtured them with earnest care, their integrity has no means of remaining whole; unless he has long favored them generously, how could their spirited resolve and courage fail eventually to bend and give way? Thus, enabling their standing to become exalted depends on an enlightened ruler’s undivided trust: Emperor Wen of Tang’s treatment of Fang Xuanling is an example. Enabling their integrity to remain whole depends on an enlightened ruler’s earnest nurturing: Emperor Taizong of Song’s treatment of Kou Zhun is an example. Enabling their spirit to remain unbending depends on an enlightened ruler’s longstanding generosity: Emperor Wen of Han’s treatment of Shentu Jia is an example. Hence it is said: taking up and putting the government of the realm in order rests with ministers; cultivating and bringing the realm’s talent to fruition rests with the ruler. This is the enlightened ruler’s private discernment, which he does not disclose to others.
Might the profound intention behind the two sage sovereigns’ compilation of the record arise from this? The Book of Documents says: “Secure the former kings’ blessings; establish the people’s livelihood forever.” When ruler and ministers cultivate a single virtue together, those above and those below …

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
允協則有賢公卿輔翼
大聖人之化焉草茅賤士其敢忘帝臣之願乎
謹對
第二問
王應時
同考試官都給事中劉批衆言淆亂折諸聖固
有是言今子論性能析諸說之異而歸諸力行
之一言子其希聖學而將有得者邪
同考試官修撰秦批性學一策士千類能言
===
之求其於諸說異同剖析明允如此篇者不多
見也豈區區記誦之學所能到邪宜錄之
考試官學士歐陽批諸子不知性善故其學起
於意見後世謂氣質有不善欲不歸罪於習而
有以自諉讀至此令人深省
考試官大學士張批性學不明以人之詳於言
而畧於行故耳此作能辨析諸家是非而歸之
力行之一言始可與論性矣錄之
性貴盡也非貴言也其言之者示人盡之
