…to bring the undertaking to completion. Since Zheng could be moved by sincerity, why resort to exhausting military force? He therefore withdrew the scouts and forbade incursions, opening his heart to Zheng; he treated the prisoners courteously and sent them back with a message, awaiting Zheng’s allegiance with an open mind. At the meeting at Xiaoyu, Duke Dao brought Zheng into submission without fighting. In consequence, relations with Chu were severed [?], and Liang Xiao was seized; Zheng thereafter remained steadfast in serving Jin. Ah! Zheng made alliances only to betray them: it was no state to be trusted. Yet because Duke Dao moved it through sincerity, its deceit had no occasion for use. Otherwise, offerings of jade and silk would have awaited whichever power was stronger, and armed conflict would never have ceased. How adept Duke Dao was at bringing Zheng into submission!
Thus Chu, though powerful, yielded to righteousness; Zheng, though rebellious, submitted to sincerity. Those skilled merely in warfare truly have no place in the age of the sage. The army of Luan Wuzi did not extend slaughter to others, and for this it received approval in the Spring and Autumn Annals. Even so, excellent as Duke Huan’s military conduct was, had Chu lacked a capable envoy, who could have exercised discretion over his ruler’s commands beyond the state’s borders? Excellent as Duke Dao’s military conduct was, had Zheng lacked capable men to deliberate on affairs of state, who could have settled the policy of that vacillating state? As for Guan Zhong’s establishment of domestic administration and Wei Jiang’s plans to give the people respite, these too enabled the achievements of the two hegemons. Such are the benefits worthy men bring to a state!
“The Viscount of Chu and the Marquis of Cai encamped at Juehe.” 〔Tenth year of Duke Wen.〕 “In spring, the Viscount of Chu attacked Jun.” 〔Eleventh year of Duke Wen.〕
Wang Yu.

When the Spring and Autumn Annals records military affairs, both those who oppress the Xia states and those who attach themselves to the Yi barbarians incur its censure. This shows how carefully the Sage guarded the distinction between Yi and Xia. Since Langyuan, Chu had not passed a day without contemplating expansion northward. Now it joined four states in encamping at Juehe, while its ruler personally led the attack on Jun. Yet Duke Huan of Qi likewise encamped before attacking. Why, then, is Chu alone censured?
The gentleman says: That the Yi should not throw the Hua into disorder is an enduring principle of Heaven and Earth; moreover, Song was the heir of a former dynasty. What was Chu, that it dared to capitalize on the awe it had inspired by destroying small states, flaunt its prowess in subduing Cheng, and encamp at Juehe? It stationed its army and plotted, awaiting an opening to act. Had Song not held the hunt at Mengzhu, the campaign at Xixue would have been directed against Song rather than Jun. In compiling the Classic, the Sage regarded Duke Huan of Qi’s encampment as an occasion for framing diplomatic statements to intimidate his enemy. Chu, however, harbored unruly ambitions to oppress the Xia. How could the two be spoken of in the same breath? Thus the attack on Jun is recorded after the encampment at Juehe: herein lies the censure.
As for making peace in order to approach Chu [?], Chen, Zheng, and Song did so too. Why, then, is Cai alone censured?
The gentleman says: To transform the Yi through Xia civilization is a principle valid in all ages, while Chu was indeed a barbarian state that usurped titles and authority. What was Cai, that it went so far as to abandon the nobility of the Ji-lineage states, willingly associate with an alien people, and follow Chu at Juehe? …in the end, when Jin convened the covenant at Xincheng, Cai alone did not participate: this clearly demonstrates its determination to abandon righteousness. In compiling the Classic, the Sage regarded the three states’ submission as an effort to relieve their troubles and secure their own safety. Cai, however, persisted without cause. How could they be judged alike? Thus he placed the Marquis of Cai below the Viscount of Chu; this, too, is how he expressed censure. If this principle prevails, the central states remain the central states, and the Yi and Di remain the Yi and Di. The central states do not pass beyond their bounds, and the Yi and Di do not enter them; the great boundary of All under Heaven is thereby established. How true the saying that none but a sage could have compiled the Spring and Autumn Annals!
Yet the greatest good fortune of the central states lies in having worthy men. At that time, Chu was the power oppressing the Xia states—but who opened the way for it? Cai was the state siding with Chu—but who permitted it? Jin presided over the covenants of the Xia states; responsibility did not rest with the other feudal lords. Zhao Dun and the other ministers cannot evade their responsibility. At this, the gentleman cannot but look back longingly to Duke Huan’s earlier time and regret that Duke Dao came so late.

…once this is taken up and applied throughout the realm, there will be no difficulty. There is good reason why the sage begins here in governing! Indeed, devotion to those nearby is the means of reaching those afar; holding to what is simple is the way to extend one's influence broadly. Examine what is given priority, and the essential character of government can be understood. Thus the sage perpetuates the brightness of Li, the trigram of fire, to illuminate all things, and responds to the active force of yang by spreading transforming influence, ruling over the myriad states. He possesses the strength of Qian, the trigram of Heaven, to decide with sole authority, rectifies his position and secures the Mandate, presiding over all activity. In attending to the age and responding to things so as to embrace and protect all under Heaven, he seeks to spread the blessings of happiness and benefit. In steadfast radiance [?], he sets forth instruction and bestows it upon the people, wishing to attain a government of splendid harmony. Could this have no starting point? That starting point is simply the way of human relationships.

For the way of human relationships lies in bringing harmony to one's kin, and nothing takes precedence over strengthening the bonds of the lineage in transforming and ordering society. The sage governs without attending separately to every thing. His Way is exalted in relationships joined by Heaven, and the constant human relationships are duly ordered, thereby setting right the foundation of all transforming influence. His affection is devoted to his kin, and the bonds of human society begin to be cultivated, thereby establishing the standard for all affairs of government. In the unity of their root, his beneficence inspires trust: he brings to fruition the harmony that unites all, and from this extends humaneness toward the people and care for other creatures. In the distinctions among their allotted relationships, principle gives them order: he broadens the proper recognition of differences, and applies this throughout the family, the state, and all within the Four Seas. Thus he fulfills human relationships and deepens transforming influence, nurturing the source from which it issues at the appropriate time. Whether his measures are gradual or urgent, he naturally has ample scope to carry them into effect.

As for rewarding merit, raising up the worthy, employing the capable, and preserving loving concern, although these all have priority in the way of government, the essential point is that one must begin with the way of human relationships. Thus the sage stands facing south as ruler, and all under Heaven is well governed. Otherwise, however earnest his desire for good government, it has no foundation. If harmony has not been achieved among those nearby, transforming influence can hardly reach those afar. How, then, could he govern all under Heaven? The worthy speaks of the harmonious response of the Three Powers—Heaven, Earth, and humanity—in a flourishing age, revealing how music arises. How abundant was the transforming vital force of high antiquity! When the Three Powers responded harmoniously, could music then be brought forth? When Zixia replied to Marquis Wen, did he not say that Heaven occupies its place above, Earth its place below, and the people dwell between them? Such is the Way of the Three Powers. title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
無私之教天地順矣吾知主宰以職則流行不
愆其序奠位以正則代謝各適其常陰陽相感
而化生焉寒暑相推而歲成焉天地官而四時
因之以不忒也使非世道之隆天地且不順况
四時乎五穀以養民民之不德則咎徵感而欲
其蕃廡難矣惟夫古者純朴天固而大道以為
公沕穆風行而敦厚以成俗民有德矣將見協
氣嘉生栽培以茂其化太和瑞應美利以溥其
施豐穰而百室盈焉順成而八蜡通焉民平康
===
而五穀因之以用成也使非世道之盛民且不
德况五穀乎夫造化之和既妙無聲之體民德
所召又涵聲氣之元此樂作於大定而平心宣
化豈溺音所得同哉抑論萬古此天地萬古此
民人則應感之盛何獨於古為然唯天子建中
和之極則與天地四時合德合序成民以阜物
而天人之和應矣是故天人者作樂之原君身
者參贊之本

punctuated:
無私之教。天地順矣，吾知主宰以職，則流行不愆其序；奠位以正，則代謝各適其常。陰陽相感而化生焉，寒暑相推而歲成焉。天地官，而四時因之以不忒也。使非世道之隆，天地且不順，况四時乎？五穀以養民，民之不德，則咎徵感，而欲其蕃廡難矣。惟夫古者，純朴天固，而大道以為公；沕穆風行，而敦厚以成俗。民有德矣，將見協氣嘉生，栽培以茂其化；太和瑞應，美利以溥其施。豐穰而百室盈焉，順成而八蜡通焉。民平康，而五穀因之以用成也。使非世道之盛，民且不德，况五穀乎？夫造化之和，既妙無聲之體；民德所召，又涵聲氣之元。此樂作於大定，而平心宣化，豈溺音所得同哉？抑論萬古此天地，萬古此民人，則應感之盛，何獨於古為然？唯天子建中和之極，則與天地四時合德合序，成民以阜物，而天人之和應矣。是故天人者，作樂之原；君身者，參贊之本。

第貳場
translation_en:
…the teaching of impartiality. Heaven and Earth were thus in accord. I know that when the ruling power fulfills its office, the course of change does not depart from its proper sequence; when positions are rightly established, successive changes each follow their constant pattern. Yin and yang respond to one another, bringing transformation and generation; cold and heat succeed one another, completing the year. Heaven and Earth fulfill their offices, and consequently the four seasons do not err. Were it not for the flourishing order of the age, even Heaven and Earth would lack accord—how much more the four seasons!

The five grains nourish the people. If the people lack virtue, portents of calamity arise in response, and it is difficult to hope for luxuriant crops. In antiquity, however, simplicity was firmly rooted in nature, and the Great Way served the common good; profound harmony spread like the wind, and sincerity and generosity formed the customs. The people possessed virtue. Thus one would see harmonious vital forces bringing forth fine growth, nurturing it so that transformation flourished; auspicious responses to supreme harmony spread their bounty through beneficial gifts. Harvests were abundant, and every household’s stores were full; the crops ripened in due season, and the eight harvest sacrifices were all duly performed. The people enjoyed peace and well-being, and consequently the five grains came to maturity. Were it not for the flourishing order of the age, even the people would lack virtue—how much more could the five grains flourish!

The harmony of creation already wondrously embodies that which is without sound; what the people’s virtue calls forth also contains the source of sound and vital force. Such music arises amid profound stability, bringing peace to the heart and spreading moral transformation. How could corrupting music compare with it? Yet these are the same Heaven and Earth throughout the ages, and these are the same people throughout the ages. Why, then, should such flourishing mutual response have occurred only in antiquity? Only when the Son of Heaven establishes the supreme standard of equilibrium and harmony does he accord in virtue with Heaven and Earth and in sequence with the four seasons, perfecting the people and making all things abundant. Then Heaven and humanity respond to one another in harmony. Thus Heaven and humanity are the source of the creation of music; the ruler’s own person is the foundation for participating in and assisting the work of Heaven and Earth.

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
無窮之心玩之有餘味矣可錄以式
聖人仁覆天下而未嘗一乎其已能故自視常
未盡自視未盡斯其為盡仁者乎夫仁天地之
大德而性於人人所以體萬物而為天地之心
者也其為道至大而至近至微而至神并包兼
濟被於天下也莫得其極而溥博淵泉出於人
心也莫竟其所際是故於物有濟可以為仁而
有一物之不濟未足以言全一念公溥可以體
仁而有一念之或間未足以言純聖人安仁無
===
違者也而天下之大未必能兼濟而無不及故
常以其所不及為未全而未嘗以其無違為已
純兹堯舜所以上下同流而猶以修己安百姓
為病也故曰聖人之心無窮非天下之至仁其
孰能與于此人之言曰凡人所孳孳而不敢苟
止者蓋事可能而已有未能雖未之能而必不
可不能者也修己之道其事為視聽言動其情
為喜怒好惡皆於身取之夫人可以與能者聖
人豈猶有所未能邪天下之大百姓至衆也欲

…the sage’s inexhaustible heart. Pondering it leaves a lingering savor. It merits inclusion as a model.
The sage’s benevolence embraces all under Heaven, yet he never rests content with what he has already accomplished [?]; thus he always regards himself as having fallen short. Is it not precisely in regarding himself as having fallen short that he fully realizes benevolence? Benevolence is the great virtue of Heaven and Earth, inherent in the nature of every person. Through it, people form one body with the myriad things and become the heart of Heaven and Earth. As a Way, it is supremely great yet supremely near, supremely subtle yet supremely wondrous. Encompassing everything and bringing aid to all, it extends throughout the world without any discoverable limit. Vast and deep as a fountainhead, it issues from the human heart, its reach unfathomable. Thus, to aid things may count as benevolence; but if even one thing remains unaided, one cannot yet speak of completeness. A single impartial and all-embracing thought may embody benevolence; but if even one thought interrupts it, one cannot yet speak of purity. The sage rests at ease in benevolence and never departs from it. Yet, given the vastness of the world, he may not be able to bring aid to everyone without exception. He therefore always considers his benevolence incomplete because of those it has not reached, and never considers it already pure merely because he has not departed from it. This is why Yao and Shun, although they flowed together with Heaven above and Earth below, still regarded cultivating themselves so as to bring peace to the common people as a daunting task. Thus it is said: “The sage’s heart is inexhaustible.” Who but one of the utmost benevolence under Heaven could attain this?

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
盡舉而安之勢有所必不能豈聖人顧汲汲焉
必能之也噫聖人之於百姓豈敢曰勢不能盡
安遂委之於不必能邪人以天地萬物為體其
安百姓盖安其四體也委四體於不必盡安惟
不仁其身者能之仁者之心固宜有汲汲不懈
者矣則夫修之已者亦豈敢曰吾已盡已能而
不復有所進邪夫人以修已為易能易盡也盖
以身為已而未嘗於其感應者觀之也今夫視
聽言動之用喜怒好惡之情凡接物而應焉者
===
已也而莫非物也微物則惡所視聽而好惡喜
怒之哉親疎遠邇智愚貴賤與夫貧窮煢獨凡
對已而感焉者物也而莫非已也微已則惡覩
其為親疎與煢獨者哉故聖人之於天下視惟
明聽惟聰而休戚誠偽之隱靡所不周言忠信
行篤敬而順逆睽合之志靡所不通喜怒不遷
好惡無作而愛憎取舍之情靡所不同茲其修
之已也皆加乎民而安之者也其於百姓惇親
及疎篤近舉遠皆在所懷而各得其欲貴貴下

安百姓蓋安其四體也委四體於不必盡安惟
不仁其身者能之仁者之心固宜有汲汲不懈
者矣則夫修之己者亦豈敢曰吾已盡己能而
不復有所述邪夫人以修己爲易能易盡也蓋
以身爲己而未嘗於其感應者觀之也今夫視
聽言動之用喜怒好惡之情凡接物而應焉者
===
己也而莫非物也微物則惡所視聽而好惡喜
怒之哉親疏遠邇智愚貴賤與夫貧窮煢獨凡
對己而感焉者物也而莫非己也微己則惡覩
其爲親疏與煢獨者哉故聖人之於天下視惟
明聽惟聰而休戚誠僞之隱靡所不周言忠信
行篤敬而順逆睽合之志靡所不通喜怒不遷
好惡無作而愛憎取舍之情靡所不同茲其修
之己也皆加乎民而安之者也其於百姓惇親
疏篤近舉遠皆在所懷而各得其敍貴貴下
punctuated: 盡舉而安之，勢有所必不能，豈聖人顧汲汲焉必能之也？噫！聖人之於百姓，豈敢曰勢不能盡安，遂委之於不必能邪？人以天地萬物為體，其安百姓，盖安其四體也。委四體於不必盡安，惟不仁其身者能之。仁者之心，固宜有汲汲不懈者矣。則夫修之已者，亦豈敢曰吾已盡已能，而不復有所進邪？夫人以修已為易能易盡也，盖以身為已，而未嘗於其感應者觀之也。今夫視聽言動之用，喜怒好惡之情，凡接物而應焉者，已也，而莫非物也。微物，則惡所視聽而好惡喜怒之哉？親疎遠邇，智愚貴賤，與夫貧窮煢獨，凡對已而感焉者，物也，而莫非已也。微已，則惡覩其為親疎與煢獨者哉？故聖人之於天下，視惟明，聽惟聰，而休戚誠偽之隱靡所不周；言忠信，行篤敬，而順逆睽合之志靡所不通；喜怒不遷，好惡無作，而愛憎取舍之情靡所不同。茲其修之已也，皆加乎民而安之者也。其於百姓，惇親及疎，篤近舉遠，皆在所懷而各得其欲；貴貴下
translation_en:
…to bring them all to peace: circumstances necessarily make some of this impossible. Would the sage nevertheless strive anxiously to accomplish it without fail? Ah! In dealing with the common people, would the sage dare say that circumstances prevent him from bringing peace to them all, and therefore abandon the task as something he need not accomplish? A person takes Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things as his own body; bringing peace to the common people is thus bringing peace to his own four limbs. Only someone without benevolence toward his own person could abandon his four limbs as things that need not all be put at ease. The benevolent heart surely must strive earnestly and without respite. In cultivating himself, then, how could he dare say, “I have exhausted the task and fulfilled my capacity,” and cease making further progress?
People consider self-cultivation easy to accomplish and complete because they identify the self with the body and have never examined it through its interactions and responses. Consider the operations of seeing, hearing, speaking, and acting, and the feelings of pleasure, anger, liking, and dislike. Whatever encounters things and responds to them is the self, yet none of this is apart from things. Without things, what would there be to see and hear, to like and dislike, or to feel pleasure and anger about? Those related closely or distantly, those near and far, the wise and foolish, the noble and lowly, together with the poor, destitute, solitary, and bereft—all who confront the self and move it are things external to it, yet none is apart from the self. Without the self, how could one perceive them as close or distant relations, or as solitary and bereft?
Thus, in his dealings with all under Heaven, the sage sees clearly and hears acutely, encompassing every hidden circumstance of well-being and distress, sincerity and falsehood. His words are loyal and trustworthy, his conduct earnest and reverent, and he comprehends every intention, whether compliant or resistant, estranged or harmonious. He does not transfer his pleasure or anger to others, nor arbitrarily arouse liking or dislike, and he shares fully in people's feelings of love and hatred, acceptance and rejection. Such is his cultivation of himself: all of it extends to the people and brings them peace. In dealing with the common people, he cherishes close relations and extends his care to distant ones, treats those nearby generously and raises up those far away. All are embraced in his concern, and each obtains what he desires. He honors the noble and humbles himself before…

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
賤尊賢容衆皆在所愛而各得其辨老老幼幼
恤不辜矜無告皆在所慈而各得其所茲其安
之也皆出乎身而修焉者也故修己者修安民
之道於己百姓安而後己之分盡自修之事畢
矣聖人有見於感應之一也以為己之分無時
而可盡自修之事無時而可畢何也百姓之衆
惡能盡舉而全安之也夫天地之大也而萬物
有未生未育人不能無憾於天地聖人之大也
而百姓有未安人不能無望於聖人而聖人豈
===
能自安於其心哉昔者堯舜大聖人也其明德
以親民者盖至於萬邦協和而四方風動矣然
其訓迪庶官勸之勿壞與其所以慎修思永者
孳孳爾也盖舜之稱堯也謂舍己稽衆不虐無
告不廢困窮惟帝能之則知人安民之道矣而
禹又以為知人則哲安民則惠雖帝亦難能焉
豈非道未易盡而堯之所能者堯亦有難焉者
哉則舜之所以孳孳如堯又可知也矣故當時
之戒羣臣也曰弼違曰無面從曰汝為汝翼汝

translation_en:
…the lowly; honoring the worthy and accommodating the multitude—all are embraced by his love, and each receives the distinctions appropriate to them. Treating the aged as the aged should be treated and the young as the young should be treated, caring for the innocent and showing compassion to those with no one to appeal to—all are embraced by his kindness, and each finds their proper place. His bringing them peace thus proceeds entirely from the cultivation of his own person. Hence, to cultivate oneself is to cultivate within oneself the Way of bringing peace to the people. Only when the common people are at peace is one’s own duty fulfilled and the work of self-cultivation complete. The sage perceives the unity of stimulus and response and considers that there is never a time when his duty can be exhausted or the work of self-cultivation completed. Why is this? With so many common people, how could he attend to every one of them and bring them all perfect peace? Great as Heaven and Earth are, among the myriad things some have yet to be brought forth or nurtured, so people cannot be without regrets concerning Heaven and Earth. Great as the sage is, some among the common people have yet to attain peace, so people cannot cease to look to the sage with expectations. How, then, could the sage feel at ease in his own heart?

In antiquity, Yao and Shun were great sages. In manifesting their virtue so as to cherish the people, they surely reached the point at which the myriad states were harmoniously united and the four quarters stirred as though moved by the wind. Yet they remained unremitting in instructing and guiding the many officials, urging them not to let things fall into ruin, and in carefully cultivating themselves with enduring consequences in mind. When Shun praised Yao, he said that only the emperor could set aside his own views and consult the multitude, refrain from oppressing those with no one to appeal to, and refrain from casting aside those in hardship and poverty. This was the Way of knowing men and bringing peace to the people. Yet Yu further held that knowing men constitutes wisdom and bringing peace to the people constitutes beneficence, and that even the emperor found these difficult to achieve. Is this not because the Way cannot readily be fulfilled in its entirety, and because even in what Yao could accomplish there remained things he himself found difficult? We can thus also understand why Shun was as unremitting as Yao. 譽咈人從欲喜起交修時幾交勅昌言交拜惴
惴焉若勉修其德而未能若經綸屯否而未底
其績者此豈不見天下理亂之形而故以為未
理不見己心危微之幾而故以為未盡哉心同
天運無有止足其視天下之大也阻飢之民豈

…my sight, and you my hearing.” When the assembled ministers offered admonitions, they too spoke of indolence, arrogance, departing from the Way to seek acclaim, and opposing others to indulge one’s own desires. The ruler’s delight and the ministers’ exertions fostered mutual cultivation; they admonished one another concerning timely action and the first stirrings of events, and bowed to one another upon hearing excellent counsel. Apprehensively, they acted as though striving to cultivate their virtue but still falling short, as though working to resolve difficulties and obstruction but not yet achieving success. Could this mean that they failed to perceive the state of order and disorder in the world and therefore deliberately deemed it not yet ordered, or failed to perceive the precarious and subtle stirrings within their own hearts and therefore deliberately deemed their work incomplete? Their hearts moved with Heaven’s course, never stopping or resting content. Considering the vastness of the world, they asked: Have all those afflicted by hunger attained ease and sufficient food? Are the five human relationships all harmonious? Have the five punishments all been set aside? Are the established rites all properly ordered? Are spirits and human beings all in harmony? Have all the Man and Yi who disturb the Chinese realm submitted? Do birds, beasts, plants, trees, and all things above and below fully delight in life? If so much remains unfulfilled in my efforts to manifest lofty virtue throughout the world, how could I rest at ease and forget vigilance?

Yao and Shun possessed sagely wisdom and spiritual insight, and their virtue accorded with Heaven. Everyone knew that they would assuredly never fall into the faults against which Yu, Yi, and the other ministers warned them. Yet only those ministers understood that they still could not rest at ease and forget vigilance. Yao and Shun trusted that their ministers could undertake difficult responsibilities, shared their sovereign’s heart, and would not forget to admonish themselves merely because no danger was apparent. To take their ministers’ warnings further and become vigilant about matters in which the ruler himself might not yet have been vigilant—this, too, only Yao and Shun could put into practice. If we consider the hearts of Yao and Shun, even if every undertaking had been fully accomplished and all things were in accord, they still could not cease the work of securing order before disorder arose. How much more was this so when, in so vast a world, there were bound to be things that did not fully satisfy their aspirations? title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
以致無數之保者猶未可以巳也况人心靡常
有未能必其無動於罔念者邪故唐虞之德光
被上下真如天地之化雖未能無一物之未生
未育然不害其為無不生育而其屈伸往來闔
闢變化則未甞因物而有所加損蓋穆然常運
而不巳也是聖人之心也聖人豈有特異于人
者哉亦曰純乎仁而巳仁者心之德也人心虛
靈天地合德其真誠惻怛明昭不昧一夫不獲
惕焉恫瘝於厥躬而一念必謹戰戰焉若氷淵
===
之臨是心體本然聖人無以異乎衆人者也衆
人之異於聖人則自雜之也是故物我相形私
利相奪忿疾暴慢猜疑刻忌紛然交作故不自
見其過而常自覺其所能則其於人也𥨊見其
可惡而不盡見其可愛見我之愛人者無不至
而人之不蒙吾愛者為自絕而不知愛人之心
久矣其窮也矣然其始蓋亦善端之動而過焉
者意有所向忽而未察其究也浸淫固滯日入
於頗側而罔覺爾聖人純乎仁而不蔽於我者

punctuated:
以致無數之保者，猶未可以巳也，况人心靡常，有未能必其無動於罔念者邪？故唐虞之德，光被上下，真如天地之化，雖未能無一物之未生未育，然不害其為無不生育，而其屈伸往來、闔闢變化，則未甞因物而有所加損，蓋穆然常運而不巳也。是聖人之心也。聖人豈有特異于人者哉？亦曰純乎仁而巳。仁者，心之德也。人心虛靈，天地合德，其真誠惻怛，明昭不昧，一夫不獲，惕焉恫瘝於厥躬，而一念必謹，戰戰焉若氷淵之臨，是心體本然，聖人無以異乎衆人者也。

衆人之異於聖人，則自雜之也。是故物我相形，私利相奪，忿疾暴慢、猜疑刻忌，紛然交作。故不自見其過，而常自覺其所能，則其於人也，𥨊見其可惡，而不盡見其可愛；見我之愛人者無不至，而人之不蒙吾愛者為自絕，而不知愛人之心，久矣其窮也矣。然其始，蓋亦善端之動而過焉者，意有所向，忽而未察，其究也，浸淫固滯，日入於頗側而罔覺爾。聖人純乎仁而不蔽於我者
translation_en:
…the means of securing unending protection still cannot be set aside. How much more so when the human heart is inconstant, and one cannot be certain that it will never be stirred into thoughtlessness? Thus the virtue of Tang and Yu shone upon all above and below, truly resembling the transforming activity of Heaven and Earth. Although there might still be some single thing not yet brought forth or nurtured, this did not detract from their bringing forth and nurturing all things. Their contraction and expansion, coming and going, closing and opening, and transformation never increased or diminished in response to particular things. Rather, they continued their solemn, harmonious operation without cease. Such is the heart of the sage. Does the sage possess anything especially different from other people? It is simply that he is pure in benevolence. Benevolence is the virtue of the heart. The human heart is empty and spiritually responsive, sharing in the virtue of Heaven and Earth. Its sincerity and compassion are radiant and undimmed. If even one person fails to find his proper place, it is alarmed and feels that person's suffering as its own; it attends carefully to every thought, trembling as though treading on ice or approaching a deep abyss. This is the original condition of the heart's substance, in which the sage is no different from ordinary people.

Ordinary people differ from the sage because they themselves introduce admixtures into it. Thus external things and the self are set against one another, private interests contend, and anger, resentment, violence, arrogance, suspicion, harshness, and jealousy arise in tangled profusion. Consequently, people fail to see their own faults while remaining constantly aware of their abilities. In their dealings with others, they increasingly [?] see what is hateful without fully seeing what is lovable. They regard their own love for others as complete in every respect, and suppose that those who do not receive their love have cut themselves off from it. They do not realize that their heart's capacity to love others has long since been exhausted. Yet at the outset this, too, was probably a stirring of the beginnings of goodness that went too far: their intentions inclined in a certain direction, and they carelessly failed to examine them. In the end, this gradually spread and became entrenched, drawing them daily into partiality and crookedness without their awareness. The sage is pure in benevolence and is not obscured by the self…

而能密察其意向之萌兢兢業業日乾夕惕若
有迫乎其中以追及乎其前雖欲已之而不得
者盖不徒以已之未易盡百姓之不能盡安而
始汲汲若是也其常覺而常愛者無待於外也
故聖人之心非警之使無窮仁本無窮也修已
以敬之極也仁道不明外安民以修已者是內
非外而不知萬物之備於我外敬以安民者徇

…Thus, being unobscured, the sage is always aware; being without selfishness, he always loves. He therefore need not wait for a fault to become flagrant before closely examining the first stirrings of his intentions. Cautious and earnest, diligent by day and vigilant at night, he seems driven by something within to catch up with what lies ahead; even if he wished to stop, he could not. It is not merely because the work upon himself is difficult to complete, or because all the common people have yet to be brought to peace, that he becomes so urgently diligent. His constant awareness and constant love depend on nothing external. Thus the sage’s heart is not made inexhaustible by keeping it alert: benevolence itself is inexhaustible. This is the highest attainment of cultivating oneself through reverence. When the Way of benevolence is not understood, those who cultivate themselves while excluding the task of bringing peace to the people affirm the inward and reject the outward, failing to understand that all things are fully present within oneself. Those who seek to bring peace to the people while excluding reverence follow the outward and neglect the inward, failing to understand that striving to treat others as oneself is rooted in the heart. Neither has attained the Way of refined singleness, free of division. Even if they work tirelessly, whatever they take up necessarily entails neglecting something else; whatever they undertake cannot remain constant and uninterrupted. Even if they stop only at death, this is still insufficient to speak of the sage’s inexhaustible heart, because they have not yet attained benevolence.
Confucius said: “Benevolence is what makes us human; affection for one’s parents is its greatest expression.” Thus, one who wishes to cultivate himself must serve his parents; one who wishes to serve his parents must understand people. Serving one’s parents is the beginning of bringing peace to the people; understanding people is understanding benevolence. Yet how could benevolence be spoken of lightly? Why is this? Benevolence is the life-generating principle of human nature. It has no sound, smell, shape, or substance that one could seek out and grasp. When Yizu first pacified All under Heaven, he urgently considered plans to recover the lost territory. When Taizong subsequently conquered Hedong, he devoted close attention to plans for securing the realm and repelling outsiders. Although the far-reaching counsels of the Director of the Secretariat offered a warning [?], the victorious strategy for the northern frontier had already come to ruin. The achievement at Zihe, witnessed once in a hundred years, might be called an act of heroic resolve; news of the victory at Baichi spread ten thousand li, an unrivaled display of grand strategy. Soon, with the opening of the Jingde era, came the campaign at Chanyuan. As in a royal hunt leaving one side open, the enemy was allowed to escape, and gold and silk instead went into their felt tents. The imperial carriage was constrained to a covenant, and for a time the beacon fires at the frontier watchposts lay idle.

Those brutish foes had long spread their wings like owls, and their cunning grew ever more unrestrained. Who could withstand [?] their boar-like charges? They wielded a hollow show of strength to shake the Central Kingdom. Insatiable in their wolf-like demands, they magnified their might and boasted throughout the northern wilderness. Recently, because the Qiang troubles had not been quelled, the outsiders’ ambitions were gradually emboldened to run unchecked. Military dispatches threw the various prefectures into confusion, and calamity became so grievous that corpses lay pillowed upon one another. Covenants were openly broken, and the two enemy powers formed a pincer movement. The fortunes of the state consequently suffered many troubles, while the people’s wealth was already exhausted by levies and deliveries of supplies. Moreover, Jingxing lies close to the enemy’s defenses, and Heshuo is indeed a strategically critical military command. Walls have been enlarged and garrisons arrayed: although the mountain and river defiles are encompassed by these defenses, guarding the passes and defending the frontier have ultimately depleted the strength of the finest troops and horses. Unless plans are carefully reckoned out beforehand, how can we bring our exertions to rest amid later…

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
艱伏念臣章句菲材詩書素業昔秉筆以
承
制既慙奉職之弗堪茲分符以課功庸免曠官
之益甚馳驅一路恐無裨補於秋毫出入
三年敢愛糜捐於暮齒昔賈誼憤匈奴苦
漢遂陳三表五餌之謀洎晁錯患謫戍危
秦因列四里十連之制雖陋如班固詆之
為疎而明若孝文用之即效爰取歲時之
更歷兼裏日夜之講求耳目得諸見聞既
===
臚陳而可指首尾識其情狀豈詮述之無
稽是因括論以成篇欲使循文而責實託
更端於客難反覆以昭利害之原借形喻
於物情校量而得短長之數言無文而可
采計施今而易行
廟議弘深豈可令
國威之不振忠思廣集將無惜虜勢之莫支
茲蓋伏遇
○○○○

爲踈而明若孝文用之卽效爰取歲時之
更歷兼裒日夜之講求耳目得諸見聞旣
===
旳陳而可指首尾識其情狀豈誑迷之無
稽是因括論以成篇欲使循文而責實託

於物情校量而得短長之數言無文而可
采計施令而易行
廟議弘深豈可今
國威之不振忠恩廣集將無惜虜勢之莫支
玆蓋伏遇
○○○○
punctuated:
艱。伏念臣章句菲材，詩書素業，昔秉筆以承制，既慙奉職之弗堪；茲分符以課功，庸免曠官之益甚？馳驅一路，恐無裨補於秋毫；出入三年，敢愛糜捐於暮齒？昔賈誼憤匈奴苦漢，遂陳三表五餌之謀；洎晁錯患謫戍危秦，因列四里十連之制。雖陋如班固，詆之為疎，而明若孝文，用之即效。爰取歲時之更歷，兼裏日夜之講求，耳目得諸見聞，既臚陳而可指；首尾識其情狀，豈詮述之無稽？是因括論以成篇，欲使循文而責實。託更端於客難，反覆以昭利害之原；借形喻於物情，校量而得短長之數。言無文而可采，計施今而易行。廟議弘深，豈可令國威之不振？忠思廣集，將無惜虜勢之莫支？
茲蓋伏遇○○○○
translation_en:
… difficulties. I humbly reflect that I, your servant, possess scant talent beyond the parsing of texts, and have made the Odes and Documents my customary study. Formerly, when I wielded the brush in obedience to imperial commands, I was already ashamed of my inability to discharge my duties. Now that I have been entrusted with regional authority and am to be judged by my achievements, how can I avoid still greater neglect of office? Hastening about throughout this circuit, I fear that I have contributed not the slightest benefit. Having served here for three years, how could I begrudge wearing myself out in my declining years?
Formerly, Jia Yi, indignant that the Xiongnu afflicted the Han, presented his plan of the Three Demonstrations and Five Baits. Later, Chao Cuo, concerned that the banishment of convicts to frontier garrisons had imperiled the Qin, set forth his system of four neighborhood units and ten linked groups. Although someone as limited as Ban Gu disparaged these proposals as impractical, a ruler as discerning as Emperor Xiaowen employed them with immediate effect. Accordingly, I have drawn upon my experience through the passing seasons and years, together with [?] my investigations by day and night. What my ears and eyes have gathered through hearing and observation can be enumerated and specifically identified; having understood the circumstances from beginning to end, how could my account lack a basis?
Thus I have gathered my discussions into a composition, intending that its claims should be tested against actual conditions. I introduce new topics through objections voiced by an imagined interlocutor, examining them repeatedly to illuminate the sources of benefit and harm. Drawing illustrative comparisons from the circumstances of things, I weigh them to determine their relative strengths and weaknesses. Though my words lack literary adornment, they merit consideration; the plans can readily be put into practice today. The court’s deliberations are broad and profound: how could they allow the empire’s martial prestige to remain unasserted? Loyal counsel is widely gathered: surely there need be no regret that the enemy’s power cannot hold out [?].
This is because I have humbly had the good fortune to encounter … ○○○○

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
恭儉宜民
寬和得衆駿業承
祖宗之盛式康庶政之惟熙
鴻仁協上下之休允底烝民於有乂納諫并
容乎訐直信賢不惑以讒邪三事無偏將
相得承於獨任四方有敗
聰明每徹於先知顧
黼扆宵旰之紆思在椎結叛回之阻化甞稟
昨畛南徼幸平夏孽今遺西陲豈靖乃耶
===
律一姓起沙漠幾二百年即靺鞨諸酋入
服屬已數十國自濫
中朝之幣予益空大內之帑藏虎北諸防既
失險以成虜據關南十縣復齎償而饋寇
資索求快遂於探囊搖脅動輕於振槁念
諸臣左計巳持倒柄之泰阿迹此虜驕心
方掠縱置之脫兎毀要言於宿好甘仇寇
之偽臣羌狄何親必中畔而復其隙舅甥
相絆聊暫連以飽所私況狠弟貪惏之方

punctuated: 恭儉宜民，寬和得衆，駿業承祖宗之盛，式康庶政之惟熙；鴻仁協上下之休，允底烝民於有乂。納諫并容乎訐直，信賢不惑以讒邪。三事無偏，將相得承於獨任；四方有敗，聰明每徹於先知。顧黼扆宵旰之紆思，在椎結叛回之阻化。甞稟昨畛，南徼幸平；夏孽今遺，西陲豈靖？乃耶律一姓起沙漠，幾二百年；即靺鞨諸酋入服屬，已數十國。自濫中朝之幣予，益空大內之帑藏。虎北諸防既失險以成虜據，關南十縣復齎償而饋寇資。索求快遂於探囊，搖脅動輕於振槁。念諸臣左計，巳持倒柄之泰阿；迹此虜驕心，方掠縱置之脫兎。毀要言於宿好，甘仇寇之偽臣。羌狄何親？必中畔而復其隙；舅甥相絆，聊暫連以飽所私。況狠弟貪惏之方
translation_en:
…Reverent and frugal, you benefit the people; generous and harmonious, you win the multitude. Your great undertaking carries forward the flourishing legacy of your ancestors, bringing peace and prosperity to the many affairs of government. Your vast benevolence unites the blessings of those above and below, truly bringing the common people under orderly rule. In accepting remonstrance, you tolerate even blunt denunciation; in trusting the worthy, you are not misled by malicious slander. The Three Dukes are impartial, and generals and chief ministers receive your undivided trust. When failures occur in the four quarters, your perceptiveness invariably grasps them beforehand. Yet what occupies your thoughts before dawn and late into the night upon the imperial throne is the resistance to civilizing influence of rebellious peoples who wear their hair in topknots. The preceding words are unclear [?]; fortunately, the southern border has been pacified. But remnants of Xia still survive: how can the western frontier be tranquil?

Now the Yelü clan arose in the desert nearly two hundred years ago; among the Mohe chieftains alone, several dozen states have already submitted to its authority. Since lavish grants of valuables began flowing from the central court, the treasury within the palace has been increasingly depleted. The defenses of Hubei [?] have already lost their strategic positions and become enemy strongholds; compensation is again furnished for the ten counties south of the passes, supplying the raiders with resources. Their demands are satisfied as readily as reaching into a bag; they resort to intimidation as effortlessly as shaking withered stalks. Consider the mistaken calculations of our ministers: they already hold the sword Tai’a with its hilt turned toward the enemy. Observe these enemies’ arrogance: they are plundering like a rabbit released to run free [?]. They break sworn pledges despite longstanding amity, willingly becoming sham subjects of our foes [?]. What affection binds the Qiang and Di? They will surely rebel midway and reopen the breach. Though bound together as maternal uncle and nephew, they maintain this alliance only temporarily, to satisfy their private interests. Moreover, the cruel younger brother’s greed is just now…

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
恣而大臣屏輔之未周鼠首以觀豈無中
說尉陀之輩蝟毛而奮何止新羅韃靼之
人觀其中外之相猜加以華畨之交亂兵
有五間操施必
仁聖而後能國無兩強爭裂豈懦庸之可制事
不圖於先試功何冀其有成欲振武以示
威在養馬練兵之弗怠思設竒而取勝惟
環車擾騎之兼長要之因外服以輯內寧
豈得惜一勞而忘永佚三空早實先占廐
廩之充盈五請速除盍究公私之匱乏由
因循之弊積故怯弱之患滋任一則權不
分莫若廢監軍而專任將威伸則和可守
大宜省歲幣而益治兵將求我志之克揚
必謹敵来之有備擁堅却銳立畫守於春
徂夏入之交批亢擣虛奮麾征於我出彼
歸之會離二虜之援於始振作三軍之氣
於方衰不畏彼侵患所以来其侵毋幸敵
亂恃已之不可亂安危在計豈容勒襲於

punctuated: 恣，而大臣屏輔之未周，鼠首以觀，豈無中說、尉陀之輩？蝟毛而奮，何止新羅、韃靼之人？觀其中外之相猜，加以華畨之交亂，兵有五間，操施必仁聖而後能；國無兩強，爭裂豈懦庸之可制？事不圖於先，試功何冀其有成？欲振武以示威，在養馬練兵之弗怠；思設竒而取勝，惟環車擾騎之兼長。要之，因外服以輯內寧，豈得惜一勞而忘永佚？三空早實，先占廐廩之充盈；五請速除，盍究公私之匱乏？由因循之弊積，故怯弱之患滋。任一則權不分，莫若廢監軍而專任將；威伸則和可守，大宜省歲幣而益治兵。將求我志之克揚，必謹敵来之有備。擁堅却銳，立畫守於春徂夏入之交；批亢擣虛，奮麾征於我出彼歸之會。離二虜之援於始，振作三軍之氣於方衰。不畏彼侵，患所以来其侵；毋幸敵亂，恃已之不可亂。安危在計，豈容勒襲於
translation_en:
…runs unchecked, while the great ministers have yet to provide full protection and support. Among those who watch furtively like rats, could there be none of the ilk of Zhongshuo [?] and Commandant Tuo? Among those who rise like a hedgehog’s bristles, could there be only men of Xinluo and the Dada? Consider the mutual suspicion between their inner and outer ranks, compounded by the disorder arising from the intermingling of Chinese and foreigners. Warfare employs five kinds of spies, but only a benevolent sage can direct their use. A state cannot contain two dominant powers: how could the cowardly and mediocre control their struggle and division? Unless affairs are planned beforehand, how can one hope for success when putting one’s capabilities to the test?

To display military might and inspire awe requires unremitting attention to raising horses and training troops. To devise unexpected tactics and secure victory requires proficiency both in forming chariot enclosures and in using cavalry to harass the enemy. In essence, we must secure submission abroad to bring peace within. How could we begrudge a single exertion and forget lasting ease? Replenish the three depleted resources promptly [?], first ensuring that the stables and granaries are full; swiftly eliminate the five requests [?]—should we not investigate the shortages afflicting both public and private resources? Because the abuses of habitual delay accumulate, the scourge of timidity and weakness grows.

When responsibility rests with one person, authority is not divided: nothing would be better than abolishing the army supervisors and entrusting command exclusively to the generals. When our might is asserted, peace can be maintained: we should certainly reduce the annual payments and devote greater effort to preparing our forces. If we would see our purposes prevail, we must take care to be prepared for the enemy’s arrival. Hold strong positions and repel their sharp assaults, laying out defensive plans [?] at the transition from departing spring to approaching summer. Strike their vital points and attack their weaknesses, vigorously directing an expedition at the moment when we advance and they withdraw. Sever the mutual support of the two enemy peoples at the outset, and revive the spirit of the armies just as it begins to flag. Do not fear their invasion; be concerned about what invites it. Do not count on disorder among the enemy; rely on making our own forces impervious to disorder. Security and peril depend on planning: how could we allow ourselves to cling [?] to…

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
故談勝敗無常可以監觀於往事臣才不
稱位力靡逮心久悉咨詢方畧足陳於指
掌叨承任使艱憂何止於恫身恐逡巡指
畫之莫施即緩急韜籌之焉濟兵難遙度
時違則變不可預期事貴權宜勢易則謀
何所卒用仰効芻蕘千慮之得冀抒葵藿
一念之忠伏惟
采之廷猷酌以

===

奪於人時兵出萬全必致兩階之舞羽
治煕一統允歌四海之建櫜臣無任瞻

聖激切屏營之至謹以禦戎論七篇隨表上
進以

故談。勝敗無常，可以監觀於往事。臣才不稱位，力靡逮心。久悉咨詢，方畧足陳於指掌；叨承任使，艱憂何止於恫身。恐逡巡指畫之莫施，即緩急韜籌之焉濟。兵難遙度，時違則變，不可預期；事貴權宜，勢易則謀，何所卒用？仰効芻蕘千慮之得，冀抒葵藿一念之忠。伏惟采之廷猷，酌以聖算。九重決勝，錄書生樽俎之長；千里折衝，舒將士鼓鼙之氣。舉事必推乎天道者，功罔奪於人時。兵出萬全，必致兩階之舞羽；治煕一統，允歌四海之建櫜。臣無任瞻天仰聖、激切屏營之至，謹以《禦戎論》七篇隨表上進以聞。

第叁場
策五道。
translation_en:
…old talk. Victory and defeat are uncertain; past events offer lessons for scrutiny. Your servant’s talents do not measure up to his position, and his strength falls short of his intentions. Having long and thoroughly considered the matters on which counsel has been sought, I can set forth strategies as clearly as if pointing to my palm. Yet, having undeservedly received this commission, my anxieties extend far beyond concern for my own person. I fear that hesitation will prevent my plans from being implemented: how, then, could strategic calculations avail in an emergency? Military affairs are difficult to assess from afar. When circumstances depart from expectations, changes cannot be foreseen. Affairs demand expedient judgment; when conditions change, what use will the plans ultimately have? I humbly offer whatever sound thought may emerge from a thousand reflections by a humble woodcutter, hoping to express my single-minded loyalty, like the mallow turning toward the sun.

I reverently beg that these proposals be taken into the court’s deliberations and weighed by Your Majesty’s sagacious calculations. In determining victory within the imperial palace, acknowledge a scholar’s ability to devise strategy over the ceremonial wine vessels; in repelling foes a thousand li away, give scope to the martial spirit of officers and soldiers stirred by drums. When undertakings invariably accord with the Way of Heaven, their success will not be thwarted by human circumstances. With troops dispatched under plans ensuring complete success, the dance with feather plumes between the two stairways will surely follow. With government flourishing in unity, all within the Four Seas may indeed sing of putting away their bows [?]. Your servant, looking up to Heaven and revering Your Majesty, is overcome with fervent emotion and trembling awe. I respectfully submit herewith, accompanying this memorial, seven discourses entitled On Resisting the Rong (Yu Rong Lun), for Your Majesty’s information.

Third Session
Five policy questions.

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
第一問
傅夏器
同考試官署郎中章批二書乃我
祖宗所以為萬世為人臣者之軌範也子衍繹其義而反覆開

First Policy Question

Fu Xiaqi

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
御製二序中為教至明切矣策問正欲諸士子知自辨自鑒將
事君之道因予之言以占其志殆誦繹
聖訓而有槩於中者乎
考試官大學士張批賢姦傳與臣鑒二書我
祖宗所以教天下人臣事君之義至詳切也子能敷繹其說而援證
有據其亦知為臣之道者他日立朝必有可觀矣
得士若此良以自慶
人君以人立政莫先擇臣之術人臣以身
任事莫急徇君之義術不先於擇臣是以
===
失委政之明義不急於徇君是以忘致身
之忠夫惟明君辨邪正於幾微以施擇臣
之術故能有所察於下而臣得自效天下
之政可立矣賢臣推得失於事理以致徇
君之義故能有所信於上而君莫之疑天
下之事可任矣此我
太祖高皇帝賢姦傳之纂
宣宗章皇帝臣鑒之錄雖專以訓臣義亦兼以
明君術也盖嘗仰讀

太祖高皇帝賢姦傳之纂
宣宗章皇帝臣鑒之錄雖專以訓臣義亦兼以

punctuated:
御製二序中，為教至明切矣。策問正欲諸士子知自辨自鑒，將事君之道，因予之言以占其志，殆誦繹聖訓而有槩於中者乎？
考試官大學士張批：賢姦傳與臣鑒二書，我祖宗所以教天下人臣事君之義，至詳切也。子能敷繹其說而援證有據，其亦知為臣之道者。他日立朝，必有可觀矣。得士若此，良以自慶。
人君以人立政，莫先擇臣之術；人臣以身任事，莫急徇君之義。術不先於擇臣，是以失委政之明；義不急於徇君，是以忘致身之忠。夫惟明君辨邪正於幾微，以施擇臣之術，故能有所察於下，而臣得自效，天下之政可立矣。賢臣推得失於事理，以致徇君之義，故能有所信於上，而君莫之疑，天下之事可任矣。此我太祖高皇帝賢姦傳之纂、宣宗章皇帝臣鑒之錄，雖專以訓臣義，亦兼以明君術也。盖嘗仰讀
translation_en:
…in the two imperially composed prefaces; their instruction is exceedingly clear and pointed. The policy question was intended precisely to make the candidates understand how to distinguish right from wrong in themselves and take warning for themselves. Concerning the way of serving a ruler, I sought through my words to discern their aspirations. Have you perhaps recited and pondered the imperial teachings and been deeply moved within?
Comment by Examiner Zhang, Grand Secretary: The two books, Biographies of Worthy and Treacherous Ministers (Xianjian zhuan) and Mirror for Ministers (Chen jian), are the means by which our imperial ancestors taught all ministers under Heaven their duty in serving the ruler, in the greatest detail and with the utmost directness. You have elaborated their teachings and supported your argument with well-founded evidence. You, too, understand the way of being a minister. When you take your place at court in the future, there will surely be much to commend. To obtain a man of such talent is truly cause for congratulating ourselves.
A ruler establishes government through the men he employs; nothing takes precedence over the art of selecting ministers. A minister undertakes responsibilities in his own person; nothing is more urgent than the duty of devoting himself to his ruler. If the ruler’s art does not give priority to selecting ministers, he loses discernment in entrusting government to others. If the minister’s sense of duty does not give urgency to devotion to his ruler, he forgets the loyalty that demands dedication of his whole person. Only an enlightened ruler distinguishes the wicked from the upright in the slightest indications and thereby exercises the art of selecting ministers. Thus he can discern the character of those below him, and his ministers can give full expression to their abilities; government throughout the realm can then be established. Worthy ministers examine what is right and wrong according to the principles governing affairs, thereby fulfilling their duty of devotion to the ruler. Thus they can win the trust of their superior, and the ruler has no doubts about them; the affairs of the realm can then be entrusted to them. This is why our Emperor Taizu Gao compiled Biographies of Worthy and Treacherous Ministers, and Emperor Xuanzong Zhang compiled Mirror for Ministers: although these works were specifically intended to instruct ministers in their duty, they also elucidate the ruler’s art. I have reverently read…

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
聖製諸序而竊敢繹其義知君臣之道必相待
而後成不可以獨競焉則二書其可為萬
世君臣之法詔矣請因執事之問究悉其
愚夫人君能以人立政不知擇臣之術不
可以言明人臣能以身任事不知徇君之
義不可以語忠是故古之明君之擇臣也
因能而授之官辨材而處之任夷能典禮
不咨以治樂契能敷教不勑以明刑開心
以受其道平志以入其謀懽然如父子之
===
相得而不可間翕然如身首之相應而無
所疆是以心志通孚之有素而意氣感合
之能常即有大姦慝動於其側則聞其聲
有以推其形觀其表有以識其裏蓋所以
用其明者審矣是故君子有所效以盡其
材小人有所懼而不得為姦慝所謂辨邪
正於幾微以施擇臣之術者此也是君之
所當察也古之人臣奮勞而不知有身竭
忠而不知有家父殛而當罪不敢以親懟

不洽以治樂契能敷教不勤以明刑開心
以受其道平志以入其謀懽然如父子之
相得而不可間翕然如身首之相應而無
所逿是以心志通乎之有素而意氣感合
之能常即有大姦慝動於其側則聞其聲

用其明者審矣是故君子有所效以盡其
材小人有所懼而不得爲姦慝所謂辨邪
正於幾微以施擇臣之術者此也是君之
所當察也古之人臣奮勞而不知有身竭
忠而不知有家父殛而當罪不敢以親懟
punctuated: 聖製諸序，而竊敢繹其義，知君臣之道必相待而後成，不可以獨競焉，則二書其可為萬世君臣之法詔矣。請因執事之問，究悉其愚。夫人君能以人立政，不知擇臣之術，不可以言明；人臣能以身任事，不知徇君之義，不可以語忠。是故古之明君之擇臣也，因能而授之官，辨材而處之任。夷能典禮，不咨以治樂；契能敷教，不勑以明刑。開心以受其道，平志以入其謀，懽然如父子之相得而不可間，翕然如身首之相應而無所疆。是以心志通孚之有素，而意氣感合之能常。即有大姦慝動於其側，則聞其聲有以推其形，觀其表有以識其裏，蓋所以用其明者審矣。是故君子有所效以盡其材，小人有所懼而不得為姦慝。所謂辨邪正於幾微以施擇臣之術者，此也，是君之所當察也。古之人臣奮勞而不知有身，竭忠而不知有家。父殛而當罪，不敢以親懟
translation_en:
…the imperially composed prefaces, and have humbly ventured to unravel their meaning. I understand that the ways of ruler and minister can be fulfilled only through their mutual reliance; neither can strive alone. These two books may thus serve as authoritative instruction for rulers and ministers for all ages. Allow me, in response to your question, to set forth fully my humble understanding.

A ruler may establish government through the men he employs, but without understanding the art of selecting ministers, he cannot be called discerning. A minister may personally undertake affairs, but without understanding the duty of devotion to his ruler, he cannot be called loyal. Thus, when discerning rulers of antiquity selected ministers, they conferred offices according to ability and assigned responsibilities after distinguishing their talents. Yi could oversee ritual, so they did not consult him about directing music; Xie could spread moral instruction, so they did not command him to administer punishments. They opened their hearts to receive their ministers’ principles and calmed their minds to admit their counsel. Their joyful accord was like that between father and son, allowing no estrangement; their harmonious responsiveness was like that between body and head, admitting no division [?]. Thus their hearts and purposes had long been joined in mutual trust, and their feelings and aspirations could remain in constant accord. Even if a profoundly treacherous man stirred at their side, from hearing his words they could infer his true character, and from observing his outward appearance they could discern what lay within. Such was the care with which they exercised their discernment.

Consequently, worthy men had opportunities to serve and fully employ their talents, while petty men had cause for fear and could not practice treachery. This is what is meant by distinguishing the wicked from the upright in the slightest signs, thereby exercising the art of selecting ministers. This is what a ruler must scrutinize.

Ministers of antiquity exerted themselves in service without thought for their own persons and exhausted their loyalty without thought for their families. If a minister’s father was put to death and the punishment fitted his crime, the minister dared not harbor resentment on account of kinship…

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
也讎舉而合公不敢以私嫉也分定而無
所陵志協而無所忌位以讓叙如五官相
使而不爭業以和成如四時相宣而不悖
是以材智攄於殫究而職業成於儆恪即
有大變患臨於其前則可隕其身而不可
詘其節可奪其位而不可易其志盖所以
篤其忠者素矣是故投之以負扆六尺之
託而不危懾之以横分九死之禍而不畏
愚所謂推得失於事理以急狥君之義者
===
此也是臣之所當厲也夫君之於臣孰不
欲擇之顧擇之有術莫要於其始也其始
何也邪正之幾微是也不審於幾微則雖
有擇臣之明其邪正無由辨矣臣之於君
孰不思狥之顧狥之有義莫難於其終也
其終何也成敗之事理是也不觀於事理
則雖有狥君之忠其得失無由論矣孟子
曰有事君人者事是君則為容悅者也有
安社稷臣者以安社稷為悅者也後之言

是以材智攄於殫究而職業成於傚恪即

託而不危懾之以橫分九死之禍而不畏
愚所謂推得失於事理以急狥君之義者
===
此也是臣之所當勵也夫君之於臣孰不
欲擇之顧擇之有術莫要於其始也其始
何也邪正之幾微是也不審於幾微則雖
有擇臣之明其邪正無由辨矣臣之於君
孰不思狥之顧狥之有義莫難於其終也
其終何也成敗之事理是也不觀於事理
則雖有狥君之忠其得失無由論矣孟子
曰有事君人者事是君則為容悅者也有
安社稷臣者以安社稷為悅者也後之言
punctuated:
也。讎舉而合公，不敢以私嫉也。分定而無所陵，志協而無所忌；位以讓叙，如五官相使而不爭；業以和成，如四時相宣而不悖。是以材智攄於殫究，而職業成於儆恪。即有大變患臨於其前，則可隕其身，而不可詘其節；可奪其位，而不可易其志。盖所以篤其忠者素矣。是故投之以負扆六尺之託而不危，懾之以横分九死之禍而不畏。愚所謂推得失於事理，以急狥君之義者，此也是。臣之所當厲也。
夫君之於臣，孰不欲擇之？顧擇之有術，莫要於其始也。其始何也？邪正之幾微是也。不審於幾微，則雖有擇臣之明，其邪正無由辨矣。臣之於君，孰不思狥之？顧狥之有義，莫難於其終也。其終何也？成敗之事理是也。不觀於事理，則雖有狥君之忠，其得失無由論矣。孟子曰：「有事君人者，事是君則為容悅者也；有安社稷臣者，以安社稷為悅者也。」後之言
translation_en:
…; when an enemy is recommended for office in accordance with the public good, they dare not resent him out of private animosity. With their allotted duties settled, they overstep no bounds; with their purposes united, they harbor no jealousy. Rank is ordered through deference, like the five organs of sense working together without contention; undertakings are accomplished through harmony, like the four seasons unfolding in succession without discord. Thus their talents and wisdom find full expression through exhaustive effort, and their official duties are accomplished through vigilance and conscientiousness. Even if great upheaval or calamity confronts them, their lives may be destroyed, but their integrity cannot be bent; their positions may be taken away, but their resolve cannot be changed. This is because their steadfast loyalty has long been cultivated. Thus, entrusted with a young sovereign who sits before the imperial screen, they do not imperil him; threatened with violent calamity [?] and almost certain death, they remain unafraid. This is what I humbly mean by weighing right and wrong according to the principles governing affairs, and making the duty of devoting oneself to one's ruler an urgent concern. It is in this that ministers should exert themselves.
What ruler does not wish to choose his ministers carefully? Yet choosing them requires a method, and nothing matters more than the beginning. What is meant by the beginning? The subtle signs of depravity and uprightness. Unless these subtle signs are scrutinized, even a ruler with the discernment to select ministers has no means of distinguishing the depraved from the upright. What minister does not think of devoting himself to his ruler? Yet such devotion must accord with righteousness, and nothing is harder than carrying it through to the end. What is meant by the end? The principles governing success and failure in affairs. Unless these principles are examined, even a minister loyal enough to devote himself to his ruler has no means of judging right and wrong. Mengzi said: “There are those who serve a ruler merely to accommodate and please him. There are ministers who secure the altars of soil and grain, taking pleasure in securing the state.” Those who spoke in later ages…

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
者乃曰天下有權臣有重臣二者其迹相
似而實不類夫權臣所為重臣之所深疾
重臣所取權臣之所不顧也故權臣天下
不可一日有而重臣天下不可一日無也
甚哉有味乎其言也由今觀之權臣内固
其君之心而外竊其威柄以予奪天下非
即孟子之所謂容悅事君者邪我
聖祖所傳之姦臣與臣鑒所載田蚡而下七十
有餘人者固皆其類也此惡可為戒者也
===
重臣内引其君於道而外謹其法制以齊
整百司非即孟子之所謂安社稷之臣者
邪我
聖祖所傳之賢臣與臣鑒所載子産而下二百
有餘人者固皆其類也此善可為法者也
以愚觀之歷代人臣賢姦之辨雖已太備
於二書然夷考
二聖序列之意所以示章癉於既往垂法戒於
方来蓋其微哉不可以不詳也執事乃欲

甚哉有味乎其言也由今觀之權臣内固
其君之心而外竊其威柄以予奪天下非
即孟子之所謂容悦事君者邪我
聖祖所傳之姦臣與臣鑑所載田蚡而下七十
有餘人者固皆其類也此惡可為戒者也
重臣内引其君於道而外謹其法制以齊
整百司非即孟子之所謂安社稷之臣者
===
邪我
聖祖所傳之賢臣與臣鑑所載子産而下二百
有餘人者固皆其類也此善可為法者也
以愚觀之歷代人臣賢姦之辨雖已大備
於二書然夷考
二聖序列之意所以示章癉於既往垂法戒於
方来盖其微哉不可以不詳也孰事為欲
punctuated:
者乃曰：「天下有權臣，有重臣，二者其迹相似而實不類。夫權臣所為，重臣之所深疾；重臣所取，權臣之所不顧也。故權臣，天下不可一日有；而重臣，天下不可一日無也。」甚哉，有味乎其言也！由今觀之，權臣内固其君之心，而外竊其威柄，以予奪天下，非即孟子之所謂容悅事君者邪？我聖祖所傳之姦臣，與《臣鑒》所載田蚡而下七十有餘人者，固皆其類也。此惡可為戒者也。

重臣内引其君於道，而外謹其法制，以齊整百司，非即孟子之所謂安社稷之臣者邪？我聖祖所傳之賢臣，與《臣鑒》所載子産而下二百有餘人者，固皆其類也。此善可為法者也。

以愚觀之，歷代人臣賢姦之辨，雖已太備於二書，然夷考二聖序列之意，所以示章癉於既往，垂法戒於方来，蓋其微哉！不可以不詳也。執事乃欲
translation_en:
…then said: “Under Heaven there are ministers who monopolize power and ministers of weight. Their outward conduct appears similar, but in substance they belong to different kinds. What the former do, the latter deeply detest; what the latter embrace, the former disregard. Thus the world cannot tolerate ministers who monopolize power for even a single day, yet cannot dispense with ministers of weight for even a single day.” How profound and rich in meaning these words are! Viewed from the present, ministers who monopolize power secure their hold upon their ruler’s heart within the court, while outside it they usurp his authority to grant and withhold throughout the realm. Are these not precisely those whom Mengzi described as serving their ruler by ingratiating themselves and pleasing him? The treacherous ministers whose lives our Sagely Progenitor recorded, together with the more than seventy men beginning with Tian Fen recorded in the Mirror for Ministers (Chen jian), all indeed belong to this category. These are examples of evil that may serve as warnings.

Ministers of weight guide their ruler toward the Way within the court, while outside it they scrupulously uphold his laws and institutions, bringing all the offices into good order. Are these not precisely those whom Mengzi called ministers who secure the altars of soil and grain—that is, the state? The worthy ministers whose lives our Sagely Progenitor recorded, together with the more than two hundred men beginning with Zichan recorded in the Mirror for Ministers, all indeed belong to this category. These are examples of goodness that may serve as models.

In my humble view, although the distinction between worthy and treacherous ministers throughout successive dynasties is already treated most fully in these two books, a careful examination of the intentions expressed in the two sage emperors’ prefatory accounts reveals how subtle their purpose is: to make praise and condemnation manifest concerning the past, and to transmit models and warnings to the future! This must be examined in detail. You, sir, now wish…

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
使承學反覆究之其敢黙焉已乎夫二書
所載賢與善者皆古重臣忠君之事也其
為道也有四以敬正事不敢冀君之知也
以道責難不敢阿君之好也内交可合曰
援黨以比周吾弗為之矣外譽可致曰違
道以要衆吾弗取之矣此四者重臣之所
執也然推其忠之所存要在殉君以行義
爾故我
聖祖於序賢臣稱其智哉忠於君而不變而臣
鑒序善可法者亦以為秉仁循義心天理
之公去之千載而有輝光矣則所謂天下
不可一日無重臣也非以其能益於國邪
所載姦與惡者皆古權臣蔽君之事也其
為道也亦有四壅主之聴將以得國之柄
也動衆之爭將以致已之威也引之以好
善之名而陰致其誣善之實欲君之善可
惑焉疆之以難從之事而因揣其易從之
志欲君之從可易焉此四者權臣之所託

之公去之千載而有輝光矣則所謂天下
不可一日無重臣也非以其能益於國邪
所載姦與惡者皆古權臣蔽君之事也其
為道也亦有四壅主之聽將以得國之柄
也動衆之爭將以致巳之威也引之以好
善之名而陰致其誣善之實欲君之善可
惑焉疆之以難從之事而因揣其易從之
志欲君之從可易焉此四者權臣之所託
punctuated:
使承學反覆究之，其敢黙焉已乎？夫二書所載賢與善者，皆古重臣忠君之事也。其為道也有四：以敬正事，不敢冀君之知也；以道責難，不敢阿君之好也；内交可合，曰：「援黨以比周，吾弗為之矣。」外譽可致，曰：「違道以要衆，吾弗取之矣。」此四者，重臣之所執也。然推其忠之所存，要在殉君以行義爾。故我聖祖於序賢臣，稱其智哉，忠於君而不變；而臣鑒序善可法者，亦以為秉仁循義，心天理之公，去之千載而有輝光矣。則所謂天下不可一日無重臣也，非以其能益於國邪？
所載姦與惡者，皆古權臣蔽君之事也。其為道也亦有四：壅主之聴，將以得國之柄也；動衆之爭，將以致已之威也；引之以好善之名，而陰致其誣善之實，欲君之善可惑焉；疆之以難從之事，而因揣其易從之志，欲君之從可易焉。此四者，權臣之所託
translation_en:
…have us students investigate these matters repeatedly and thoroughly. How could we dare remain silent and leave it at that? The worthy and good men recorded in these two books all exemplify how great ministers of antiquity served their rulers loyally. Their way of acting had four aspects: they rectified affairs with reverence, never presuming to seek their ruler’s recognition; they invoked the Way to demand difficult achievements of him, never daring to flatter his tastes; when they could form connections at court, they said, “I will not enlist a faction and engage in collusion”; and when they could acquire a reputation outside the court, they said, “I will not violate the Way to win over the multitude.” These four principles were what great ministers upheld. Yet, tracing their loyalty to its source, its essence lay simply in devoting themselves to their ruler in order to carry out righteousness. Thus, in his preface concerning worthy ministers, our Sagely Progenitor praised their wisdom [?] and their unwavering loyalty to their ruler. Likewise, the preface to the Mirror for Ministers held that those whose goodness could serve as a model embraced benevolence, followed righteousness, and took the impartiality of Heaven’s principle to heart; even a thousand years later, they still shone with glory. Hence the saying that the realm cannot be without great ministers for even a single day: is this not because they can benefit the state?
The treacherous and wicked men recorded there all exemplify how ministers who monopolized power deceived their rulers in antiquity. Their way of acting likewise had four aspects: they blocked what their ruler could hear, intending to gain control of the state; they stirred up contention among the multitude, intending to establish their own authority; they guided him under the pretext of loving goodness, while secretly bringing about the actual slandering of good men, intending to confound his sense of goodness [?]; and they pressed him with matters difficult to assent to, then gauged his inclination toward what he could readily accept, intending to make his assent easy to obtain [?]. These four were what ministers who monopolized power relied upon…

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
也然推其欺之所著要在蔽君以行私爾
故我
聖祖於序姦臣指其恃要持權窺覘人主之意
臣鑒序惡可戒者亦斥其挾姦縱私傷仁
敗德百世聞其姓名猶起人忿憾不平之
氣矣則所謂天下不可一日有權臣也非
以其能害於政邪夫語其不可無也不能
預畜之以有待知其不可有也不能决去
之而無疑斯則人主擇臣之失術徒託所
===
以垂之論誡者也且夫不察其心而求其
迹則重臣之直行不顧孰與權臣之恭退
有禮也不觀其度而信其才則權臣之敏
給便事孰與重臣之質疆少文也慶賞爵
予君所以惠下重臣用之以張公朝權臣
亦用之以厚私門而有不知其竊者矣刑
罰誅奪君所以威眾重臣取之以行公法
權臣亦取之以快私志而有不知其假者
矣故處有重臣之朝者君子赴義小人畏

聖祖於庠姦臣指其恃要持權窺覘人主之意
臣鑒庠惡可戒者亦庠其挾姦縱私傷仁

之而無疑斯則人主擇臣之失術往記所

權臣亦取之以快私忿而有不知其假者
矣故處有重臣之朝者君子赴義小人畏
punctuated:
也。然推其欺之所著，要在蔽君以行私爾。故我聖祖於序姦臣，指其恃要持權、窺覘人主之意；臣鑒序惡可戒者，亦斥其挾姦縱私、傷仁敗德。百世聞其姓名，猶起人忿憾不平之氣矣。則所謂天下不可一日有權臣也，非以其能害於政邪？夫語其不可無也，不能預畜之以有待；知其不可有也，不能决去之而無疑。斯則人主擇臣之失術，徒託所以垂之論誡者也。
且夫不察其心而求其迹，則重臣之直行不顧，孰與權臣之恭退有禮也？不觀其度而信其才，則權臣之敏給便事，孰與重臣之質疆少文也？慶賞爵予，君所以惠下，重臣用之以張公朝，權臣亦用之以厚私門，而有不知其竊者矣。刑罰誅奪，君所以威眾，重臣取之以行公法，權臣亦取之以快私志，而有不知其假者矣。故處有重臣之朝者，君子赴義，小人畏
translation_en:
…Yet if we examine the manifestations of their deceit, its essence lies simply in keeping the ruler in ignorance so as to pursue private interests. Thus, in his preface concerning treacherous ministers, our Sagely Progenitor pointed out how they relied on strategic positions, wielded power, and watched for the sovereign’s intentions. The Mirror for Ministers (Chen jian), in recounting evils that should serve as warnings, likewise condemns their harboring treachery, indulging selfish desires, injuring benevolence, and corrupting virtue. Even a hundred generations later, hearing their names still arouses indignation and resentment at injustice. Thus, when it is said that the realm cannot tolerate even a single day with overmighty ministers, is this not because they can harm its government? Yet although a ruler speaks of being unable to do without weighty ministers, he fails to nurture them beforehand and hold them in readiness; although he knows that overmighty ministers must not be tolerated, he fails to remove them decisively and without hesitation. This is a failure in the sovereign’s art of selecting ministers: he merely entrusts the lesson to admonitory discussions handed down to posterity [?].
Moreover, if one does not examine their hearts but looks only for outward conduct, how will the weighty minister’s forthright and unheeding actions compare with the overmighty minister’s respectful reserve and observance of propriety? If one does not observe their moral bearing but trusts their abilities, how will the overmighty minister’s quick-witted facility in handling affairs compare with the weighty minister’s plain strength and lack of polish? Rewards and the bestowal of ranks are the means by which a ruler extends favor to those below. Weighty ministers use them to strengthen the public authority of the court; overmighty ministers also use them, but to enrich their private households—and some rulers fail to recognize this usurpation. Punishments, executions, and deprivation of rank or property are the means by which a ruler overawes the multitude. Weighty ministers employ them to enforce impartial law; overmighty ministers also employ them, but to gratify their private desires—and some rulers fail to recognize this appropriation. Thus, at a court that has weighty ministers, men of virtue hasten toward righteousness, while petty men fear…

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
法天下之政無一不出於公者國家所以
日興於治也處有權臣之朝者小人赴勢
君子畏禍天下之政無一不出於私者國
家所以日入於亂也是故人君綜攬萬幾
觀化原於物理之著攝御群臣辨人品於
心術之微察事之無形以推其形之所示
審幾之欲動以知其動之所由夫然後天
下之材可得而知天下之情可得而校而
重與權之分賢與姦之判不待數計物索
===
已昭昭乎不可盖匿矣抑權臣之不可有
世皆知之而重臣之不可無非深明於治
體者不足與識之也盖天下有危疑不制
之變非重臣孰能定之人君有沮易難持
之計非重臣孰能决之故僕固之難六師
攻之不克汾陽一出卒著免冑之勲光獻
之疑天下憂之莫解稚圭數語迄成撤簾
之功彼其德信感人之深故意動而中外
咸服威朢繫人之久故語出而上下不疑

之功彼其德信感人之深故意動而中外

punctuated:
法，天下之政無一不出於公者，國家所以日興於治也。處有權臣之朝者，小人赴勢，君子畏禍，天下之政無一不出於私者，國家所以日入於亂也。是故人君綜攬萬幾，觀化原於物理之著；攝御群臣，辨人品於心術之微；察事之無形，以推其形之所示；審幾之欲動，以知其動之所由。夫然後天下之材可得而知，天下之情可得而校，而重與權之分、賢與姦之判，不待數計物索，已昭昭乎不可盖匿矣。

抑權臣之不可有，世皆知之；而重臣之不可無，非深明於治體者，不足與識之也。盖天下有危疑不制之變，非重臣孰能定之？人君有沮易難持之計，非重臣孰能决之？故僕固之難，六師攻之不克，汾陽一出，卒著免冑之勲；光獻之疑，天下憂之莫解，稚圭數語，迄成撤簾之功。彼其德信感人之深，故意動而中外咸服；威朢繫人之久，故語出而上下不疑。
translation_en:
…the law, and every act of government throughout the realm proceeds from public interest: this is why the state advances daily toward good order. In a court with a minister who monopolizes power, petty men flock to power and gentlemen fear calamity; every act of government throughout the realm proceeds from private interest: this is why the state sinks daily into disorder. Thus, in taking comprehensive charge of the myriad affairs of government, the ruler observes the source of transformation in the manifest principles of things; in directing his ministers, he distinguishes their character through the subtleties of their intentions. He examines affairs before they take shape, to infer what their eventual form will reveal; he scrutinizes incipient developments on the verge of movement, to understand what gives rise to that movement. Only then can the talents of the realm be known and its actual circumstances assessed. The distinction between a weighty minister and one who monopolizes power, and the division between the worthy and the treacherous, will then be so clear that they cannot be concealed, without any need for laborious reckoning or investigation of each particular.

Now, everyone knows that ministers who monopolize power must not be allowed to exist. But only those who profoundly understand the essentials of government can recognize that weighty ministers are indispensable. When the realm faces dangerous and uncertain upheavals that defy control, who but a weighty minister can settle them? When the ruler has plans that are vulnerable to obstruction and alteration and difficult to sustain, who but a weighty minister can bring them to a decision? Thus, during the rebellion of Pugu, the imperial armies attacked but could not prevail; yet once Fenyang—Guo Ziyi—went forth, he ultimately won distinction by removing his helmet. During the uncertainty concerning Guangxian, the whole realm was anxious, and no one could resolve the matter; yet a few words from Zhigui—Han Qi—finally secured the withdrawal of the curtain of regency. Because such ministers’ virtue and trustworthiness have moved people deeply, as soon as they form an intention, those at court and beyond all submit; because their authority and prestige have long held people’s allegiance, as soon as they speak, neither high nor low has any doubt…

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
以之靖亂則吳楚之難淮蔡之功不動聲
色而可定以之寄命則產祿之變思訓之
謀無煩指顧而能安後世惟不得重臣用
之故帷幄無參决之倚則弘石之姦得肆
筦樞乏耆舊之託則李鄭之難由作此禍
亂所為相尋於無窮也然所謂重臣者豈
可遽得於一旦哉非君任之素專則其體
無由而尊養之素篤則其節無由而完優
寵之素厚則其英毅果敢之氣幾何不至
===
遂撓屈也故體能使之尊明主之專任也
唐文皇之於房玄齡是已節能使之完明
主之篤養也宋太宗之於寇準是已氣能
使之不撓屈明主之素優予也漢文帝之
於申屠嘉是已故曰天下之政舉而修之
在臣天下之材作而成之在君此明主之
獨璧不以語人者也
二聖纂錄之深意得無有出於是乎書曰克綏
先王之祿永底烝民之生一德交修上下

punctuated: 以之靖亂，則吳楚之難、淮蔡之功，不動聲色而可定；以之寄命，則產祿之變、思訓之謀，無煩指顧而能安。後世惟不得重臣用之，故帷幄無參决之倚，則弘石之姦得肆；筦樞乏耆舊之託，則李鄭之難由作。此禍亂所為相尋於無窮也。然所謂重臣者，豈可遽得於一旦哉？非君任之素專，則其體無由而尊；養之素篤，則其節無由而完；優寵之素厚，則其英毅果敢之氣，幾何不至遂撓屈也？故體能使之尊，明主之專任也，唐文皇之於房玄齡是已；節能使之完，明主之篤養也，宋太宗之於寇準是已；氣能使之不撓屈，明主之素優予也，漢文帝之於申屠嘉是已。故曰：天下之政，舉而修之在臣；天下之材，作而成之在君。此明主之獨璧，不以語人者也。二聖纂錄之深意，得無有出於是乎？《書》曰：「克綏先王之祿，永底烝民之生。」一德交修，上下
translation_en:
…Employ such ministers to quell disorder, and troubles like the rebellion of Wu and Chu, or campaigns like that against Huai and Cai, can be settled without any outward show of agitation. Entrust the fate of the state to them, and upheavals like that of Lü Chan and Lü Lu, or the plot of Sixun [?], can be brought under control without so much as a gesture of command. In later ages, rulers failed to obtain and employ such weighty ministers. Thus, when there was no one in their inner councils upon whom to rely for deliberation and decision, the villainy of Hong Gong and Shi Xian went unchecked; when there were no venerable senior servants to whom the central direction of government could be entrusted, disasters such as that involving Li Xun and Zheng Zhu arose. This is why calamity and disorder followed one another without end.

Yet could such weighty ministers suddenly be obtained in a single day? Unless the ruler has long entrusted them with undivided responsibility, their standing cannot become exalted; unless he has long nurtured them with earnest care, their integrity cannot remain whole; unless he has long treated them with generous favor, how can their heroic resolve and courage avoid eventually being bent and broken? Thus, enabling their standing to become exalted depends upon an enlightened ruler’s undivided trust: Emperor Wen of Tang’s treatment of Fang Xuanling exemplifies this. Enabling their integrity to remain whole depends upon an enlightened ruler’s earnest nurturing: Emperor Taizong of Song’s treatment of Kou Zhun exemplifies this. Enabling their spirit to remain unbowed depends upon an enlightened ruler’s longstanding generosity: Emperor Wen of Han’s treatment of Shentu Jia exemplifies this. Hence the saying: bringing the government of the realm into good order rests with ministers; cultivating and perfecting the talents of the realm rests with the ruler. This is the enlightened ruler’s uniquely treasured jade [?], of which he does not speak to others.

Might the profound intention behind the two sage sovereigns’ compilation of this record have arisen from this very principle? The Book of Documents says: “Be able to preserve the blessings of the former kings and secure forever the livelihood of the multitude.” When ruler and ministers cultivate one another through a shared virtue, those above and those below…

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
允協則有賢公卿輔翼
大聖人之化焉草茅賤士其敢忘帝臣之願乎
謹對
第二問
王應時
同考試官都給事中劉批衆言淆亂折諸聖固
有是言今子論性能析諸說之異而歸諸力行
之一言子其希聖學而將有得者邪
同考試官修撰秦批性學一策士子類能言
===
之求其於諸說異同剖析明允如此篇者不多
見也豈區區記誦之學所能到邪宜錄以式
考試官學士歐陽批諸子不知性善故其學起
於意見後世謂氣質有不善故不歸罪於習而
有以自諉讀至此令人深省
考試官大學士張批性學不明以人之詳於言
而畧於行故耳此作能辨析諸家是非而歸之
力行之一言始可與論性矣錄之
性貴盡也非貴言也其言之者示人盡之

punctuated:
允協，則有賢公卿輔翼大聖人之化焉。草茅賤士，其敢忘帝臣之願乎？謹對。

第二問
王應時

同考試官都給事中劉批：衆言淆亂，折諸聖，固有是言。今子論性，能析諸說之異，而歸諸力行之一言，子其希聖學而將有得者邪？

同考試官修撰秦批：性學一策，士子類能言之。求其於諸說異同剖析明允如此篇者，不多見也。豈區區記誦之學所能到邪？宜錄以式。

考試官學士歐陽批：諸子不知性善，故其學起於意見。後世謂氣質有不善，故不歸罪於習，而有以自諉。讀至此，令人深省。

考試官大學士張批：性學不明，以人之詳於言而畧於行故耳。此作能辨析諸家是非，而歸之力行之一言，始可與論性矣。錄之。

性貴盡也，非貴言也。其言之者，示人盡之
translation_en:
…are truly in accord, then worthy dukes and ministers will assist the transforming influence of the great sage. Would a humble scholar from the countryside dare forget his aspiration to serve as the emperor’s minister? Respectfully submitted in reply.

Second Question
Wang Yingshi

Comment by Associate Examiner Liu, Chief Supervising Secretary: “When the many voices are confused, judge them by the sages”: this is indeed an established saying. Now, in discussing human nature, you distinguish the differences among the various explanations and bring them back to the single injunction to practice earnestly. Are you perhaps one who aspires to the learning of the sages and is about to attain something of it?

Comment by Associate Examiner Qin, Senior Compiler: On this policy question concerning the study of human nature, most candidates can say something. But few essays analyze the similarities and differences among the various explanations as clearly and judiciously as this one. Could mere learning by memorization and recitation reach this level? It should be recorded as a model.

Comment by Examiner Ouyang, Academician: The various thinkers did not understand that human nature is good, so their teachings arose from personal opinions. Later generations asserted that the psychophysical endowment contains what is not good; thus they failed to blame habituation and had a means of excusing themselves. Reading to this point prompts deep reflection.

Comment by Examiner Zhang, Grand Secretary: The study of human nature remains obscure simply because people are detailed in their words but cursory in their practice. This composition distinguishes what is right and wrong in the various schools and brings it back to the single injunction to practice earnestly. Only then can one discuss human nature with its author. Record it.

What matters is fully realizing one’s nature, not talking about it. Those who speak of it show people how to realize it fully…

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
之功也言貴行也不貴辯也其辯之者欲
人行之無惑也盖人性本善而或梏之聖
人有憂焉於是言其所深造自得者牖人
心而反之善故其言非使人通曉辯說已
也欲其好學力行得之深而居之安故言
必可教教必可學學必可以成己成物而
徒言非所貴也盖嘗觀古之言性矣言乎
若性而有恒焉言乎節性而日邁焉言乎
率性以為道焉言乎誠善以盡性焉凡以
===
教力行也教慎習也盖聖人恒其性之中
矣欲夫人若焉而無敢戾致其性之和矣
欲夫人節焉而無敢縱盡其性之善矣欲
夫人率焉而無敢賊全其性之誠明矣欲
夫人思誠而無敢妄不戾不縱不賊不妄
而聲色臭味得其正喜怒哀樂中其節君
臣父子兄弟夫婦朋友盡其分習與性成
教之極功也道與時降勢以時異堯舜文
武之時教立於上而君師之道一道德齊

教之極功也道與時降勢以時異堯舜文
武之時教立於上而君師之道一道德齊
punctuated:
之功也。言貴行也，不貴辯也；其辯之者，欲人行之無惑也。盖人性本善，而或梏之，聖人有憂焉。於是言其所深造自得者，牖人心而反之善。故其言非使人通曉辯說已也，欲其好學力行，得之深而居之安。故言必可教，教必可學，學必可以成己成物，而徒言非所貴也。盖嘗觀古之言性矣：言乎若性而有恒焉，言乎節性而日邁焉，言乎率性以為道焉，言乎誠善以盡性焉，凡以教力行也，教慎習也。盖聖人恒其性之中矣，欲夫人若焉而無敢戾；致其性之和矣，欲夫人節焉而無敢縱；盡其性之善矣，欲夫人率焉而無敢賊；全其性之誠明矣，欲夫人思誠而無敢妄。不戾、不縱、不賊、不妄，而聲色臭味得其正，喜怒哀樂中其節，君臣、父子、兄弟、夫婦、朋友盡其分，習與性成，教之極功也。

道與時降，勢以時異。堯舜文武之時，教立於上，而君師之道一，道德齊
translation_en:
…the work of fully realizing it. What is valued in words is putting them into practice, not disputation; explanations are offered so that people may practice without perplexity. Human nature is originally good, yet it may become fettered, and this concerned the sages. They therefore spoke of what they had attained through profound study and grasped for themselves, opening people’s minds and returning them to goodness. Their words were not intended merely to make people conversant with arguments and explanations. They wanted people to love learning and exert themselves in practice, to attain a deep understanding and abide securely in it. Thus their words must be fit to teach; their teachings must be possible to learn; and learning must enable people to perfect themselves and others. Mere words are not what is valued. I have considered what the ancients said about human nature: they spoke of following one’s nature with constancy, of regulating one’s nature and advancing daily, of following one’s nature as the Way, and of making goodness authentic so as fully to realize one’s nature. All this was to teach strenuous practice and care in forming habits. The sages maintained the equilibrium of their nature and wished everyone to follow it without daring to deviate. They brought their nature into harmony and wished everyone to regulate it without daring to indulge it. They fully realized the goodness of their nature and wished everyone to follow it without daring to injure it. They preserved the full sincerity and clarity of their nature and wished everyone to strive for sincerity without daring to be false. With no deviation, indulgence, injury, or falsity, sounds, sights, smells, and tastes find their proper measure; joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure accord with their due bounds; and ruler and minister, father and son, elder and younger brothers, husband and wife, and friends fully discharge their respective duties. Habit becomes one with nature: this is the highest achievement of teaching.

The Way declined with the passage of time, and circumstances changed with the age. In the days of Yao, Shun, King Wen, and King Wu, teaching was established by those above, and the roles of ruler and teacher were united: they guided through virtue and regulated through…

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
禮而人莫不敬應故行有枝葉言畧而功
倍孔子孟軻之時教立於下而君師之道
二百家殊方而人各為異說故詞有枝葉
言詳而功半蓋至於言詳而德行之教衰
意見之習盛於是人才風俗寖不逮古矣
嗟乎三代而下何其紛紛也孟子道性善
而羣喙競起衆言殽亂曰性惡者曰善惡
混者曰善惡各有定者曰無善無惡者各
是其是互相評譏其意則皆欲人為善易
===
惡者也而孟子闢之不遺餘力豈好為嘵
嘵者自今觀之孟子之言善也本之天命
徵之正情若曰能率其性斯無不善不可
反其性而為惡也諸子則或離情以為言
或雜習以為言若曰人當治其性以為善
不可以其性入於不善也故孟子之學順
理而無為也若决江河以注之海而無汎
濫焉雖困勉之功至於人十己千皆無為
而為性也非意也諸子之學刻意而有作

punctuated:
禮，而人莫不敬應，故行有枝葉，言畧而功倍。孔子、孟軻之時，教立於下，而君師之道二，百家殊方，而人各為異說，故詞有枝葉，言詳而功半。蓋至於言詳，而德行之教衰，意見之習盛，於是人才風俗寖不逮古矣。
嗟乎！三代而下，何其紛紛也！孟子道性善，而羣喙競起，衆言殽亂：曰性惡者，曰善惡混者，曰善惡各有定者，曰無善無惡者，各是其是，互相評譏。其意則皆欲人為善易惡者也，而孟子闢之不遺餘力，豈好為嘵嘵者？自今觀之，孟子之言善也，本之天命，徵之正情，若曰能率其性，斯無不善，不可反其性而為惡也。諸子則或離情以為言，或雜習以為言，若曰人當治其性以為善，不可以其性入於不善也。故孟子之學，順理而無為也，若决江河以注之海，而無汎濫焉。雖困勉之功至於人十己千，皆無為而為，性也，非意也。諸子之學，刻意而有作
translation_en:
…through ritual, and everyone responded reverently. Thus conduct branched out into its ramifications: words were brief, yet their effect was doubled. In the time of Confucius and Meng Ke, teaching was established among those below, and the ways of ruler and teacher became separate. The hundred schools pursued different methods, and people each advanced divergent doctrines. Thus words acquired branches and leaves: discourse was detailed, yet its effect was halved. Once discourse became detailed, education in virtue and conduct declined, while the habit of advancing personal opinions flourished. Consequently, human talent and social customs gradually fell short of those of antiquity.
Alas! After the Three Dynasties, how confused and contentious things became! Mencius spoke of the goodness of human nature, but a multitude of voices arose in rivalry, their assertions mingled in confusion. Some said that human nature was evil; some that it was a mixture of good and evil; some that goodness and evil were each fixed; and some that it was neither good nor evil. Each affirmed the correctness of his own position, and they criticized and disparaged one another. Their intention was in every case to have people do good and reform their evil, yet Mencius spared no effort in refuting them. Was he someone who delighted in wrangling? Viewed from the present, Mencius’s account of goodness was rooted in Heaven’s mandate and corroborated by rightly ordered feelings. It was as though he said: if people can follow their nature, nothing will be other than good; they must not turn against their nature and do evil. The other thinkers, however, either framed their arguments apart from feelings or mixed acquired habits into their accounts. It was as though they said: people should regulate their nature to become good and must not allow their nature to lead them into what is not good. Thus Mencius’s teaching follows principle and acts without contrivance. It is like opening channels for the Yangzi and Yellow Rivers to flow into the sea without overflowing. Even when the effort of persevering through difficulty reaches the point of doing a thousand times what others do ten times, it is all action without contrivance: it proceeds from one’s nature, not from deliberate intention. The teaching of the other thinkers strains deliberate intention and resorts to contrived action…

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
也若堤江河而鑿之道使無汎濫焉即功
力之熟至於不待思勉皆有作而成意也
非性也夫一陰一陽之道在天曰命命之
流行曰氣氣之凝聚曰質質之虛靈曰心
心之生理曰性性之發動曰情情之作止
反復曰習本末一原者也性者習之體習
者性之用性習而善惡分習與性成而善
惡不移始同終異者也故無不善者性之
常習而後有不善則逆其常者也然為善
===
斯慊不善斯不慊蓋根諸心而不可欺者
未始易乎其常孔子言性近習遠以至於
上智下愚此本末始終之別也孟子承之
謂善端為固有謂得之失之由於求舍謂
相倍蓰而無筭非才之罪此明其順逆常
變者也諸子則迷其本始故混其順逆而
以為皆其常然者以是為教而道人於善
其究也反害之矣何也意見作而天性賊
也夫楊朱無見於性之義則取為我以為

punctuated: 也，若堤江河而鑿之道，使無汎濫焉。即功力之熟，至於不待思勉，皆有作而成，意也，非性也。夫一陰一陽之道，在天曰命，命之流行曰氣，氣之凝聚曰質，質之虛靈曰心，心之生理曰性，性之發動曰情，情之作止反復曰習，本末一原者也。性者，習之體；習者，性之用。性習而善惡分，習與性成而善惡不移，始同終異者也。故無不善者，性之常；習而後有不善，則逆其常者也。然為善斯慊，不善斯不慊，蓋根諸心而不可欺者，未始易乎其常。孔子言性近習遠，以至於上智下愚，此本末始終之別也。孟子承之，謂善端為固有，謂得之失之由於求舍，謂相倍蓰而無筭，非才之罪，此明其順逆常變者也。諸子則迷其本始，故混其順逆，而以為皆其常然者。以是為教而道人於善，其究也反害之矣。何也？意見作而天性賊也。夫楊朱無見於性之義，則取為我以為
translation_en:
…like embanking rivers and cutting channels for them so that they do not overflow. Even when practiced effort reaches such mastery that neither reflection nor exertion is needed, all this is achieved through deliberate action: it belongs to intention, not to human nature.

The Way of alternating yin and yang is called the Mandate in Heaven; the flowing operation of the Mandate is called vital energy (qi); the condensation of vital energy is called physical constitution; the numinous receptivity of physical constitution is called the heart-mind; the life-giving principle of the heart-mind is called nature; the stirring of nature is called feeling; and the repeated arising and cessation of feeling is called habituation. Root and branches share a single source. Nature is the substance of habituation; habituation is the functioning of nature. As nature undergoes habituation, good and evil diverge; when habit and nature have formed together, good and evil become fixed. Thus what is alike at the beginning differs at the end. To be entirely good is therefore nature’s constant condition; when evil appears after habituation, this runs counter to that constant condition. Yet doing good brings inward satisfaction, and doing evil brings dissatisfaction. What is rooted in the heart-mind and cannot be deceived has never departed from its constant condition.

Confucius spoke of people being close in nature but becoming distant through habituation, extending his account to those of the highest wisdom and the lowest stupidity. This distinguishes root from branches and beginning from end. Mengzi followed him, saying that the beginnings of goodness are inherently present; that attaining or losing them depends on seeking or abandoning them; and that people may differ twofold, fivefold, or beyond reckoning, without this being the fault of their native endowment. This makes clear what accords with nature and what opposes it, what is constant and what changes. The other thinkers, however, lost sight of the root and beginning. They consequently confused what accords with nature with what opposes it, regarding both as its normal condition. If one uses this as a teaching to guide people toward goodness, the ultimate result is instead to harm them. Why? Because preconceived opinions arise and injure Heaven-endowed nature. Yang Zhu, failing to perceive the righteousness inherent in nature, adopted the principle of acting for oneself and took it to be …

title: 嘉靖二十九年會試錄
text:
義墨翟無見於性之仁則兼愛以為仁子
莫無見於性之中則執一以為中告子之
不動心鄉愿之德許行之無為皆無見於
性之本故以其意見者為學而思以易天
下使天下皆能為為我之義兼愛之仁執
一之中猶未免為矯情鑿真況必不能為
也必不能為而又不知所為則恣情迷真
者仁義充塞中庸晦蝕而天下日入於亂
譬諸養生然黍稷稻粱其常也而必熊蹯
===
猩唇以充膳豈惟自伐天和将世之不能
皆得者有坐而甘餓或相食以斃耳至是
而後知諸說之紛紛不啻驅人於溺而率
之左衽而孟子之論所以距詖行正人心
者其為實用真足以比功禹周非無益之
空言也矣後人又推所未備将以輔行其
說乃以善歸性以不善歸氣質則信辯矣
然氣之冲和偏勝也質之剛柔明暗也本
天命之流行凝聚繼善而成性者也故曰
